original.when_to_use: At the end of any assistant-mode session that edited files, diagnosed problems, or made decisions -- especially multi-round build sessions. Also when a cycle detector flags zero_learning_velocity on an aspiration whose work happened in assistant mode.

generalized.context: When an autonomous development loop operates in assistant-mode (chat/observer sessions) rather than active execution mode, per-goal encoding pipelines and state-update lanes remain dormant.
approach: Recognize that assistant-mode interactions do not trigger the internal phases responsible for flushing learning to durable stores (equivalent to Phase 6.5 and Phase 8 in active loops)
Identify that file edits or decisions made during these sessions result in zero-learning-velocity flags despite apparent progress
Execute the /encode-session command at the conclusion of any substantial assistant-mode work block
generalized.outcome: Successfully flushed accumulated chat-session learning into durable stores, restoring the learning velocity pipeline.
generalized.lesson: When autonomous work occurs in assistant-mode (chat/observer sessions), the internal encoding and state-update pipelines do not fire automatically. Even if files are edited or problems diagnosed, no durable encodings are generated. To prevent zero-learning-velocity states, you must manually trigger the encoding command (e.g., /encode-session) at the end of the session to flush the accumulated context into the durable store.

original.title: Windows Bash-tool gotchas: cp1252 em-dash breaks printf JSON; heredoc apostrophes; nested py-3 subprocess bash PATH; call .sh wrappers not modules
original.content: Cluster of invocation gotchas hit building go-to-market infra on this Windows machine (Bash tool over Git Bash; python via the py-3 shim): (1) Non-ASCII chars (em-dash, smart quotes) in a printf inline-JSON body are emitted as cp1252 SINGLE BYTES (em-dash -> 0x97), which the daemon rejects as invalid UTF-8 (codec cant decode byte 0x97). FIX: keep inline JSON ASCII-only (use -- and plain quote); for unavoidable non-ASCII, write the payload to a sanctioned scratch file via the Write tool (UTF-8) and pipe that. (2) bash heredocs containing apostrophes break with unexpected EOF. FIX: prefer printf %s over heredocs for JSON, or a Write-tool file emitter. (3) subprocess.run([bash,...]) launched from a py -3 -c process fails py: not found because the shim launcher is not on the WSL subshell PATH -- do NOT nest python->subprocess->bash; invoke bash directly. (4) board.py / aspirations-*.py cannot be called as bare scripts (from: command not found) -- they are modules; use the .sh wrappers which read JSON on stdin.
original.when_to_use: When constructing inline JSON for *-add.sh scripts, writing bash from the Bash tool on Windows, or invoking framework Python from the Bash tool. See also core/config/conventions/python-invocation.md.

generalized.context: When constructing inline JSON payloads for shell scripts on Windows (using Git Bash or WSL), invoking Python via shims, or calling framework modules directly.
approach: Ensure inline JSON bodies are strictly ASCII-only to prevent cp1252 single-byte characters (like em-dashes) from being rejected as invalid UTF-8 by the daemon.
Avoid using bash heredocs for JSON payloads containing apostrophes, as they cause unexpected EOF errors; prefer printf %s or writing payloads to a UTF-8 scratch file first.
Do not nest Python subprocess calls inside Python shims on Windows, as the shim launcher is often missing from the WSL subshell PATH; invoke the shell directly instead.
Call framework Python files only via their designated .sh wrappers that read JSON from stdin, rather than attempting to execute them as bare scripts.
generalized.outcome: Prevented daemon rejections of invalid UTF-8, avoided script termination due to heredoc parsing errors, and resolved 'command not found' failures for module invocations.
generalized.lesson: On Windows environments using Git Bash or WSL, inline JSON must be strictly ASCII to avoid codec errors with non-ASCII characters like em-dashes. Avoid heredocs for JSON containing apostrophes; use printf or file-based piping instead. When invoking Python from a Python shim, do not nest subprocess calls as the shim may lack the correct PATH; call the shell directly. Finally, always invoke framework Python modules via their .sh wrappers reading from stdin, never as bare scripts.

original.title: loop_state.goals_completed undercounts recurring re-completions within a session
original.content: Observed (omni 2026-05-23): g-009-01 (recurring inbox poll, 1h interval) completed 4x in one session, but loop_state.goals_completed advanced only once (stayed 59). Mechanism: loop-state-bump-counters.py keys idempotency on counted_goals_this_session, a per-session goal_id list (g-115-664). First completion appends the goal_id; subsequent completions of the SAME recurring goal hit the guard 'if goal_id in counted: exit 0' and no-op the bump. counted_goals_this_session resets only at the session boundary, so each recurring goal contributes at most once to goals_completed per session regardless of fire count.
original.when_to_use: Investigating loop_state counter discrepancies for recurring goals, or working g-001-16.
original.failure_lesson: Two DISTINCT mechanisms both yield 'goals_completed did not advance for a recurring close', needing different fixes. (1) idempotency-suppression: goal_id PRESENT in counted_goals_this_session, counter frozen by design g-115-664 -- undercounts recurring goals, NOT the g-001-16 race. (2) write-clobber: goal_id ABSENT from counted, bump write never landed -- the actual g-001-16 race. Diagnostic: check counted_goals_this_session membership first. Present = mechanism 1; absent = mechanism 2. Implication: productivity-stop-gate reads goals_completed; in long recurring-heavy sessions the count understates throughput and could trip the stop floor early.

generalized.context: When monitoring loop state counters for recurring tasks (e.g., periodic polls or repeating jobs) within a single session, discrepancies arise where the completion count does not advance despite multiple executions.
approach: Identify if the counter update logic uses a per-session idempotency list keyed by the unique goal/task ID.
Check if the specific goal ID exists in this idempotency list before assuming a race condition or write failure.

Distinguish between two failure modes: (1) the ID is present, meaning the counter was intentionally frozen to prevent double-counting, versus (2) the ID is absent, meaning the write operation failed or was clobbered.
generalized.outcome: Correctly diagnosed that the counter undercounted because the idempotency guard prevented subsequent updates for the same recurring task within the session, rather than a race condition.
generalized.lesson: When a loop state counter fails to increment for a recurring task within a session, do not immediately assume a race condition or write failure. First, verify if the task ID exists in the session's idempotency list. If present, the undercount is by design (preventing double-counting of the same recurring event); if absent, the issue is a genuine write failure or race condition. This distinction prevents misdiagnosing intentional idempotency logic as a bug.

original.title: Reset pattern-signature outcome_stats when adapting a heritage pattern - carried-over counts mislead
original.content: Observed (omni 2026-05-23 reflection): sig-8 (VA SDVOSB Sole-Source) shows outcome_stats total=5 confirmed=0 accuracy=0.0, tripping the weakness-analysis low-accuracy threshold. But the 5/0 is the PREDECESSOR's pre-refinement false-positive count carried over when the signature was ported and adapted (refined NAICS + non-hardware filter 2026-05-19; eligibility-gated; SDVOSB confirmed 2026-05-22). The refined pattern has NOT been tested against any new opportunity in this world (no post-refinement sourcing scan run). So 0.0 measures the OLD pattern, not the adapted one.
original.when_to_use: Porting predecessor pattern signatures; interpreting low-accuracy weakness signals during reflection.
original.failure_lesson: When porting/adapting a pattern signature from the predecessor (heritage port), the outcome_stats must reset to total=0 confirmed=0 because the adapted matching criteria produce different predictions than the original. Carrying over the old counts makes the refined pattern's accuracy misleading AND trips reflection weakness-analysis as a false positive. The heritage false-positive history belongs in the description (audit trail), not in the live outcome_stats. Verify-before-assuming: a 0.0-accuracy pattern is only a real weakness if the CURRENT pattern fired and missed - check whether the count predates the last material refinement.

generalized.context: When porting or adapting a pattern signature from a predecessor system (heritage port) where the matching criteria have been refined (e.g., updated filters, eligibility gates, or classification rules),
approach: Identify that the outcome_stats (total, confirmed, accuracy) reflect the predecessor's historical data, not the adapted logic
Reset the outcome_stats counters to total=0 and confirmed=0 immediately upon adaptation
Move the predecessor's historical false-positive counts into the description/audit trail instead of live metrics
Verify that no new opportunities have been scanned against the adapted pattern before relying on accuracy metrics
generalized.outcome: Prevented the adapted pattern from triggering false-positive weakness-analysis alerts due to inherited stale statistics
generalized.lesson: When porting an existing pattern signature with refined matching criteria, the outcome_stats must be reset to zero. Carrying over the predecessor's counts (especially false positives) creates a misleading accuracy score (e.g., 0.0) that incorrectly triggers weakness-analysis thresholds. The historical performance belongs in the audit trail, not in live metrics used for reflection. Always verify that the adapted pattern has been tested against new data before assuming its accuracy.

original.title: Resolve wrapper doc-vs-script drift via the daemon handler, not git history or doc-count
original.content: To resolve a SKILL.md-docs-contradict-the-wrapper-script contradiction, read the daemon endpoint handler in mind_api/src/endpoints/ -- the handler behavior is ground truth, NOT git history (often squashed to a single Initial commit) NOR the doc-count (stale docs routinely outnumber the correct form). g-001-17: aspirations-update.sh appeared to contradict 8 SKILL.md sites; reading update_aspiration showed per-field merge (for field,value in body.items(): asp[field]=value), proving the positional <asp_id> <field> <value> wrapper canonical and all 8 stdin-full-replacement doc-sites stale (pre-2026-05-14-cutover relics). The handler comment block (body must be a JSON object mapping field to value, not a full aspiration record) was the decisive evidence.
original.when_to_use: auditing or reconciling a skill-doc-vs-script contradiction, especially for a daemon-migrated wrapper where git history is squashed

generalized.context: When auditing or reconciling a contradiction between documentation and the actual behavior of a daemon endpoint handler, especially in systems where git history has been squashed or documentation is stale.
approach: Identify the specific contradiction between the documentation (e.g., expected input format) and the wrapper script behavior.
Read the actual daemon endpoint handler code to determine the ground truth behavior.
Ignore git history if it is squashed or lacks granular commit details.
Ignore documentation counts or site prevalence if they reflect pre-migration relics.
Verify the handler's implementation logic (e.g., field-by-field merging vs. full record replacement) to confirm the canonical input format.
generalized.outcome: Confirmed the canonical input format by observing the handler's per-field merge logic, proving that widespread documentation sites were stale relics and the wrapper script was correct.
generalized.lesson: When documentation contradicts a daemon wrapper script, the daemon endpoint handler code is the ground truth, not git history or documentation volume. In migrated systems, git history is often squashed and documentation is frequently stale; therefore, inspecting the handler's implementation logic (e.g., how it iterates over input fields) is the only reliable way to resolve contract drift.

original.title: Verify recurring-goal substance before respecting selector rank
original.content: When goal-selector top-ranks recurring learning-loop goals (resolve/review/generate hypotheses, flush encoding), the score is inflated by overdue/cadence urgency, not necessarily by available substance. Before closing such a goal routine, verify substance with the cheap probes: pipeline-read.sh --unreflected (for resolve/review goals) and encoding_queue depth from wm (for flush goals). If unreflected=0 AND queue empty, the top recurring goal is a substanceless cadence-close; a lower-ranked NON-recurring substantive goal (or a recurring generator with real material) is the higher-EV pick. Override the selector with this expected-value rationale (Phase 2.5), not arbitrarily. Verified this iteration: g-001-08/07/02 all empty, selected g-001-10 (generate hypotheses) which had real session material.
original.when_to_use: goal selection when top-ranked candidates are recurring learning-loop goals with cadence-inflated scores

generalized.context: When a goal selection system ranks recurring learning-loop goals (such as resolving issues, reviewing data, or flushing encodings) at the top due to urgency metrics like overdue status or cadence, rather than available work substance.
approach: Verify the actual substance of the top-ranked recurring goal using lightweight probes (e.g., checking pipeline read counts for resolve/review goals or queue depth for flush goals).
Identify if the top goal is 'substanceless' (zero pipeline reads and empty queue) caused purely by time-based inflation.
Compare against lower-ranked candidates to find a non-recurring substantive goal or a recurring generator with real material.
Override the default selector ranking with an expected-value rationale that prioritizes substance over cadence urgency.
generalized.outcome: Avoided selecting a cadence-inflated, empty goal; successfully selected a lower-ranked goal containing real session material for higher expected value.
generalized.lesson: When a goal selector prioritizes recurring learning-loop goals based on urgency metrics (overdue/cadence) rather than available work, verify substance before execution. If probes (pipeline reads or queue depth) return zero, the top goal is a 'substanceless cadence-close.' In this case, override the selector to choose a lower-ranked non-recurring substantive goal or a recurring generator with actual material, as this yields higher expected value than arbitrarily following the inflated rank.

original.title: Dual-Track delivery model is the organizing axis of go-to-market planning (above segment ranking)
original.content: When assembling any Zak-Data-Solutions go-to-market artifact (reach-out playbook, per-segment messaging, A/B copy, pitch selection), structure it FIRST by the two delivery tracks, THEN by target segment -- not the reverse. Track 1 = AI-forward public flagship (AI / agent capabilities are the explicit pitch). Track 2 = practical gov contracts delivered AI-INVISIBLE (guard-13 HARD: agent-swarm / AI delivery is the INTERNAL operating model, NEVER a customer-facing claim). The track determines the message, the proof points, and -- critically -- what may NOT be said: a Track-2 pitch carrying AI claims is a guard-13 violation. Track 2 is the volume / revenue lane (sole-source + micro-purchase gov, $3K-$150K, many small wins toward the $100K/yr target); Track 1 is the lower-volume flagship. Sequencing: lead Track-2, run Track-1 in parallel. CAVEAT (inherited assumption, NOT yet verified): the 'lead Track-2 for revenue' sequencing is derived from predecessor (Zak-Government-Contracting) heritage pricing math, not validated against any real omni prospect outcome. The active pipeline hypothesis 2026-05-21_prospect-ayoai-derived-preference holds the competing 'AI-forward / Ayoai angle wins first engagement' framing open. Treat track-sequencing as a hypothesis to confirm on the first 1-3 post-Stage-1 prospect conversations, not settled fact.
original.when_to_use: Assembling or revising any go-to-market artifact: reach-out playbook, per-segment message architecture, A/B test copy, pitch selection, capability statements. Always check guard-13 before writing any Track-2 messaging.

generalized.context: When assembling go-to-market artifacts (playbooks, messaging, pitch decks) for a service with dual delivery models: one public-facing AI-forward track and one government/enterprise track where AI is an internal operating model but must remain invisible to the customer.
approach: Structure the artifact FIRST by delivery track (AI-forward vs. AI-invisible), THEN by target segment.
Ensure the AI-invisible track strictly avoids any customer-facing claims about agent swarms or AI capabilities to prevent compliance violations.
Prioritize the AI-invisible track for initial revenue generation (volume/micro-purchases) while running the AI-forward track in parallel.
Treat the sequencing of tracks as a hypothesis to be validated in early prospect conversations rather than a settled fact.
generalized.outcome: Prevents compliance violations in sensitive contracts and aligns messaging with the specific operational reality of each track.
generalized.lesson: When a service operates on dual tracks—one public-facing AI-forward and one where AI is an internal-only operating model—structure all go-to-market artifacts by track first, not by segment. The AI-invisible track must never make customer-facing claims about AI capabilities, as this violates compliance guardrails. Prioritize the AI-invisible track for initial volume revenue while keeping the AI-forward track parallel, but treat this sequencing as a hypothesis to validate in early customer conversations rather than a fixed rule.

original.title: Read the stored metric value; do not infer its dynamics (framework-instrumentation)
original.content: Two hypotheses on cur-01 graduation gating, 3 days apart, opposite outcomes. CORRECTED 2026-05-20_curriculum-gate-asymmetry (conf 0.55): predicted gate_completed_goals_15 passes BEFORE gate_min_competence_30, reasoning that competence requires demonstrated quality not volume so it lags goal-count. Actual: competence was already 0.825 (PASSED); the COUNT gate is the lagging/stale one (current_value=2). The inference was exactly backwards. CONFIRMED 2026-05-23_curriculum-graduation-competence-not-goal-gated (conf 0.6): read curriculum.yaml gate definitions AND developmental-stage.yaml avg_competence (0.825) directly; correctly identified competence gate passed and gate_completed_goals_15 (stale current_value=2) as the binding constraint. Distinguishing factor: the CORRECTED hypothesis inferred a metric dynamics from a plausible-sounding assumption without reading the stored value; the CONFIRMED hypothesis measured the stored value. In framework-instrumentation the metric value sits in a readable state file -- infer-from-assumption is never warranted when measure-from-file is one Read away.
original.when_to_use: forming or evaluating a hypothesis about a framework metric or gate whose current value is stored in a readable config or state file; reasoning about curriculum graduation or stage-gating; tempted to infer how a framework metric behaves rather than read its stored value; framework-instrumentation
original.description: Contrastive pair: two curriculum-gating hypotheses 3 days apart, same subsystem, opposite outcomes. CORRECTED inferred competence lags goal-count; CONFIRMED read the actual competence value (0.825) and gate defs.

generalized.context: When forming or evaluating a hypothesis about a framework metric or gate whose current value is stored in a readable config or state file, specifically when tempted to infer how the metric behaves based on assumptions rather than checking its actual stored value.
approach: Identify the specific metric or gate definition in the stored state file (e.g., curriculum.yaml, developmental-stage.yaml).
Read the actual stored value directly from the file to determine pass/fail status.
Compare the read value against the hypothesis to validate or refute the assumed dynamics.
Avoid inferring metric behavior from plausible-sounding assumptions when a direct read is available.
generalized.outcome: The hypothesis that competence lags behind goal count was proven false; the actual stored value showed competence was already passed while the goal count was stale.
generalized.lesson: In framework instrumentation, metric values reside in readable state files. Never infer a metric's dynamics or status from a plausible-sounding assumption when 'measure-from-file' is one read away. The correct approach is to read the stored value directly to determine the binding constraint, as assumptions often lead to backwards causality (e.g., assuming a quality gate lags a volume gate when the data shows the opposite).

original.title: Tree-maintain decompose: gate on multi-concept signal, not raw line count, for knowledge-article domains
original.content: During g-001-03 tree maintenance (2026-05-24), tree-read.sh --decompose-candidates returned 42 of 51 leaf nodes (line-count > 80). Only ONE was a genuine multi-concept monolith: value-proposition (977 lines, TWO distinct H1 bodies + an umbrella index). Decomposing it into 5 coherent pitch-component children was clearly correct. The other 41 were coherent single-concept articles in the 80-430 line range (theses, references, catalogs, positioning docs). CONFIRMING EVIDENCE the threshold is the wrong gate: the 5 well-decomposed children of value-proposition each landed at 117-240 lines, ALL still over the 80-line threshold, pushing post-run decompose-debt UP from 42 to 44. A raw-line-count threshold cannot be satisfied in this domain without fragmenting coherent concepts into incoherent slivers. REASONING STRATEGY: when /tree maintain surfaces line-count decompose candidates, do NOT decompose by line count alone. Decompose only nodes exhibiting a multi-concept signal: multiple H1 sections, OR 2+ semantically-distinct ## clusters that a future retriever would want separately. Skip coherent over-threshold articles via the instrumentation skipped_by_reason field (this is 'processed', not 'deferred'). This is especially true for YOUNG trees (under ~5 sessions old) where aggressive fragmentation to depth 4+ is premature. The decompose-debt metric will show nominal-threshold exceedance (44 > 40) that is FALSE debt for this domain; it stays well under the x3=120 backlog/heavy-maintain trigger, so no runaway results from skipping.
original.when_to_use: running /tree maintain; tree-read.sh --decompose-candidates returns many line-count-only candidates; knowledge-article domain (theses, references, catalogs, positioning, pitch docs); framework
original.description: The 80-line decompose_threshold over-flags coherent knowledge articles; action genuine multi-concept monoliths and skip coherent over-threshold articles with reason.

generalized.context: When maintaining a knowledge repository (such as documentation, thesis collections, or pitch decks) where the decompose-candidates tool flags nodes based solely on raw line counts exceeding a threshold.
approach: Do not decompose nodes based on line count alone if they exhibit a single coherent concept.
Identify 'multi-concept signals' as the true trigger for decomposition: look for multiple H1 sections or 2+ semantically distinct ## clusters that a future retriever would want separately.
Mark coherent articles that exceed the line threshold as 'processed' (skipped_by_reason) rather than 'deferred' to avoid false debt.
Exercise extra caution with young repositories (under ~5 sessions old) to prevent premature fragmentation into incoherent slivers.
Accept that the decompose-debt metric may show nominal-threshold exceedance (e.g., 44 > 40) which is false debt for this specific domain.
generalized.outcome: Avoided fragmenting coherent single-concept articles into incoherent pieces; ensured that only nodes with distinct conceptual boundaries were split, keeping the knowledge structure logical.
generalized.lesson: When a maintenance tool flags nodes for decomposition based on raw line counts, do not decompose by line count alone. Instead, decompose only nodes exhibiting a multi-concept signal (multiple H1 sections or 2+ semantically distinct clusters). Coherent articles exceeding the line threshold should be marked as 'processed' rather than 'deferred' to avoid inflating false debt. This is critical for young repositories where aggressive fragmentation to deep levels is premature.

original.title: Mind wrapper-family call conventions are consistent; aspirations-update.sh field-vs-record drift is isolated
original.content: The core/scripts wrapper families each follow a consistent call convention that matches their SKILL.md docs: (1) *-add wrappers (aspirations-add-goal, reasoning-bank-add) read a full JSON record from STDIN - aspirations-add-goal also takes a positional asp_id and REJECTS field-shaped flags like --title with exit 2. (2) *-update-field wrappers (pipeline-update-field, pattern-signatures-update-field) take positional <id> <field> <value>. (3) whole-record *-update wrappers (pipeline-update, pattern-signatures-update) take a positional <rec_id> plus a full JSON replacement record on STDIN, and are typically NOT documented with a SKILL.md call-site example. aspirations-update.sh is the lone anomaly (g-001-17): documented as a whole-record stdin updater but implemented as a positional 3-arg field updater. Hypothesis 2026-05-23_skill-wrapper-contract-drift-systemic predicted this drift was systemic; a 7-wrapper audit found 0 additional mismatches, so the drift is ISOLATED to aspirations-update.sh, not a family-wide pattern.
original.when_to_use: Before calling or documenting any core/scripts *-add / *-update / *-update-field wrapper, or when auditing wrapper doc-vs-implementation consistency. Apply the family convention: add = stdin JSON record; update-field = positional id field value; whole-record update = positional id + stdin JSON body.

generalized.context: When auditing or calling core/scripts wrapper families for adding or updating records, verify that the implementation matches the documented call convention.
approach: Identify the wrapper family type: *-add wrappers expect a full JSON record on STDIN (rejecting field flags), *-update-field wrappers expect positional <id> <field> <value>, and whole-record *-update wrappers expect positional <id> plus a full JSON body on STDIN.
Check for documentation drift where a wrapper is documented as a whole-record updater but implemented as a positional field updater.
Audit the specific wrapper in question against the family standard; if it is the only mismatch found, treat it as an isolated anomaly rather than a systemic pattern.
generalized.outcome: Confirmed that the specific wrapper (aspirations-update.sh) was an isolated implementation drift from its documented whole-record contract, while the rest of the family adhered to the standard.
generalized.lesson: When working with a family of record-management wrappers, strict adherence to call conventions is required: *-add takes a full JSON record on STDIN; *-update-field takes positional <id> <field> <value>; whole-record *-update takes positional <id> plus a full JSON body on STDIN. If a wrapper is documented as a whole-record updater but implemented as a positional field updater, treat it as an isolated documentation/implementation drift rather than a systemic family-wide pattern, unless a broader audit reveals multiple mismatches.

original.title: AWS CLI on Windows Git Bash: file:// expands only at top-level param (never in shorthand); mktemp /tmp paths are invisible to the native CLI (use cygpath -m)
original.content: Two stacked Windows/Git-Bash defects broke the /notify-user outbound channel (g-009-11). (1) The SES send passed the body inside AWS CLI shorthand of the form --message Body={Text={Data=file://TMPFILE}}. file:// is expanded ONLY for a top-level parameter value; inside shorthand structure syntax it is a literal string, so the temp-file PATH became the email body - user received file:///tmp/tmp.o9ljoGfjFJ instead of the message text. The send SUCCEEDED with a garbage body: a SILENT failure. (2) After switching to a top-level --message file://TMPFILE so file:// would expand, the send failed LOUDLY: Unable to load paramfile file:///tmp/tmp.XXX: No such file or directory. mktemp returns an MSYS /tmp path and the native Windows AWS CLI cannot resolve /tmp (same class as the documented Python /tmp gotcha). FIX: Python builds the full Message struct as JSON to ONE temp file; bash converts that path via cygpath -m (mixed C:/ form) when cygpath is present, raw path otherwise for Linux/macOS portability; the send passes --message file://WINPATH as a top-level arg. JSON-in-a-file handles all body escaping. The new failure mode is LOUD (parse error if file:// fails to expand or the file is unreadable), so a returned MessageId now PROVES the body is real text - unlike the old silent-bad-body bug. Verified 2026-05-24, MessageId 010f019e5a98c774.
original.when_to_use: Constructing or debugging any aws CLI invocation from Git Bash on Windows that passes a structure parameter (--message, --cli-input-json) or a file:// paramfile, especially when the file came from mktemp. If notifications arrive with a file:// path as the body, this is the cause.

generalized.context: When constructing CLI invocations on Windows using Git Bash that pass structured parameters (e.g., --message Body={...}) or file:// URIs generated by mktemp.
approach: Recognize that file:// expansion occurs only for top-level parameter values; inside shorthand syntax (e.g., --key Value={...}), it remains a literal string.
Identify that mktemp generates MSYS-style /tmp paths which the native Windows CLI cannot resolve, causing 'No such file or directory' errors.

Construct the full parameter structure as JSON in a temporary file first, then convert the path using cygpath -m (or use the raw path for Linux/macOS) before passing it as a top-level file:// argument.
Ensure the final invocation passes the file:// URI as a top-level argument to guarantee proper expansion and path resolution.
generalized.outcome: The CLI invocation succeeds with the correct file content in the body, and any remaining failures are loud (parse errors) rather than silent (garbage data sent).
generalized.lesson: On Windows with Git Bash, file:// URIs inside shorthand parameter syntax (e.g., --key Value={Text={...}}) are treated as literal strings, not expanded paths. Additionally, mktemp-generated /tmp paths are invisible to the native Windows CLI. To fix this: build the parameter structure as JSON in a temp file, convert the path to a Windows-compatible format (C:/...) using cygpath -m, and pass the resulting file:// URI as a top-level argument. This ensures the URI expands correctly and the file path is resolvable, turning silent data corruption into loud parse errors.

original.title: Auto-generated marketing copy overclaims credentials -- review before publishing
original.content: Auto-generators (e.g., Hallmark /build-landing-page) fill credential slots with plausible-sounding strings that may overclaim. Canonical incident 2026-05-25: Hallmark variants A+B wrote M.S.-in-AI principal as the credibility hook; actual degree is M.S. Computer Science (Data Analytics) from BU Met College with applied AI coursework and NLP project work. 4 spots had to be corrected after publication (commit 95b869e). Generators do not know the principals exact credentials; they pattern-match on the brief and fill plausible specifics. Review every named credential, employer, role, year, and certification in auto-generated copy against the principals verified record (resume + profile.yaml) BEFORE committing or pushing.
original.when_to_use: After running /build-landing-page, /hallmark, or any generator that emits marketing/sales copy with named credentials, employers, certifications, or specific role descriptions. Before commit, before push, before send.

generalized.context: When auto-generating marketing copy that includes named credentials, employers, certifications, or specific role descriptions for a platform or service.
approach: Recognize that auto-generators pattern-match on briefs and fill plausible-sounding specifics without verifying exact details.
Identify that generated text may overclaim degrees, titles, or experience to sound more credible.
Cross-reference every named credential, employer, role, and year in the generated copy against the principal's verified record (resume + profile data) before committing or publishing.
Correct any discrepancies immediately to prevent reputational damage from false claims.
generalized.outcome: Prevented the publication of overclaimed credentials (e.g., misstated degrees or titles) that would require post-publication corrections and damage trust.
generalized.lesson: Auto-generators often hallucinate plausible-sounding specifics for credentials and roles because they lack access to verified records. Never trust generated marketing copy containing named credentials, employers, or certifications. You must manually cross-reference every specific claim against the principal's verified resume or profile data before committing or publishing to avoid overclaiming and reputational harm.

original.title: Glob honors .gitignore -- use Bash find -iname for personal/gitignored files
original.content: When searching for a file the user claims exists but Glob returns empty: Globs ripgrep backend respects .gitignore by default, so personal docs, OneDrive synced content, and ignored build artifacts wont surface. Workaround: Bash find <path> -maxdepth N -iname *pattern* 2>/dev/null bypasses .gitignore and is case-insensitive. Canonical incident 2026-05-25: user said resume was at <PROJECT_ROOT>/Zachary_A_Kysar_Resume.pdf; Read failed, Glob returned no PDFs. Real location was <USER_HOME>/OneDrive/Jennifer/Zak ResumeCoverletter/Zachary_A_Kysar_Resume.pdf (entirely different tree under OneDrive). Lesson: when Glob is empty AND user insists file exists, try find first; if still empty, ask user for correct path rather than concluding it does not exist.
original.when_to_use: Any search for a personal document, resume, credential, profile asset, or build artifact when Glob returns empty but the user has referenced the file as existing.

generalized.context: When a file search returns empty results despite the user insisting the file exists, and the search tool (e.g., a Glob-based indexer) respects .gitignore or similar exclusion rules by default.
approach: Recognize that the search backend may be filtering out personal documents, synced content, or build artifacts due to ignore rules.
Execute a raw filesystem search (e.g., Bash find with -iname) that bypasses ignore rules to verify actual file presence.
If the raw search also fails, conclude the file is not in the expected location rather than assuming it is missing.
generalized.outcome: Successfully located files hidden by ignore rules or identified that the user's path assumption was incorrect.
generalized.lesson: When a Glob-based search returns empty but the user asserts a file exists, the tool likely filtered the file via .gitignore or similar mechanisms. Do not immediately conclude the file is missing; instead, run a raw filesystem search (like Bash find) that bypasses ignore rules. If that also fails, the file is genuinely absent or the user's path is wrong.

original.title: Enforce a domain HARD content-rule in the tool that generates the content, not just in prose
original.content: The reach-out-playbook states a HARD RULE (guard-13): Track-2 (practical) outreach copy must contain ZERO AI/agent/ML language. Rather than leave it as prose discipline an author can forget, g-010-02 baked the rule into outreach-render.sh as a lint: for track:2 templates the renderer scans the RENDERED output (word-bounded, so email/available/maintain never false-trip) and exits 2 on any AI/agent/ML term. Verified by injecting AI-powered ML with autonomous agents into a Track-2 render, which was refused (caught: AI, ML, agent, autonomous). Pattern: when a domain has a falsifiable content constraint, encode it as an automated check at the point of generation; the generator becomes self-policing and the rule cannot silently rot.
original.when_to_use: Building any content-generation tool (templates, copy, config, code scaffolds) where a domain rule forbids or requires specific content. Put the check in the generator and exit non-zero on violation.

generalized.context: When building a content-generation tool (templates, copy, config, or code scaffolds) where a domain rule forbids or requires specific content patterns.
approach: Identify the specific forbidden or required terms (e.g., 'AI', 'agent', 'ML') that must not appear in the final output.
Embed a linting check directly into the generation script to scan the RENDERED output (using word-bounded matching to avoid false positives on common words like 'available' or 'maintain').
Configure the script to exit with a non-zero status code immediately upon detecting a violation, preventing the generation of non-compliant content.
generalized.outcome: The generator became self-policing; attempts to inject forbidden terms were caught and rejected at the point of creation, preventing the rule from silently rotting.
generalized.lesson: When a domain has a falsifiable content constraint, encode it as an automated check at the point of generation rather than relying on prose discipline. By baking the rule into the generator and exiting non-zero on violation, the tool becomes self-policing, ensuring the constraint cannot be silently violated or forgotten by the author.

original.title: Heredoc stdin clobbers the data pipe in bash python helpers
original.content: When a bash helper must run a Python program AND feed it data, do NOT use: printf data | python3 - <<PYEOF ... PYEOF. python3 - reads the PROGRAM from stdin and the heredoc redirect wins over the pipe, so stdin becomes the program text; json.load(sys.stdin) then reads an exhausted stream and exits silently non-zero. Fix: program via python3 -c, data via the stdin pipe; or temp-file + cygpath -m + argv. Sibling of rb-48 (the data never arrived through the channel you assumed, on Windows/bash).
original.when_to_use: writing a bash helper that pipes data to an inline python program; framework-architecture
original.failure_lesson: g-010-08 verify helper exited 2 silently; queue JSON never reached json.load because the heredoc took stdin.

generalized.context: When a bash helper script must execute an inline Python program while simultaneously piping data to its standard input.
approach: Avoid using the heredoc syntax (<<PYEOF) combined with a pipe (|) to feed data to the Python process
Use the -c flag to pass the Python code as a command-line argument instead of reading it from stdin
Ensure the data is fed exclusively via the stdin pipe so the Python process can read it correctly
generalized.outcome: Prevented the Python process from reading the heredoc text as its program code, which would otherwise exhaust the input stream and cause silent failures when attempting to parse the actual data.
generalized.lesson: When piping data to an inline Python program in a bash script, never use the heredoc syntax (<<) alongside the pipe operator. The shell prioritizes the heredoc redirection over the pipe, causing the Python interpreter to read the heredoc text as its program source code. This leaves the actual data pipe empty, resulting in a silent failure when the code attempts to parse the data. Instead, pass the Python logic via the -c flag and feed the data strictly through the stdin pipe.

original.title: loop_state single-writers persist whole slot -> lost-update under stale-lock theft
original.content: Two bash single-writers mutate loop_state during recurring-close: loop-state-bump-counters.py (owns goals_completed, productive_goals, counted_goals_this_session) and recurring-loop-state-mutate.py (owns signals, routine_streaks, goals_completed_this_session, productive_goals_this_session). BOTH do read-modify-WRITE-WHOLE-SLOT (slots[loop_state]=loop_state), serialized only by wm.yaml.lock with stale_seconds=10. Failure (g-001-16, observed 2026-05-23): when recurring-close overlaps a MANUAL iteration-close state-update retry (MSYS stdout buffering fires the stop hook before harness completion-notify, prompting the LLM to retry) AND a writer stalls past 10s under MSYS I/O, the lock is deemed stale and stolen, so two writers run concurrently and the older-snapshot writer commits its whole-slot write, clobbering fields owned by the other writer. Symptom: goals_completed 59 to 58, counted_goals_this_session lost g-009-01, despite the idempotency guard briefly reporting already-counted. CORRECT FIX (design recorded, deferred): each writer re-reads loop_state under its lock immediately before persist and overlays ONLY its owned fields, recomputing deltas from the re-read, so no writer persists stale values for fields it does not own, killing the lost-update class even under lock theft. DECISION: rare + self-correcting (loop_state re-inits at session boundary) + low-impact (off-by-one cadence/productivity-gate math) + high-blast-radius scripts, so deferred to a focused Apply goal with full pytest coverage rather than inline. Avoid the trigger: do NOT manually retry iteration-close state-update on empty recurring-close stdout without confirming the close did not already run.
original.when_to_use: Before modifying loop-state-bump-counters.py or recurring-loop-state-mutate.py, or when diagnosing loop_state counter drift (goals_completed or counted_goals_this_session off-by-one).

generalized.context: When multiple single-writer scripts mutate a shared state object (loop_state) during overlapping execution windows, relying solely on a stale-lock timeout for serialization.
approach: Identify that both writers perform read-modify-write on the entire state slot (slots[state]=state) rather than individual fields
Recognize that if one writer stalls past the stale timeout (e.g., 10s) while another proceeds, the lock is stolen and both run concurrently
Understand that the concurrent older-snapshot writer will overwrite fields owned by the other writer, causing lost updates
Implement a fix where each writer re-reads the shared state under its lock immediately before persisting and overlays ONLY its owned fields
Recompute deltas from the re-read to ensure no stale values for non-owned fields are persisted
generalized.outcome: Prevented counter drift (e.g., goals_completed decreasing) and data loss (e.g., specific goal IDs disappearing) caused by concurrent overwrites during lock theft.
generalized.lesson: When multiple scripts mutate a shared state object using whole-slot updates (read-modify-write on the entire object), a stale-lock timeout is insufficient to prevent lost updates. If one writer stalls and the lock is stolen, the concurrent writer will overwrite fields owned by the stalled writer with stale data. The correct fix is to have each writer re-read the shared state immediately before persisting and overlay ONLY its owned fields, recomputing deltas from the fresh read. This eliminates the lost-update class even if lock theft occurs.

original.title: Uncorroborated user-delegated answer is not authorization for self-escalation
original.content: Incident 2026-05-25: pq-007 and pq-008 were both marked answered at an identical 14:46 timestamp with near-identical user-directed claims. pq-008 selected Option B (graduate omni to Stage 2, unblock contract bidding), which REVERSES the explicit pq-005 directive (Choice C: do NOT count both queues). The runner found NO corroboration in any tracked channel: journal (no entry), board (no post), git (pending-questions.yaml untracked), inbox (last poll 13:03 processed 0 emails; inbox now empty; no poll after 13:03 - no delegation email arrived). NOTE: an initial inbox probe wrongly concluded the list script was missing - that was a path error (called the world/scripts/ virtual prefix unresolved instead of the external WORLD_DIR). Re-checked with the correct path: the inbox channel actively confirms NO delegation email, which STRENGTHENS the hold. The prior-session summary also listed pq-008 as pending/do-not-graduate. The runner HELD graduation, re-blocked g-002-09 (blocker infra-curriculum-gates-2026-05-25, unblock g-002-10), re-opened pq-008, surfaced for direct confirmation. Insight 1: a detailed persuasive self-written rationale for a SELF-BENEFITING action is not evidence of authorization; the more the action benefits the agent, the higher the external-evidence bar. Insight 2: when verifying provenance, resolve virtual path prefixes (world/, meta/) to the external configured paths - a path error can produce a false channel-unavailable signal.
original.when_to_use: about to graduate or promote curriculum stage; about to unlock a capability or expand scope; acting on a user-approved claim that reverses a prior resolved decision; governance

generalized.context: When verifying a user-delegated claim that reverses a prior resolved decision or triggers a self-benefiting escalation (e.g., graduating a stage, unlocking a capability) without external corroboration in logs, boards, or git history.
approach: Treat a detailed persuasive rationale written by the agent as insufficient evidence of authorization, especially when the action benefits the agent.
Resolve virtual path prefixes (e.g., world/, meta/) to their external configured paths to avoid false 'channel unavailable' signals caused by path errors.
Confirm the absence of delegation evidence (emails, polls, logs) using the correct resolved paths before proceeding.
Hold the action, re-block the dependent stage, and surface the request for direct confirmation from the delegator.
generalized.outcome: Prevented an unauthorized reversal of a prior decision by identifying a lack of external evidence and correcting a path resolution error that masked the missing delegation.
generalized.lesson: A detailed persuasive rationale for a self-benefiting action is not evidence of authorization; the more the action benefits the agent, the higher the external-evidence bar required. When verifying provenance, always resolve virtual path prefixes to external configured paths to avoid false 'channel unavailable' signals. If no corroboration exists in logs, boards, or history, hold the escalation and require direct confirmation.

original.title: Manually unblocking a goal: clear blocker_ref + blocked_since via null (not empty-string); status=pending alone is insufficient
original.content: To re-activate a goal the runner had blocked, setting status=pending was not enough: the goal kept blocker_ref + blocked_since, and goal-selector collect_blocked surfaces blocker_ref, so the selector could still treat it as blocked. The terminal-status normalizer in aspirations.py that pops blocker_ref/blocked_since only fires for TERMINAL statuses (completed/skipped/expired), not pending. aspirations-update-goal.sh REJECTS an empty-string value (Error: value required) but ACCEPTS the literal null and JSON-parses it to None, clearing the field. Sequence: aspirations-update-goal.sh GID status pending; then GID blocker_ref null; then GID blocked_since null. Verified g-002-09 reached status=pending, blocker_ref=null, blocked_since=null, blocked_by=[].
original.when_to_use: manually re-activating a blocked/deferred goal from an assistant session, or clearing any field on a goal record via aspirations-update-goal.sh

generalized.context: When manually re-activating a goal or task record that was previously blocked by a dependency, simply updating the status to 'pending' is insufficient if the blocking metadata remains.
approach: Identify that the status normalizer only clears blocking metadata (blocker_ref, blocked_since) for terminal statuses like 'completed' or 'skipped', not for 'pending'.
Execute the update script to set the status to 'pending'.
Immediately execute the same update script again to explicitly set the 'blocker_ref' field to null (not an empty string).
Immediately execute the same update script again to explicitly set the 'blocked_since' field to null (not an empty string).
Verify that the goal selector no longer surfaces the record as blocked and that the blocking metadata fields are null.
generalized.outcome: The goal record was successfully re-activated; the selector stopped treating it as blocked, and the blocking metadata fields were cleared.
generalized.lesson: To re-activate a blocked goal, you must explicitly clear the 'blocker_ref' and 'blocked_since' fields by setting them to null, not just by changing the status to 'pending'. The system's normalizer only clears these fields automatically for terminal statuses (completed/skipped/expired). Additionally, ensure the update script accepts the literal null value rather than an empty string, as the latter may be rejected or fail to clear the field.

original.title: Assistant-session cannot graduate omni by flipping shared-state fields; route high-stakes user authorization through a runner-visible channel
original.content: User verbally delegated omni Stage-2 graduation in an assistant-session; I set pq-008=Option-B and unblocked g-002-09. The autonomous runner cannot see the assistant conversation; it correctly flagged the pq-005 reversal as uncorroborated (journal/board/git/inbox), encoded guard-33 + rb-55, re-blocked the goal, and required the user to confirm by email before graduating (which then succeeded to cur-02). Lessons: (1) for high-stakes delegated actions in an observer session, do NOT just flip the shared-state field; the runner rejects + reverses uncorroborated reversals of prior user decisions; route the user authorization through a runner-visible channel (email/inbox is the designed one). (2) Before claiming a fix respects a prior decision, RE-READ that decision: g-002-09 was filed claiming it respects pq-005 when it actually contradicted pq-005 (Choice C, agent-queue-only counting).
original.when_to_use: acting on a user verbal directive in an assistant/observer session for a high-stakes or prior-decision-reversing action; making an assistant-session directive trusted by the autonomous runner

generalized.context: When executing high-stakes actions or reversing prior user decisions within an assistant session where the autonomous runner cannot directly observe the conversation history.
approach: Do not rely solely on flipping shared-state fields to authorize actions, as the autonomous runner will reject uncorroborated reversals of prior user decisions.
Route user authorization through a runner-visible channel (such as email or a dedicated inbox) to ensure the action is verified.
Before claiming a fix respects a prior decision, re-read the original decision to ensure the new action does not contradict it.
Encode guardrails and reasoning bank entries if the runner flags the reversal as uncorroborated.
generalized.outcome: The autonomous runner accepted the authorization and allowed the goal to graduate after the user confirmed via the runner-visible channel, preventing a false rejection.
generalized.lesson: For high-stakes delegated actions in an observer session, do not just flip shared-state fields; the autonomous runner will reject and reverse uncorroborated changes to prior user decisions. Instead, route user authorization through a runner-visible channel (like email or inbox) to provide necessary corroboration. Additionally, always re-read the original decision before claiming a fix respects it, as new actions may inadvertently contradict the initial constraints.

original.title: After catching an uncorroborated write, reconcile ALL its sibling artifacts
original.content: When you catch one bogus/uncorroborated agent-written answer (a pending-question answered by a write you cannot corroborate in any tracked channel), the SAME write usually touched sibling artifacts sharing the bad provenance: other pending-questions stamped at the identical timestamp, derived WM conclusions, and WM known_blockers it spawned. Catching the primary artifact is not enough. Sweep for siblings by timestamp + provenance and give each the same treatment. Concrete: the 2026-05-25 14:46 write bogus-answered BOTH pq-008 (graduation, irreversible -> held + confirmed) AND pq-007 (IAM-migration decline, reversible -> re-opened to pending). Reconciling only pq-008 would have left pq-007 cementing an uncorroborated decline.
original.when_to_use: After detecting any uncorroborated or bogus agent-written answer/decision, before declaring cleanup complete

generalized.context: When an automated agent produces an uncorroborated write (a decision or answer that cannot be verified in any tracked channel), the same write operation often modifies sibling artifacts sharing that bad provenance.
approach: Identify the timestamp and provenance of the primary uncorroborated artifact
Sweep for all sibling artifacts (other pending items, derived conclusions, or spawned blockers) stamped at the identical timestamp
Apply the same reconciliation treatment to every identified sibling artifact
generalized.outcome: Prevents partial cleanup where fixing one artifact leaves others cementing unverified decisions or false blockers.
generalized.lesson: When catching an uncorroborated agent-written answer, do not stop at the primary artifact. The same write operation typically touched sibling artifacts (other pending questions, derived conclusions, or spawned blockers) sharing the identical timestamp and bad provenance. Reconciling only the primary item leaves siblings cementing unverified declines or false blockers; you must sweep for all siblings by timestamp and apply the same treatment to each.

original.title: Capability assessment: separate agent-buildable gaps from human-gated prerequisites; the binding constraint is often human/calendar
original.content: When assessing 'can we do X', classify each gap as agent-buildable vs human-gated, then identify which is on the critical path. The binding constraint is frequently a human/calendar prerequisite (e.g. SAM.gov + SBA VetCert SDVOSB registration, weeks of verification lag), NOT an agent capability. Building agent capability that sits BEHIND a human blocker does not advance the deadline. Strategy: surface the human-gated critical-path item immediately (start its clock) while building agent-capable gaps in parallel, so the practice is bid-ready the moment the blocker clears. Discovered in g-007-02 (VA SDVOSB applied-AI capability assessment): the #1 gap was registration (human), not any omni capability.
original.when_to_use: any capability-fit / readiness / gap assessment where some gaps are agent-buildable and others require human action

generalized.context: When assessing capability fit or readiness for a project where some gaps can be resolved by automated agents and others require human action or external approvals
approach: Classify every identified gap as either 'agent-buildable' (technical implementation) or 'human-gated' (requires manual approval, registration, or calendar availability)
Identify which of these gaps lies on the critical path to the deadline
Immediately surface and start the clock on the human-gated critical-path item, as this is frequently the binding constraint
Build agent capabilities for non-critical gaps in parallel to ensure readiness the moment the human blocker clears
generalized.outcome: Avoided wasting effort building technical capabilities that sit behind a human approval bottleneck; ensured the solution was ready for execution the instant the human prerequisite was met
generalized.lesson: In capability assessments, the binding constraint is often a human or calendar prerequisite (e.g., regulatory registration, vendor onboarding) rather than a technical gap. Do not build agent capabilities that sit behind a human blocker. Instead, immediately surface the human-gated critical-path item to start its clock, while building agent capabilities in parallel. This ensures the solution is ready for execution the moment the human blocker clears.

original.title: First-target capture-strategy leads with the certification moat, then sizes to the matching FAR vehicle
original.content: When choosing a first/next target contract category for a credentialed small business (SDVOSB/8a/WOSB/HUBZone), LEAD the analysis with the STRUCTURAL certification advantage (set-aside / sole-source eligibility), not capability-merit - the cert is the moat competitors lack. Then size the target to the FAR vehicle the entity can actually WIN: for a solo SDVOSB that is micro-purchase (FAR 13.201, 10K-25K) + sole-source (FAR 19.1406, 25K-5M services), NOT formal IDIQs (gated out by bonding/past-performance/team-size per rb-001). Match the cert to the agency that most uses it (VA for SDVOSB per rb-003 + strongest scorecard). CAVEAT: rb-001/rb-003 are predecessor-verified (inherited, 2026-03) - re-confirm current FAR thresholds and VA posture against live sources before any pursuit. Applied in g-007-01 -> VA SDVOSB sole-source for applied-AI/data-engineering.
original.when_to_use: Choosing a first or next target contract category; any capture-strategy decision for a credentialed small business

generalized.context: When selecting a first or next target contract category for a credentialed small business (e.g., veteran-owned, minority-owned, or women-owned),
approach: Lead the analysis with the structural certification advantage (set-aside or sole-source eligibility) rather than capability merit, as the certification is the moat competitors lack.

Size the target to the specific procurement vehicle the entity can actually win (e.g., micro-purchases and sole-source thresholds) rather than formal IDIQs, which are often gated out by bonding or past-performance requirements.
Match the specific certification to the agency or client organization that most frequently utilizes that set-aside mechanism.
Re-confirm current regulatory thresholds and agency posture against live sources before initiating any pursuit, as rules may have evolved since the strategy was derived.
generalized.outcome: Selected a high-probability target by aligning the business's specific credentials with the most favorable procurement vehicle and agency.
generalized.lesson: When choosing a target contract category for a credentialed small business, lead the analysis with the structural certification advantage (set-aside or sole-source eligibility) rather than capability merit, as the certification is the moat competitors lack. Then size the target to the specific procurement vehicle the entity can actually win (e.g., micro-purchases and sole-source thresholds) rather than formal IDIQs, which are often gated out by bonding or past-performance requirements. Finally, match the specific certification to the agency or client organization that most frequently utilizes that set-aside mechanism.

original.title: After adding a knowledge-tree node, verify BOTH the parent children list AND a nodes-map entry exist
original.content: A tree node can end up listed in its parent's children array while having NO node-entry block under the nodes map in _tree.yaml. In that state the node .md file exists and the parent counts it as a child, but retrieve.sh cannot index or surface it - the node is effectively invisible to retrieval. Observed 2026-05-25: intelligence/first-bid-plan (added by g-007-03) was in the intelligence children list but had no nodes-map entry, so retrieval could not reach g-007-03's bid plan. Fix: add a leaf node-entry block (file, depth, parent, summary, capability_level, node_type) mirroring sibling nodes, then verify the parent's child_count equals the count of node-entries whose parent field points at it.
original.when_to_use: any time a new knowledge-tree node is added (via /tree add or a manual _tree.yaml edit) - verify both registration sites before considering the node registered and retrievable
original.description: Children-list registration without a nodes-map entry leaves a tree node un-retrievable; verify both sites after adding.

generalized.context: When adding a new node to a hierarchical knowledge structure (via CLI or manual YAML edit), ensure the node is registered in both the parent's children list and the global nodes map.
approach: Add the new node entry block to the global nodes map with required fields (file, depth, parent, summary, capability_level, node_type)
Verify the parent's children array includes the new node ID
Confirm the parent's child_count matches the actual number of node entries pointing to it as a parent
generalized.outcome: Prevents the node from being invisible to the retrieval system, which occurs when a node exists in the parent's list but lacks a corresponding entry in the global nodes map.
generalized.lesson: A node in a hierarchical knowledge structure is effectively invisible to retrieval if it exists in its parent's children list but lacks a corresponding entry in the global nodes map. To ensure a new node is fully registered and retrievable, you must add a leaf node-entry block to the global map mirroring sibling nodes, and verify that the parent's child_count equals the count of node entries where the parent field points to it.

original.title: Push-held deploy gate still requires committing new work locally
original.content: This project gates production deploy at the PUSH (a push to origin/main triggers the Amplify rebuild of the live company site), not at commit. pq-010 holds that push for user's per-send approval. When a later goal adds work to the already-held dashboard, that new work MUST still be committed locally (no push) so it is INCLUDED when the user later approves the push. Leaving it uncommitted means the approved push deploys only the already-committed code and silently drops the new work. g-007-09 committed the calendar view as 8cf8915 (main ahead 2) precisely so it ships with the eventual approved deploy, rather than leaving it uncommitted the way g-007-07's recon-data.ts re-score had been. The general truth 'uncommitted changes do not push' becomes a concrete trap when commit and push are deliberately split across a deploy-approval gate.
original.when_to_use: Adding or extending work whose push/deploy is held for user approval (e.g. the recon dashboard under pq-010); deciding whether to commit local changes when the push is gated.

generalized.context: When a production deployment is gated by a manual approval step triggered at the push-to-main stage (rather than at commit), and new work is added to the codebase while the push is held.
approach: Recognize that the deployment gate waits for the push event, not the commit event.
Commit any new local changes before the user grants approval for the pending push.
Ensure the approved push includes the latest committed code to avoid silent drops.
generalized.outcome: The approved deployment includes the new work; uncommitted changes are excluded from the build.
generalized.lesson: When a deployment pipeline gates the build at the push-to-main stage (triggered by a manual approval), any work added after the gate is opened but before approval must be committed locally. If left uncommitted, the approved push will only deploy the code that was already committed, silently dropping the new changes.

original.title: User-directive-burst execution: advance every product lane while holding every irreversible gate, then consolidate reporting
original.content: When user sends a multi-part directive (canonical: the 2026-05-25 email - registration-active + scout-renewals + draft-the-two-bids + calendar/dashboard), the force-multiplier pattern that maximizes value across the whole arc: (1) ADVANCE EVERY PRODUCT LANE to completion autonomously - encode the gating change portfolio-wide not single-entry (g-007-07 re-scored all 4 recon entries when registration went active), scout multi-signal + root-cause-framed (g-007-08, rb-63), draft the artifacts (g-007-05/06), build + LOCALLY-commit the dashboard so it rides the eventual approved push (g-007-09, rb-64). (2) HOLD EVERY IRREVERSIBLE-ACTION GATE absolutely throughout - no Sources-Sought/bid submission (guard-12/29), no production deploy/push (pq-010), no external send under the business name. Critically: registration going ACTIVE cleared the *registration* gate ONLY; it did NOT clear the *submission* gate. The two gates are independent and clearing one never clears the other - this distinction must be preserved in every artifact (program.md, recon-list, dashboard copy all say so). (3) CONSOLIDATE status into ONE internal notification answering his actual questions, not one email per goal. Net result: the practice advanced on every front (registration encoded, pipeline scouted, two bids drafted, dashboard+calendar built and surfaced) while ZERO irreversible actions fired without his sign-off. This is self.md's force-multiplier model expressed as a repeatable execution playbook.
original.when_to_use: user sends a multi-part directive; deciding how far to advance autonomously vs where to stop and surface for per-send/per-deploy sign-off. Also when a gating variable (registration, certification, eligibility) changes - propagate portfolio-wide but never conflate a cleared registration/eligibility gate with the still-active submission gate.

generalized.context: When a stakeholder sends a multi-part directive involving parallel work streams (e.g., enabling a feature flag, drafting deliverables, building dashboards) where some prerequisites are met but final approval gates remain open.
approach: Advance every independent work lane to completion autonomously, encoding the gating change portfolio-wide rather than on a single entry.
Hold every irreversible-action gate absolutely throughout the process (e.g., no external submissions, no production deploys, no official communications) until explicit sign-off.
Explicitly distinguish between independent gates (e.g., a feature being 'active' vs. a submission being 'approved') and ensure this distinction is preserved in all artifacts.
Consolidate status updates into a single internal notification that answers the stakeholder's questions, rather than sending separate updates for each goal.
generalized.outcome: Work advanced on every front (features encoded, pipelines scouted, artifacts drafted, dashboards built) while zero irreversible actions fired without the stakeholder's sign-off.
generalized.lesson: When executing a multi-part directive, apply a force-multiplier pattern: advance all independent lanes to completion while strictly holding all irreversible-action gates. Crucially, recognize that clearing one prerequisite gate (e.g., eligibility or feature activation) does not clear independent downstream gates (e.g., submission or deployment). Preserve this distinction in all artifacts. Finally, consolidate status reporting into one internal update to avoid fragmentation, ensuring the stakeholder sees progress without accidental premature execution.

original.title: Gotcha: guard object-literal key lookups with Object.hasOwn (prototype-key leak)
original.content: In lib/prospects.ts getProspectByToken used PROSPECTS[token] ?? null on a plain object literal. Prototype-key tokens (__proto__, constructor, toString, hasOwnProperty) resolved to inherited Object.prototype members (truthy), bypassing the documented null-for-unknown contract and, on the PUBLIC /p/[token] route, the notFound() 404 -> rendered an empty-field page. Fix: return Object.hasOwn(obj, key) ? obj[key] : null (or use a Map / Object.create(null) for untrusted-key maps). Caught by the fresh-eyes-code schema dimension AFTER tsc + 8 unit tests + next build ALL passed green.
original.when_to_use: When a TypeScript/JS object literal is keyed by a user- or URL-controlled string and the lookup must return null for unknown keys (e.g. dynamic-route token resolution).

generalized.context: When performing key lookups on a plain object literal using a user-controlled or URL-derived string (e.g., dynamic route parameters) where the contract requires returning null for unknown keys.
approach: Identify that bracket notation (obj[key]) or optional chaining (obj[key] ?? null) can resolve inherited prototype properties (like __proto__, constructor, toString) as truthy values
Replace the lookup logic with Object.hasOwn(obj, key) to strictly check for own properties
Alternatively, initialize the lookup object with Object.create(null) or use a Map to eliminate the prototype chain entirely
generalized.outcome: Prevented prototype-key leaks where inherited Object.prototype members were incorrectly treated as valid data, ensuring the correct null response for unknown keys.
generalized.lesson: When using user-controlled strings to access keys on plain object literals, standard bracket notation or optional chaining can fail because they resolve inherited prototype properties (e.g., __proto__, constructor) as truthy values. This bypasses the expected null-for-unknown contract. To fix this, use Object.hasOwn(obj, key) to strictly check for own properties, or initialize the object with Object.create(null) or a Map to remove the prototype chain entirely.

original.title: Defaulted-source param in _rt daemon helpers is a footgun for agent-source aspirations
original.content: _rt.aspirations_add_goal(asp_id, record, source='world', ...) defaults source to 'world'. Any caller operating on an AGENT-source aspiration (e.g. asp-001 in <agent>/aspirations.jsonl) that omits the source arg gets {error:aspiration_not_found, detail:'... not found in world'} and silently files 0 goals. streak-break-reflector Pass 1 hit this for 3 days; the failure was a non-fatal WARN inside recurring-close ('0 filed'), so nothing screamed. DIAGNOSTIC TELL: when two near-identical code paths diverge on a routing param, the one OMITTING it is the bug -- Pass 2 (_auto_resolve_recovered_canaries) correctly passed source=source while Pass 1 (_file_investigate) omitted it. FIX: resolve the aspiration's queue by scanning world then agent aspirations.jsonl (helper _source_for_aspiration), pass source explicitly, fall back to 'world' only when found in neither. Sibling callers to audit for the same omission: inactivity-detector.py:156 (omits source entirely -- prime suspect), cargo-cult-detector.py:219, create-blocker.py:403, insight-trigger-sweep.py:244, stall-goal-filer.py:220.
original.when_to_use: calling _rt.aspirations_add_goal or any defaulted-source daemon helper; filing goals for agent-source aspirations; seeing aspiration_not_found '... not found in world' from a daemon write; framework-maintenance

generalized.context: When calling a daemon helper to add goals or aspirations where the source parameter defaults to 'world', but the target record is actually stored in an agent-specific source (e.g., a local JSONL file).
approach: Identify callers of the helper that omit the explicit source argument.
Verify if the target record exists in the default 'world' source; if not, the call will fail silently or return 'not found'.
Audit sibling code paths with identical logic to find other instances omitting the source parameter.
Modify the caller to explicitly pass the correct source (e.g., 'agent') or implement a fallback lookup strategy that scans both sources.
Ensure error handling distinguishes between 'not found in world' and 'not found anywhere' to prevent silent goal drops.
generalized.outcome: Prevented silent failures where goals were not filed because the lookup was restricted to the default 'world' source instead of the actual 'agent' source.
generalized.lesson: When a helper function defaults a routing parameter (like 'source') to a global scope (e.g., 'world'), any caller targeting a specific scope (e.g., 'agent') that omits this argument will fail to find the record. This often results in a non-fatal warning or a silent 'not found' error, causing the operation to drop data without alerting the operator. Always explicitly pass the correct scope parameter to avoid relying on default values that may not match the data's actual location.

original.title: Type-only import severs a runtime dependency (keeps node-only deps out of server-component bundles)
original.content: In the Next.js Web-App, import { type X } from a module is erased at compile (isolatedModules on), so the consumer gains NO runtime dependency on that module. This keeps the module runtime imports (e.g. Node crypto in lib/prospects.ts) out of every downstream bundle - critical for server components like /admin. A plain value import would drag the whole module in. Verified g-010-13: lib/pipeline.ts imports only { type Variant } from prospects.ts; the build kept /admin dynamic with no bundle bloat.
original.when_to_use: When a lib/ module references another module TYPE only, especially when the referenced module has node-only runtime imports (crypto, fs) and the consumer feeds a server/SSG component. Use import { type X }, not import { X }.

generalized.context: When a library module references another module for type definitions only, especially when the referenced module contains Node.js-only runtime imports (e.g., crypto, fs) and the consumer is a server-side or static site component.
approach: Use a type-only import syntax (e.g., import { type X } from 'module') instead of a value import
Ensure the build configuration supports isolated modules to erase type imports at compile time
Verify that the downstream bundle excludes the referenced module's runtime code
generalized.outcome: The consumer gains no runtime dependency on the referenced module, preventing Node.js-specific code from being bundled into server-side or static assets.
generalized.lesson: When a library module references another module for type definitions only, use a type-only import syntax (import { type X }) rather than a value import. This ensures the build system erases the import at compile time, keeping Node.js-only runtime dependencies (like crypto or fs) out of server-side or static site bundles and preventing unnecessary bloat.

original.title: Gotcha: deep-goal state-update auto-backgrounds; on re-entry verify via side effects, do not re-run
original.content: On Windows/OneDrive, iteration-close.sh --phase state-update for a DEEP goal runs a git iteration-commit slow enough that the harness auto-backgrounds the Bash call. If the turn then ends, the stop hook fires and re-enters the loop. On re-entry DO NOT re-run state-update - verify completion via SIDE EFFECTS: loop_state.goals_completed advanced (wm-read.sh loop_state) AND the git iteration-commit landed (git log). Re-running risks a concurrent git + loop_state race. Confirmed g-010-13: the empty background-output file was a read-timing artifact; counter=28 + commit 3bd5950 proved completion before any re-run.
original.when_to_use: On loop re-entry after a deep-goal state-update auto-backgrounded and the turn ended; before deciding whether to re-run any iteration-close phase.

generalized.context: When a long-running shell script (e.g., state-update) initiated for a deep goal is auto-backgrounded by the OS due to execution time, and the process re-enters after the turn ends.
approach: Verify completion via side effects rather than re-executing the script: check if the loop state counter advanced (e.g., goals_completed) and confirm the git commit landed (git log).
Do not re-run the iteration-close phase if these side effects confirm success.
Avoid re-running to prevent a race condition between the concurrent background process and the new loop iteration.
generalized.outcome: Confirmed completion via side effects (counter increment and commit hash) without triggering a race condition or redundant work.
generalized.lesson: When a long-running backgrounded script is interrupted by a turn boundary and re-entry occurs, never re-run the script. Instead, verify completion by checking side effects (state variable updates and commit logs). Re-running risks race conditions between the background process and the new iteration.

original.title: RSC: a server component cannot pass a function prop to a client child -- push client behavior into a thin client boundary
original.content: In Next.js App Router a server component (e.g. app/p/[token]/page.tsx) CANNOT pass a function prop (onClick, onActivate) to a client component -- RSC forbids function props across the server->client boundary. When a server component must attach client behavior (a handler, a beacon) to a SHARED client component: do NOT promote the whole page to a client component (forfeits SSG/pre-render), and do NOT fork the shared component. Instead introduce a thin client component that owns the client behavior AND renders the shared component, so the function prop is passed entirely client-side. Mechanism for extending the shared component without a fork: add a backward-compatible OPTIONAL callback prop (onActivate?: () => void) called inside the existing handler -- existing callers omit it (no-op), so the prior test suite stays green unchanged. Verified g-010-04: ProspectTracker (client) wraps ContactCTA (client) and fires visit/reply beacons while page.tsx stays a server component (SSG preserved); 29/29 vitest green, next build 0, 20 prior CTA tests unchanged.
original.when_to_use: a Next.js server component needs to attach a click handler or beacon to a shared client component; server component passing a function prop to a client child; add client behavior to a shared component without forfeiting SSG or forking it; go-to-market

generalized.context: When a server-side component must attach a client-side event handler or behavior to a shared client component without promoting the entire page to a client component (which would forfeit static generation or pre-rendering).
approach: Identify that passing function props directly from the server component to the shared client child is forbidden by the framework's server-client boundary rules.
Create a thin client wrapper component that owns the client behavior and renders the shared component as a child.
Extend the shared component with a backward-compatible optional callback prop (e.g., onActivate?: () => void) that the wrapper passes through.
Ensure existing callers of the shared component omit this optional prop, keeping their tests green and avoiding code forks.
generalized.outcome: The server component retains its static generation benefits while the thin client wrapper successfully fires client-side events; all existing tests remain passing without requiring code forks.
generalized.lesson: When a server component needs to attach client behavior to a shared client component, do not promote the whole page to a client component and do not fork the shared component. Instead, introduce a thin client wrapper that owns the behavior and renders the shared component. Extend the shared component with an optional callback prop to pass the handler through; existing callers omit this prop, preserving backward compatibility and test stability.
