Lesson: banner scope (vocabulary) != decision scope (vocab + architecture + cross-doc). Audit every implication axis of a decision change via a multi-lens classifying sweep, not a keyword grep.
original.when_to_use: After a decision/naming/architecture change is propagated through multiple documents and you must confirm zero contradictions remain -- especially when a transitional-mapping banner is in play, since the banner creates false confidence that the docs are fully clean.

generalized.context: When propagating a decision change through multiple strategy or technical documents, especially when a transitional-mapping banner (e.g., 'wherever X, read Y') is used to cover vocabulary substitutions.
approach: Recognize that a transitional banner only covers vocabulary substitutions and does not cover architecture, topology, or semantic assertions.
Execute a multi-lens adversarial sweep across all decision axes (noun, tiers, version-invariant, topology, core-diff, cross-doc, completeness) instead of relying on keyword grep.
Classify findings into 'real-contradiction' versus 'by-design-transitional' for each axis.
generalized.outcome: Detected semantic contradictions (e.g., conflicting infrastructure topology assertions) that were invisible to keyword grep and falsely assumed clean by the banner.
generalized.lesson: A transitional-mapping banner covers vocabulary substitutions only; it does not cover architecture, topology, or semantic assertions. Relying on keyword grep or banners creates false confidence. To ensure zero contradictions after a decision change, audit every implication axis via a multi-lens adversarial sweep that classifies real contradictions against by-design transitions.

original.title: A goal description premise can be wrong - verify the data before a reconcile/delete instruction
original.content: g-012-36 was auto-filed from website error reports as: reconcile orphaned send doe-osdbu-intro-1 because prospect doe-osdbu-2026-06-02 is missing. A DynamoDB get-item BEFORE any delete showed the prospect EXISTS in DDB - never orphaned. The real bug was code: dispatchApprovedSend resolved prospects via the in-memory PROSPECTS seed only, with no DynamoDB fallback (unlike the approvals page, which already merges fetchProspects). A runner-drafted DDB-only prospect therefore resolved on the page but threw on Approve-and-Send, crashing the route. Executing the literal goal instruction (delete the orphan) would have destroyed a valid drafted outreach to a real prospect. The data probe was signal-2 that falsified the goal premise and redirected the fix from data-deletion to a code DDB-fallback.
original.when_to_use: Any goal whose instruction is delete/reconcile/clean-up based on a missing-X or orphaned-Y premise - especially goals auto-filed from an error report or alert (the report names a symptom, not a verified root cause). Verify X/Y is actually missing via a single-item store read BEFORE any destructive action. The premise in the goal description is a hypothesis, not ground truth.

generalized.context: When a system receives an instruction to delete, reconcile, or clean up an entity based on a premise that it is missing or orphaned, especially if the instruction was auto-generated from an error report.
approach: Treat the missing/orphaned premise in the goal description as a hypothesis, not ground truth.
Execute a single-item store read (e.g., DynamoDB get-item) to verify the entity's actual existence before performing any destructive action.

If the entity exists, pivot the investigation from data deletion to code logic, checking if the resolution path relies on an incomplete data source (e.g., in-memory cache) rather than the persistent store.
Redirect the fix to implement a fallback mechanism (e.g., merging cache with store) instead of deleting valid data.
generalized.outcome: Prevented the destruction of a valid drafted outreach to a real prospect by identifying that the entity existed but was not being resolved by the current code path.
generalized.lesson: When a goal instruction mandates a destructive action (delete/reconcile) based on a 'missing' or 'orphaned' premise, verify the entity's existence via a direct store read before acting. The goal description is often a hypothesis derived from a symptom, not ground truth. If the entity exists, the root cause is likely a code logic gap (e.g., resolving from an in-memory cache without a persistent store fallback) rather than data corruption. Redirect the fix to address the code gap instead of deleting valid data.

original.title: Diagnosing a DMARC/email-auth report: read rua= first, then SPF/DKIM/MX, cross-check a 2nd resolver
original.content: To answer 'what is this email-auth report / why am I getting it' for any domain: (1) dig _dmarc.<domain> TXT and read the rua= address -- if it is the asker's own inbox, that IS why they receive the report (DMARC reports route to the rua= destination). (2) Read p= to know if anything is enforced (none=monitor-only, nothing blocked; quarantine/reject=enforced). (3) dig <domain> apex TXT for SPF (v=spf1); no TXT at apex = no SPF = mail claiming From:<domain> gets SPF 'none'. (4) dig <selector>._domainkey.<domain> for DKIM (google._domainkey for Workspace). (5) dig MX to see receive-config (inbound-smtp.<region>.amazonaws.com = AWS SES inbound). (6) Cross-check any 'none' against a 2nd independent resolver (e.g. 8.8.8.8) before asserting it. Then map: send-configured (SPF+DKIM present) vs receive-only/monitor-only. Tighten p=none->quarantine->reject ONLY after SPF+DKIM exist, else legit mail risks failing.
original.when_to_use: Any DMARC aggregate-report, SPF/DKIM, or email-deliverability question about a ZDS product domain

generalized.context: When analyzing an email authentication report (DMARC aggregate report) to determine why a domain is generating reports or failing authentication checks.
approach: Query the domain's _dmarc TXT record to read the 'rua=' address and confirm if the report destination matches the observer's inbox.
Read the 'p=' policy tag to determine enforcement level (none=monitor-only vs quarantine/reject=enforced).
Query the domain apex TXT record for SPF (v=spf1) and note that a missing record results in an implicit 'none' result.
Query the specific selector._domainkey TXT record to verify DKIM signatures are configured.
Query the MX record to identify the inbound mail server configuration.
Cross-check any 'none' results against a second independent DNS resolver before concluding the configuration is missing.
generalized.outcome: Mapped the current state to 'send-configured' (SPF+DKIM present) versus 'receive-only/monitor-only', preventing premature policy tightening.
generalized.lesson: To diagnose email authentication reports, first verify the DMARC 'rua=' address explains the report receipt. Then, systematically check the apex TXT for SPF and the selector TXT for DKIM; note that a missing apex TXT record defaults to an SPF 'none' result. Only tighten the DMARC policy from 'none' to 'quarantine' or 'reject' after confirming both SPF and DKIM are explicitly configured, otherwise legitimate mail risks failing authentication. Always cross-check ambiguous 'none' results with a second independent resolver to avoid false negatives.

original.title: Single-file semantic migration: per-site change/keep classification + a mandatory adversarial verify stage
original.content: For a vocab/semantic doc migration (e.g. propagating a locked naming model through a body), structure it as discover -> classify -> apply -> verify, NOT a blanket find-replace. The per-site CHANGE/KEEP classification is what prevents over-reach: in the g-016-32 pearl propagation (2026-06-04, wf_f866c7f3) it correctly changed consumer-unit world->environment and Open/Shared/Vault->public/selective/private while KEEPING the grouping/cross-world world sense, the claude-mind vault METAPHOR, and dated historical/changelog entries (overreach_count=0). Critically, the adversarial VERIFY stage is NOT optional even when the apply looks clean: it found 2 real misses the single-writer apply left behind (old_vocab_remaining=2: a World-Contract sentence equating world with a single environment, and a SHARED build-step label) that a human eyeball + the apply agent both missed. A single file cannot be parallel-edited (Edit races), so use ONE writer for apply but keep discover/verify parallel and adversarial. Skipping verify on a simple propagation would have shipped the 2 misses.
original.when_to_use: Migrating vocabulary, renames, or semantic changes through one or more documents after a decision lands -- especially when some instances of the old term must be PRESERVED (grouping sense, metaphor, historical record). Classify per-site; always run an adversarial verify even if the apply looks complete.

generalized.context: When migrating vocabulary, renaming terms, or applying semantic changes across documents where some instances of the old term must be preserved (e.g., historical records, metaphors, or specific grouping contexts).
approach: Structure the migration as a four-stage pipeline: discover -> classify -> apply -> verify, avoiding a blanket find-replace operation.
Perform per-site classification to explicitly mark each instance as CHANGE or KEEP based on context (e.g., distinguishing a literal term from a metaphor or historical entry).
Execute the apply stage using a single writer agent to prevent edit races and ensure consistency.
Run a mandatory adversarial verify stage where the verification logic actively attempts to find missed instances, even if the apply stage appears complete.
generalized.outcome: Prevented over-reach by catching 2 real misses (a World-Contract sentence equating a term with a single environment and a SHARED build-step label) that a standard apply or human review had overlooked.
generalized.lesson: For semantic migrations where context matters, never use a blanket find-replace. Instead, classify every instance as CHANGE or KEEP to preserve necessary historical or metaphorical usage. Crucially, always run an adversarial verify stage that actively hunts for missed instances; skipping this verification on simple propagations risks shipping errors that standard application logic or human eyeballing will miss.

original.title: Sutton 'Toward Enactive AI' - top-prestige citation for the continual-learning pitch + the ayoai pattern-break differentiator
original.content: Rafiee & Sutton (2026, arXiv 2605.24238 'Toward Enactive AI') supplies three reusable positioning assets. (1) The Big World Hypothesis ('the world is orders of magnitude larger than the agent and thus is perceived as ever-changing') is the deepest, most authoritative WHY behind continual learning - stronger than the a16z essay because it is Sutton, the RL pioneer, himself. Use in Lodestar / continual-learning positioning. (2) The paper's sharpest LLM critique - LLMs 'are not able to evaluate their own outputs without outsourcing evaluation to external signals' - NAMES the exact gap our verification / learning-gate / hypothesis-resolution architecture fills. Position Mind as the self-evaluation scaffold LLMs lack. (3) Differentiator line for ayoai: 'a generative model continues a pattern, whereas an enactive agent decides what to do next when the pattern breaks.' That is the gap between a chatbot and ayoai's perceive-act loop - a clean investor/prospect line. Full alignment scorecard in tree node enactive-ai-sutton.

generalized.context: When positioning a system that moves beyond static generative responses to dynamic, self-evaluating action loops.
approach: Cite the 'Big World Hypothesis' (the environment is orders of magnitude larger than the agent, making it perpetually changing) as the authoritative theoretical foundation for continual learning.
Highlight the critique that standard generative models cannot evaluate their own outputs without external signals, positioning the system as the necessary self-evaluation scaffold.
Use the differentiator that a generative model merely continues a pattern, whereas an enactive agent decides the next action specifically when the pattern breaks.
generalized.outcome: Establishes a high-authority theoretical basis for continual learning and clearly distinguishes the system's active decision-making capability from passive pattern completion.
generalized.lesson: To differentiate a dynamic agent from a static chatbot, leverage the 'Big World Hypothesis' to argue that the environment is too vast and changing for static models. Explicitly state that standard generative models lack the ability to self-evaluate their outputs without external signals, creating a gap that your system fills by acting as a self-evaluation scaffold. Finally, define the core differentiator: a generative model continues an existing pattern, while an enactive agent actively decides what to do next specifically when that pattern breaks.

original.title: 'The world is its own best model' (Sutton enactive-AI) - weight live re-perception over the internal knowledge tree
original.content: Sutton & Rafiee's enactive-AI thesis (arXiv 2605.24238) carries a standing design pressure for any Claude-Mind-style agent: 'the world is its own best model' - no internal surrogate captures the world's inexhaustible richness. Our knowledge tree IS such a surrogate. We already partially honor the imperative via the retrieval-escalation ladder (tree -> codebase -> web search), which prefers the live source when the internal model is thin. The enactive lesson: keep raising the weight of live re-perception (escalation tiers 2-3) relative to the compressed tree, and treat 'consult the tree first' as a reflex to interrogate rather than a default to trust. A more enactive Mind re-perceives the world instead of leaning on its memory of it. Actionable follow-up (not yet done): turn this into a concrete retrieval-weighting change.

generalized.context: When designing an agentic system that relies on an internal knowledge base (e.g., a reasoning bank or knowledge tree) alongside live external data sources (e.g., codebase, web search, or API endpoints)
approach: Acknowledge that the internal knowledge base is a compressed surrogate that cannot capture the world's full richness
Implement a retrieval-escalation ladder that prioritizes live sources over internal memory when the internal model is thin
Increase the weighting of live re-perception (escalation tiers 2-3) relative to the compressed internal store
Reframe 'consult the tree first' as a reflex to interrogate the internal model's validity rather than a default to trust it
generalized.outcome: The system shifts from relying on static memory to actively re-perceiving the current state of the environment, reducing hallucinations caused by outdated or incomplete internal models.
generalized.lesson: Treat the internal knowledge base as a fallible surrogate rather than ground truth. Because no internal model can capture the world's inexhaustible richness, the system must actively raise the weight of live re-perception (escalation tiers 2-3) relative to the compressed tree. Do not default to trusting the internal store; instead, use it as a starting point to interrogate, then immediately escalate to live sources when the internal representation is thin.

original.title: Verify framework-code claims against the FRONTIER repo, not a downstream deployments CLAUDE.md
original.content: When verifying a claim about framework env-vars/scripts during a multi-deployment migration, the authoritative source is the frontier repos OWN docs and code - not a downstream deployments CLAUDE.md, which lags. Near-miss 2026-06-05: alpha classified MIND_AGENT as zero production reads. ZDS-Mind CLAUDE.md states MIND_AGENT is the ONLY mechanism for agent resolution - a direct contradiction that nearly made omni distrust a correct finding. Grep of the frontier (Ayoai-Mind) showed it already moved agent/world/meta resolution to MIND_* (bash-agent-inject.py, _paths.py); MIND_AGENT is a vestigial cross-deploy test alias there. Both docs were true for their own repo; the downstream CLAUDE.md was simply un-migrated.
original.when_to_use: Verifying a claim about framework code/env-vars when frontier and downstream deployments are mid-migration and may diverge

generalized.context: When verifying claims about framework environment variables or scripts during a multi-deployment migration where upstream and downstream repositories may diverge.
approach: Identify the authoritative source as the upstream framework repository's own documentation and codebase.
Avoid relying on downstream deployment documentation (e.g., local CLAUDE.md files) which may lag behind upstream changes.
Cross-reference specific mechanism names (e.g., agent resolution logic) against the upstream code to detect if they are vestigial or have been renamed.
Recognize that documentation in both upstream and downstream repos may be technically correct for their respective contexts, but the downstream doc may simply be un-migrated.
generalized.outcome: Prevented a false negative where a downstream documentation file incorrectly claimed a mechanism was the sole resolver, while the upstream code had already migrated to a new implementation.
generalized.lesson: During multi-deployment migrations, always verify claims about framework code or environment variables against the upstream repository's authoritative documentation and code, not downstream deployment guides. Downstream docs often lag and may describe legacy mechanisms as current, leading to false contradictions. If a downstream doc claims a specific mechanism is the only one, grep the upstream code to check if that mechanism has been renamed or replaced; both docs might be 'true' for their specific scope, but the downstream one is simply outdated.

original.title: Exact-var allowlist beats prefix-widening for a credential-adjacent env filter
original.content: When de-overloading an env-var prefix that doubles as a credential allowlist, enumerate the exact known var names rather than broadening the prefix tuple. Prefix-widening (startswith of several new prefixes) re-opens a collision/leak surface: any host/CI var with common prefixes (STORAGE_, RUNTIME_, ENVIRONMENT_) could load. An exact frozenset of the ~12 known vars is strictly safer (zero leak, zero future collision) at negligible maintenance cost, AND it completed the N3 de-overload cleanly - collapsing MIND_ to credentials-only (startswith MIND_AWS_), matching the design intent that the MIND_ prefix IS the security filter. Verified in mind_api/src/__main__.py _N3_ALLOWED_EXACT, 2026-06-05.
original.when_to_use: Designing or reviewing an env-var allowlist filter, especially one that gates credentials

generalized.context: When designing or reviewing an environment variable allowlist filter that also serves as a credential gate, specifically when de-overloading a prefix that previously mixed credentials with other data.
approach: Enumerate the exact set of known variable names rather than broadening the prefix tuple (e.g., using a frozenset of specific names instead of startswith checks for multiple prefixes)
Avoid prefix-widening strategies that could inadvertently include common host or CI variable prefixes (like STORAGE_, RUNTIME_, ENVIRONMENT_)
Ensure the filter strictly matches only the intended security scope to prevent future collisions or data leaks
generalized.outcome: Achieved a zero-leak, zero-future-collision security posture with negligible maintenance cost, while cleanly separating credential logic from general environment data.
generalized.lesson: When an environment variable filter doubles as a credential allowlist, an exact enumeration of known variable names is strictly safer than prefix-widening. Broadening prefixes (e.g., using startswith on common categories like STORAGE_ or RUNTIME_) re-opens a collision surface where legitimate host or CI variables could be incorrectly loaded as credentials. An exact set provides a hard security boundary that prevents future leaks without increasing maintenance overhead.

original.title: The first real cut through new release/migration tooling is itself a test - it exercises write-paths dry-runs miss
original.content: Dry-runs and unit tests of new release rails exercise the happy read-path but often skip the real write-path; the first genuine cut surfaces latent bugs there. Canonical 2026-06-05 (v1.0.0 N3 cut): the cut exposed _release_lib.rollback_path_for using str(Path()) which emits Windows backslashes - a POSIX downstream would read the rollback path as one literal filename and fail validation. All prior dry-runs missed it; the real cut caught it (fixed with .as_posix() + regression test). Budget for a first-cut shakedown and treat the first real release through new tooling as a verification event, not a formality.
original.when_to_use: Cutting the first real release/migration through newly-built tooling

generalized.context: When deploying the first genuine release or migration through newly built tooling, where dry-runs and unit tests have only exercised the happy read-path.
approach: Recognize that dry-runs often skip the actual write-path execution required for real deployments
Treat the first real cut through the new tooling as a critical verification event rather than a formality
Expect latent bugs in write-path logic (e.g., path formatting, file locking, state mutation) to surface only during this first execution
generalized.outcome: Latent bugs in the write-path are exposed that were invisible to dry-runs and unit tests, allowing for immediate detection and correction before broader rollout.
generalized.lesson: Dry-runs and unit tests of new release tooling often validate the happy read-path but miss the real write-path; the first genuine cut is the only event that exercises the actual write logic. Budget for a first-cut shakedown and treat the first real release through new tooling as a verification event, not a formality, because it is the only time latent bugs in write-path operations (such as path serialization or state mutation) will surface.

original.title: Defer a plan-docs field guess to the implementer once the field gains a precise, validated meaning
original.content: A forward-plan written before the machinery exists may guess a typed fields value loosely; once the field is implemented with a precise validated meaning, the implementers reading wins - reconcile the plan doc to match. Canonical 2026-06-05: the pearl said the naming release should be cross_world true (loose sense: flows through the promotion chain). The built rails define cross_world true to MECHANICALLY require world/meta snapshot+restore markers in the recipe; N3 migrates env-keys + code, not world/meta data, so true would HARD-FAIL validation. alpha set false; omni verified against _release_lib.py and corrected the pearl. Cross-world PROPAGATION is handled by the promotion chain - a separate mechanism from the cross_world recipe flag.
original.when_to_use: A plan documents value for a typed/validated field conflicts with what the implemented system enforces

generalized.context: When a forward-looking plan document specifies a loose or guessed value for a typed field that conflicts with the strict validation rules enforced by the implemented system.
approach: Identify the precise, validated meaning enforced by the current implementation (e.g., specific markers required for cross-environment propagation).
Verify that the plan's loose interpretation would cause a hard failure against these implementation constraints.
Reconcile the plan document to match the implementation's strict requirements rather than forcing the implementation to match the plan.
generalized.outcome: The plan document was corrected to reflect the actual mechanical constraints of the system, preventing future validation failures.
generalized.lesson: When a plan document contains a loose guess for a typed field that conflicts with the strict validation logic of the implemented system, the implementation's constraints take precedence. Do not force the implementation to accommodate the plan's ambiguity; instead, update the plan to match the precise, validated behavior enforced by the code.

original.title: Migration scope is gated by the target deployment backend, not by the migration existing at the frontier
original.content: During the N4 own-cloud AWS-resource rename review (Ayoai-Mind v2.0.0), the assumption that the migration would seed to every downstream deployment was tested against the live target before being accepted. zds-mind runs the LOCAL storage backend, verified two independent ways on 2026-06-05: .env.example carries zero own-cloud keys (only SES email + a mail-capture bucket); mind_api/src has zero lodestar / STORAGE_BACKEND / own-cloud references; and __main__.py:179 defaults STORAGE_BACKEND to local. Because N4 only renames own-cloud lodestar-* resources, it is a complete no-op for zds-mind (the recipe FROM-state guard finds no lodestar-data bucket and exits inert), which saved the entire N4 seed-down work-stream. LESSON: a framework migration scope is gated by the TARGET deployment backend and config, not by the migration existing at the frontier. Before assuming a release applies downstream, read the target live config (env + daemon source) and confirm the migration FROM-state actually exists there. Same meta-pattern as rb-150 (verify scope against live source before gating) and verify-before-assuming.md.
original.when_to_use: When assessing whether a framework migration or release applies to a given deployment, or scoping any cross-deployment change. Check the target backend/config before assuming the change is in scope.

generalized.context: When assessing whether a framework migration or release applies to a specific deployment, or scoping any cross-deployment change.
approach: Read the target live configuration (environment variables and daemon source code) to identify the active backend.
Verify that the migration's 'FROM-state' (e.g., specific resource names or bucket references) actually exists in that target configuration.
Confirm that the migration logic will execute or exit inertly based on the presence or absence of those specific resources.
generalized.outcome: Identified that the migration was a complete no-op for the target deployment because the required source resources did not exist in its local configuration, saving the entire seed-down work-stream.
generalized.lesson: A framework migration scope is gated by the TARGET deployment backend and configuration, not by the migration existing at the frontier. Before assuming a release applies downstream, read the target live config (env + daemon source) and confirm the migration FROM-state actually exists there. Do not assume a migration affects a deployment just because the migration code exists; verify the specific resources it targets are present in that deployment's environment.

original.title: S3 bucket-name global-namespace collision; provision-bucket-first ordering enabled a clean abort
original.content: N4 (Ayoai-Mind v2.0.0 own-cloud rename) aborted SAFE at the first AWS call: create_bucket(zds-data) returned BucketAlreadyExists - S3 bucket names are unique across ALL accounts and zds-data was owned by a third party (lodestar-data only worked because it was claimed first). TWO lessons. (1) NAMING: a brand-prefixed name is not guaranteed free in a global namespace; probe with head-bucket before committing it in a recipe (see the S3-naming guardrail). Resolved name: zds-own-cloud-data (env-agnostic, to preserve the shared-bucket env-id-key-prefix topology; DDB tables zds-locks/zds-sessions are account-scoped so they did not collide). (2) DESIGN: the recipe ran provision_bucket BEFORE provision_tables/provision_user and BEFORE any state flip, and the H3b snapshot ran before any AWS mutation. So the most-collision-prone op ran first and the failure aborted with ZERO partial state: no zds- resources created, .env.local never flipped, lodestar-data untouched. REUSABLE: in a destructive or move-all-state migration, order the highest-failure-risk operation first (global-namespace creates, capacity checks) so failures abort cheaply, and snapshot before the first mutation.
original.when_to_use: Designing or reviewing a migration/provisioning recipe that creates global-namespace resources or moves live state.

generalized.context: When designing or reviewing a migration or provisioning recipe that creates global-namespace resources (like unique bucket names) or moves live state.
approach: Probe for resource existence (e.g., head-bucket) before committing to a creation operation in the recipe.
Order the highest-failure-risk operations (global-namespace creates, capacity checks) to run first in the sequence.
Execute a snapshot before the first mutation occurs.
Ensure the recipe aborts cleanly if the first operation fails, preventing partial state updates.
generalized.outcome: The failure aborted at the first AWS call with zero partial state created; no downstream resources were provisioned, and the environment configuration remained untouched.
generalized.lesson: In destructive or state-moving migrations, order the highest-failure-risk operations (such as creating unique global-namespace resources) to run first. Because these operations are prone to collisions or external conflicts, running them first ensures that any failure aborts the entire process cheaply, preventing partial state updates and leaving the system in a clean, unmodified state.

original.title: Do not push a release tag until the state it describes exists; an unpushed tag re-cuts cleanly
original.content: On N4 the recommendation was to HOLD the v2.0.0 push until the live migration proved healthy, not publish first. That paid off twice. (1) When the migration aborted on the bucket-name collision, v2.0.0 (unpushed, never deployed) could be cleanly RE-CUT: delete the local tag, fix the bucket constant + IAM ARN, re-cut - no lineage to preserve, because nothing had consumed it. A pushed tag could not have been re-cut this cleanly (others may have pulled; published history would describe a state that never materialized). (2) A v2.0.1 patch was rejected in favor of re-cut precisely because an unpushed or never-deployed tag is not yet a real release. PRINCIPLE: publish a release tag only when the thing it describes actually exists; until pushed a tag is amendable, so prefer re-cut over patch for an unpushed tag.
original.when_to_use: Deciding whether to push a release tag before a live migration, or whether to re-cut vs patch an unpushed tag.

generalized.context: When deciding whether to push a release tag before a live migration or infrastructure change, or when determining whether to re-cut versus patch an unpushed tag.
approach: Hold the release tag push until the live migration or state change proves healthy
If a migration fails (e.g., due to configuration collisions), delete the local unpushed tag and re-cut with the corrected configuration
Reject the idea of patching an unpushed tag in favor of re-cutting, as the tag does not yet represent a deployed state
generalized.outcome: Avoided preserving lineage to a state that never materialized and enabled clean re-cuts without affecting other consumers
generalized.lesson: A release tag should only be pushed when the state it describes actually exists in the live environment. Until a tag is pushed, it is not a real release and can be safely deleted and re-cut to fix issues. If a tag is pushed before a migration succeeds, re-cutting becomes difficult because other systems may have pulled it, and the published history would describe a state that never materialized. Therefore, prefer re-cutting over patching for unpushed tags.

original.title: Verify whether a writer is daemon-owned or agent-owned before specifying a quiesce method
original.content: My N4 Gate-3 runbook said to quiesce own-cloud writes by stopping the agent loops. That was mechanism-wrong: the own-cloud mirror sweep is a DAEMON-owned background thread (mind_api/src/__main__.py ~170-230, name owncloud-sync) that pushes local->S3 every ~120s on its own timer, regardless of whether any agent loop is active. Stopping the agents does NOT quiesce it. The designed switch is OWNCLOUD_SYNC_DISABLE=1 + daemon restart (early-returns before the thread starts at __main__.py:181-185; HTTP server stays up; key is in _N3_ALLOWED_EXACT). LESSON: before assuming a quiesce method works, identify the owner and lifecycle of the writer (daemon thread vs agent loop vs cron). A quiesce aimed at the wrong owner leaves the real writer running - here that would have lost any write landing in the copy->flip window. Caught by alpha firsthand + a 3-lens panel, then confirmed by my own firsthand read of the frontier source.
original.when_to_use: Planning to quiesce writes before a migration or maintenance window - identify the writer owner and lifecycle before choosing the stop method.

generalized.context: When planning to quiesce writes before a migration or maintenance window, verify whether the writer is owned by a daemon thread, an agent loop, or a cron job.
approach: Identify the specific owner and lifecycle of the writer process (daemon thread vs. agent loop vs. scheduled task)
Check the source code or configuration for the initialization logic to confirm if the writer starts independently of the main application loop

Apply the correct quiesce mechanism: stop the specific owner (e.g., disable the daemon flag or restart the service) rather than stopping unrelated components (e.g., agent loops) that do not control the writer
generalized.outcome: Ensured the actual writer process was stopped, preventing data loss during the copy-to-flip window.
generalized.lesson: Before assuming a quiesce method works, identify the owner and lifecycle of the writer. A quiesce aimed at the wrong owner (e.g., stopping an agent loop when the writer is a background daemon thread) leaves the real writer running, causing data loss during the write window. Always verify the initialization logic to ensure the stop mechanism targets the correct process.

original.title: Coordination cadence: checkpoint on irreversibility, not on wave or iteration count
original.content: Through the multi-day N3/N4 refactor as the review and coordination hub, the cadence that worked: run free and BATCH on reversible, test-gated work (verify a recipe, draft a convention, encode), and STOP to checkpoint with the principal only at genuine boundaries - (a) a breaking-release sign-off, (b) a deploy/push/public/secrets/live-infra action, (c) genuine ambiguity needing a human or brand decision. Do NOT checkpoint merely because N waves or iterations elapsed. This kept the partner agent working long stretches between human gates while still putting a human hand on every irreversible step (Gate 3 live AWS, the bucket name, the push). REUSABLE: the right granularity for human-in-the-loop is the IRREVERSIBILITY boundary, not a fixed wave count - widen batches between gates, narrow to a stop at each irreversible, outward, or ambiguous step.
original.when_to_use: Pacing a multi-step collaboration with a human or partner agent - decide where to checkpoint by irreversibility, not elapsed waves.

generalized.context: When pacing a multi-step collaboration with a human or partner agent across a complex workflow involving code refactoring, configuration changes, or infrastructure updates.
approach: Run free and batch reversible, test-gated work (verifying recipes, drafting conventions, encoding logic) without interruption.

Stop and checkpoint with the principal only at genuine boundaries: breaking-release sign-offs, deploy/push/public/secrets/live-infrastructure actions, or genuine ambiguity requiring human/brand decisions.
Do not checkpoint merely because a fixed number of waves or iterations have elapsed.
generalized.outcome: Kept the partner agent working long stretches between human gates while ensuring a human hand verified every irreversible step.
generalized.lesson: The right granularity for human-in-the-loop is the IRREVERSIBILITY boundary, not a fixed wave count. Widen batches between gates to maximize throughput, but narrow to a stop at each irreversible, outward-facing, or ambiguous step to ensure proper decision authority.

original.title: Tenant isolation is per-customer (separate buckets), not env-id-prefix-in-shared-bucket
original.content: Principal directive 2026-06-06: different customers must NOT share AWS buckets (all of ayoai-mind should not share buckets with all of zds-mind). This REVISES the prior shared-bucket-with-env-id-key-prefix model (Gate-2 topology rb-189; roadmap Step 3.1 partition-prefix + IAM-fence). Decided model: within the single shared AWS account (accounts not split, locked 2026-06-04), each CUSTOMER gets its own bucket + per-customer IAM fence; environmentId is a key-prefix WITHIN a customer bucket. Levels: customer (owner/account-of-record) -> bucket; environment (environmentId) -> key-prefix; agent -> within an environment. N4 is undisturbed: zds-own-cloud-data is grandfathered as the ayoai-mind (first own-cloud customer) bucket; customer 2 gets its own bucket under the same convention, no immediate rename. Rationale: tenant isolation + the privacy-first product positioning; key-prefix isolation in a shared bucket is weaker than bucket-level IAM isolation for distinct customers. Cross-ref: company-strategy.md Environment Profiles section, daemon-architecture node, rb-189.
original.when_to_use: Designing multi-tenant storage isolation, naming customer buckets, or refining the per-world isolation step (roadmap 3.1).

generalized.context: When designing multi-tenant storage isolation within a single cloud account where distinct customers must not share data.
approach: Assign a dedicated storage bucket to each customer rather than using a shared bucket with environment-specific key prefixes.
Implement per-customer IAM fences to enforce strict access boundaries at the bucket level.
Use the environment ID only as a key prefix within the customer's dedicated bucket to organize data.
Grandfather existing customer data under the new convention without immediate renaming to ensure continuity.
generalized.outcome: Achieved stronger tenant isolation and privacy compliance by elevating the isolation boundary from key-prefix to bucket-level IAM enforcement.
generalized.lesson: For multi-tenant systems requiring strict privacy or regulatory isolation, do not rely solely on key-prefix separation within a shared bucket. Instead, assign a dedicated bucket to each customer and enforce access via per-customer IAM policies. Key-prefix isolation is insufficient for distinct customers because it relies on application logic to prevent leakage, whereas bucket-level IAM isolation provides a stronger, infrastructure-enforced boundary.

original.title: Generalization proving-experiment: structural PASS is necessary not sufficient (utility metric is a proxy)
original.content: Ran Lodestar proving-experiment.test.ts firsthand 2026-06-06 (70 traces: zds-mind 18, ayoai-mind 50, zds-parent 2). v1 CoarseInducer drops k-aggregation quarantine 88.6%->8.6% while holding median structural utility 0.567 (>=0.4): VERDICT PASS, conclusive (>=50 patterns). The quarantine-everything problem (R11) is solved. BUT scorePatternUtility is a STRUCTURAL heuristic (steps/tools/roles/cross-source), not retrieval demand -- the test file states a real score would use downstream feedback. Emitted patterns are structural shells: top is a 17-step interaction (system, user, assistant) attested across 39 sources, structurally rich yet semantically generic -- the exact zero-commercial-value shape the single-biggest-risk warns of. Lesson: a structural PASS is necessary but not sufficient. The selective tier is NOT proven until a downstream-relevance metric (held-out cross-world query match, 0..1, median) also passes. That ~1-2 day metric is the genuine hardening, not the experiment itself (which already exists and runs).
original.when_to_use: When interpreting a generalization-engine proving-experiment PASS, or assessing whether the selective tier is commercially viable. A structural-utility PASS clears the privacy-gate/quarantine hurdle but not retrieval demand.

generalized.context: When interpreting a proving experiment for a generalization engine where a structural utility metric passes but the metric relies on static analysis rather than downstream feedback.
approach: Verify that the structural utility score (based on steps, tools, and roles) meets the threshold to clear privacy or quarantine gates
Recognize that the passing structural score only confirms the existence of a valid interaction shell, not its commercial relevance
Identify that the emitted patterns may be semantically generic despite being structurally rich (e.g., a 17-step system-user-assistant flow)
Execute a downstream-relevance metric (such as held-out cross-world query match) to validate actual retrieval demand
generalized.outcome: The structural PASS cleared the quarantine hurdle but revealed that the generated patterns were 'shells' with zero commercial value until validated by a real-world relevance metric.
generalized.lesson: A structural PASS in a proving experiment is necessary but not sufficient for commercial viability. Because structural metrics (steps/tools/roles) are heuristics and not proxies for retrieval demand, a passing score only confirms the existence of a valid interaction shell. The selective tier is not proven until a downstream-relevance metric (e.g., held-out cross-world query match) also passes, as this is the only way to verify that the patterns meet actual user needs rather than just satisfying a privacy gate.

original.title: Verify the tool, do not trust its error message (cross-agent lesson from alpha N4)
original.content: From alpha N4 frontier-migration handoff: the promote-to-upstream script gh-detection had a PATH bug and reported gh not installed when gh WAS installed. Alpha trusted the error message and handed user manual PR steps he did not need. Lesson: when a tool reports a capability missing or an operation impossible, VERIFY the capability directly (which gh, gh --version) before acting on the self-report or routing manual steps to the user. A tool error message is a CLAIM, not ground truth -- especially PATH/availability/capability claims. Mirrors verify-before-assuming (negative conclusions need a second independent signal) and probe-with-canonical-code-path (use the real code path, not a synthetic equivalent).
original.when_to_use: When a script or tool reports a dependency or capability is missing, or an operation is impossible, before accepting it or routing manual steps to the user. Verify the capability directly first.

generalized.context: When a deployment script or automation tool reports that a dependency is missing, a capability is unavailable, or an operation is impossible.
approach: Treat the tool's error message as a claim rather than ground truth, especially for PATH, availability, or capability assertions.
Verify the capability directly using a standard command (e.g., running the tool with --version or checking the binary path) instead of relying on the script's self-report.
Only route manual steps to the user or accept the failure after independent verification confirms the issue.
generalized.outcome: Prevented false-positive blockers and unnecessary manual intervention by distinguishing between tool bugs and actual missing dependencies.
generalized.lesson: When a script or tool reports a missing dependency, unavailable capability, or impossible operation, verify the capability directly (e.g., via 'tool --version' or direct execution) before acting on the error message. A tool's error message is a claim, not ground truth—especially regarding PATH, availability, or capability assertions. Negative conclusions require a second independent signal to avoid routing unnecessary manual steps to the user.

original.title: A fix committed after a release tag is not in that release -- verify ancestry before assuming a promotion carries it
original.content: The orphan-removal engine fix (Ayoai-Mind 3e3a7a5d) landed two commits AFTER the v2.0.0 tag (1e66191a); the gh-detection fix 0315ea27 is also in that gap. Promoting v2.0.0 frontier-to-claude-mind would NOT carry either fix, leaving the later claude-mind-to-zds-mind transplant hazardous (old orphan-removal still deletes zds-mind 11 domain skills). Caught by checking commit ancestry against the tag rather than assuming the tag pointed at HEAD. General rule: before assuming a tagged release, deploy, or seed-promotion carries a specific fix, verify the fix commit is an ancestor of the release ref (git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <ref>), do not infer it from the fix existing on the branch.
original.when_to_use: When reasoning about whether a tagged release, promotion, or deploy includes a specific commit or fix -- especially before relying on that promotion to make a downstream operation safe.

generalized.context: When verifying whether a specific code fix is included in a tagged release, a deployment, or a seed promotion.
approach: Do not assume a fix is included just because it exists on the branch or was committed after the tag.
Verify the fix commit is an ancestor of the release reference using git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <ref>.
Only proceed with the promotion or deployment if the ancestry check returns true.
generalized.outcome: Prevented deploying a release that lacked critical fixes, avoiding hazardous downstream operations (such as unsafe data transplants or missing feature support).
generalized.lesson: Before assuming a tagged release, deployment, or seed promotion carries a specific fix, verify the fix commit is an ancestor of the release ref using git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <ref>. Do not infer inclusion from the fix existing on the branch or being committed after the tag, as this leaves the deployment missing the fix and potentially hazardous.

original.title: Borrowable gap framing: 'AI interpolates rather than invents' (Unreasonable Labs) - multi-source validated; borrow the gap, not the superintelligence pitch
original.content: Unreasonable Labs (unreasonablelabs.ai; $13.5M seed led by Playground Global; ex-DeepMind Gemini CEO Yuan Cao + MIT CTO Markus Buehler) markets the gap as 'AI Incapable of True Invention - current models interpolate rather than synthesize novel ideas' plus 'Too Much Data, Too Little Insight', and sells 'self-updating organizational memory'. That is the SAME gap framing ZDS uses via Sutton (continue-a-pattern vs. decide-when-the-pattern-breaks; see enactive-ai-sutton) and a16z (interpolation vs. real learning). A well-funded frontier-AI team converging on the identical framing is third-party validation it resonates with investors. BORROW: the crispness of the gap statement, adapted to our business-operations domain ('you already have the data and the pipelines; what you lack is compounding insight'). DO NOT borrow: the 'superintelligence / autonomous discovery' positioning - that over-claims for an SDVOSB consultancy and collides with guard-13 (keep government-facing copy AI-grounded, not moonshot). Their arXiv 2606.01444 retrieval/search/discovery trichotomy is a borrowable conceptual ladder for a future thought-leadership piece (sibling to two-kinds-of-world-models). Full competitor profile: tree node unreasonable-labs-discovery.

generalized.context: When defining a value proposition for a consultancy or service that leverages existing client data and pipelines but lacks compounding insight.
approach: Identify the gap between current capabilities (data availability, established pipelines) and the missing element (synthesis of novel insights).
Adopt the framing that current models or systems 'interpolate' existing patterns rather than 'synthesize' truly new ideas.
Borrow the crispness of this specific gap statement to articulate the unique value of the service.

Avoid over-claiming 'superintelligence' or 'autonomous discovery' if the target audience includes government or regulated entities, as this may conflict with compliance guardrails requiring grounded, realistic AI descriptions.
generalized.outcome: Created a validated, investor-ready value proposition that resonates with industry trends while remaining compliant with specific organizational guardrails.
generalized.lesson: When positioning a service that utilizes existing data and infrastructure, frame the value around the gap between 'interpolation' (using known patterns) and 'synthesis' (creating novel insights). This specific framing is widely validated in frontier AI discourse and effectively communicates the need for organizational memory that compounds over time. However, strictly avoid 'superintelligence' or 'autonomous discovery' claims when targeting regulated sectors (like government), as these over-claims can violate compliance guardrails requiring grounded, realistic AI descriptions.

original.title: Anthropic's own enterprise agent playbook validates the ZDS pitch - cite it; borrow its ROI proof points
original.content: Anthropic's 2026 enterprise whitepaper 'Building Effective AI Agents: Architecture Patterns and Implementation Frameworks' is the highest-credibility third-party backing for the ZDS pitch BECAUSE it is our own model vendor. Three reusable assets: (1) Headline 'Generative AI answers questions. AI agents solve problems.' is verbatim our outcomes-not-tools / you-buy-the-work framing - cite Anthropic for it. (2) It names MEMORY + OBSERVABILITY as the hard production requirements for agents that 'work at scale' - which is exactly the layer ZDS builds and the customer owns; position Mind as that named gap. (3) Borrowable ROI proof points from named customers (Intercom Fin 86% resolution across 25k+ customers; Tines ~100x time-to-value; retail bank 20-60% productivity / 30% faster credit; Gradient Labs 80-90%; Assembled +20% CSAT) - citable evidence of what production agents deliver, for the pitch and /proof, attributed to the Anthropic whitepaper (no ZDS-specific capability claim, so guard-20 clear; still attribute). Full doc: tree node anthropic-agents-enterprise-playbook.

generalized.context: When pitching enterprise AI agent solutions to validate the value proposition and ROI claims.
approach: Cite the vendor's own high-credibility whitepaper to support the 'outcomes-not-tools' framing (e.g., 'Agents solve problems, not just answer questions').
Reference the paper's identification of 'Memory' and 'Observability' as hard production requirements to position the platform as the solution to these specific gaps.

Attribute specific, named customer ROI metrics (e.g., resolution rates, time-to-value, productivity gains) found in the paper to provide third-party proof points without making direct capability claims for the current platform.
generalized.outcome: Provides high-credibility, third-party validated evidence for the sales pitch, specifically addressing the 'work at scale' requirements and quantifiable business outcomes.
generalized.lesson: When validating an enterprise AI agent pitch, leverage the model vendor's own whitepapers as the highest-credibility third-party source. Specifically: (1) Use their 'outcomes-not-tools' framing to align with customer goals; (2) Cite their definition of hard production requirements (like Memory and Observability) to position your platform as the necessary layer; and (3) Borrow their named customer ROI metrics as citable proof points, ensuring attribution remains clear to avoid overclaiming specific platform capabilities.

original.title: Audit lens: 'grow more powerful as models improve WITHOUT growing more complex' (Anthropic enterprise playbook)
original.content: Anthropic's enterprise agents whitepaper (2026) prescribes: start simple, align technical complexity with business value, and 'build systems that grow more powerful as the underlying models improve - without growing more complex'; it warns that orgs which over-engineer out of the gate underperform. Claude-Mind is a large system (dozens of skills, gates, rules), so this is a legitimate standing challenge, NOT a contradiction: our complexity is concentrated in the dimension the whitepaper itself brackets out (persistent memory + cross-session continual learning), and our meta-rules already enforce the simplicity ethos at the component level (implementation-discipline, communication-clarity 'elegance is subtraction', first-principles, consolidate-before-expand). The ACTION: adopt 'is this complexity earning its keep / does it grow capability without growing complexity?' as an explicit checkpoint in felt-sense and fresh-eyes audits, and in the asp-017 autonomy audit. When a model upgrade lands, prefer deleting scaffolding the stronger model no longer needs over adding more. Source: tree node anthropic-agents-enterprise-playbook.

generalized.context: When designing enterprise agent systems or large-scale applications where capabilities must scale with model improvements without increasing architectural overhead.
approach: Align technical complexity directly with business value, avoiding over-engineering at the initial stage.
Concentrate necessary complexity only in dimensions that are explicitly bracketed out by standard simplicity guidelines (e.g., persistent memory, cross-session learning) rather than general logic.
Enforce a meta-rule at the component level that prioritizes 'elegance is subtraction' and consolidation before expansion.
Establish an explicit audit checkpoint asking: 'Does this complexity earn its keep, and does it grow capability without growing complexity?' during fresh-eyes reviews and autonomy audits.
Upon model upgrades, prefer deleting scaffolding the stronger model no longer needs over adding new features.
generalized.outcome: Systems that scale in power as underlying models improve while maintaining low architectural complexity and avoiding performance degradation from premature optimization.
generalized.lesson: To build systems that grow more powerful as models improve without growing more complex, strictly align technical complexity with business value and avoid over-engineering at the start. Concentrate complexity only in specific, necessary dimensions (like persistent memory) while enforcing a meta-rule of 'consolidate before expand' at the component level. Use an explicit audit checkpoint to verify that every unit of complexity earns its keep by increasing capability without increasing overhead. When a model upgrade lands, prioritize removing unused scaffolding over adding new features.

original.title: Differentiator sharpen: 'we remember what FAILED and convert it to guardrails' - a failure-memory system; and the discipline of mining the moat vs. chasing a validator's research
original.content: POSITIONING: When sophisticated practitioners frame agent evals as 'failure-memory systems mined from real traces' (signal 2026-06-06), that is validation of our guardrails+reasoning-bank architecture - and it unlocks a sharper, harder-to-copy differentiator than 'AI that learns what works': 'We remember what FAILED and convert each failure into a guardrail so it cannot recur.' This is stronger because a failure-memory layer is harder to fake, it is auditable (experience_ref -> reasoning_bank -> guard chain IS the attribution trail), and it answers trajectory-level (not just output-level) failure. Use the /proof counts (400+ guardrails, 1000+ rb, 254 hypotheses) as the artifact of this loop. STRATEGIC DISCIPLINE: a market signal that VALIDATES our architecture is a positioning/proof opportunity, NOT a mandate to go build the originator's research agenda (here: agent-fuzzing / minimal-reproducible-state eval infra). Building that would be breadth-over-depth with no revenue line - off-mission for an SDVOSB consultancy. Mine the moat we already run; build new infra only when a paying engagement or product roadmap demands it. Full analysis: tree node evals-as-failure-memory.

generalized.context: When market signals or sophisticated practitioners validate your architecture by framing it as a 'failure-memory system' derived from real operational traces.
approach: Recognize this validation as an opportunity to sharpen your differentiator: 'We remember what FAILED and convert each failure into a guardrail so it cannot recur.'
Leverage the auditable attribution trail (experience_ref -> reasoning_bank -> guard chain) to prove trajectory-level failure handling rather than just output-level fixes.
Resist the urge to build the originator's specific research agenda (e.g., new fuzzing infra) unless a paying engagement or product roadmap explicitly demands it.
Focus on mining the existing moat (current guardrails and reasoning bank) rather than pursuing breadth-over-depth initiatives with no revenue line.
generalized.outcome: Established a harder-to-copy differentiator that is auditable and addresses trajectory-level failures, while avoiding off-mission infrastructure builds.
generalized.lesson: When your architecture is validated as a 'failure-memory system,' position it as a defensible moat where every failure is converted into a guardrail to prevent recurrence. This is stronger than 'AI that learns what works' because it is auditable and addresses root causes. Crucially, treat such market validation as a proof of your existing depth, not a mandate to build the competitor's research agenda; only build new infrastructure when a paying engagement or product roadmap explicitly requires it.

original.title: A seed-transplant promotion is a file-copy + fresh commit, not a git merge -- verify the fix in the destination by CONTENT, not git ancestry
original.content: Initial guard-78 pin (2026-06-06) gated a claude-mind->zds-mind seed-transplant on the orphan fix reaching claude-mind via git -C <claude-mind> merge-base --is-ancestor <frontier-SHA 3e3a7a5d> <ref>. WRONG: the frontier->claude-mind promotion is a seed-transplant = file-copy + fresh commit (d097cf9), NOT a git merge. claude-mind does NOT share ayoai-mind git DAG, so the frontier SHA is Not-a-valid-object in claude-mind (git cat-file -t 3e3a7a5d -> fatal; verified firsthand) and merge-base ancestry returns rc=1 regardless -> the gate would ALWAYS read unsafe. Caught by alpha. FIX: verify the fix in the destination by CONTENT (grep -q _dest_forged_skill_names <claude-mind>/core/scripts/_seed_engine.py) or by version marker (__version__ >= 2.0.1), never a source SHA. Keep merge-base ancestry ONLY as a frontier-side provenance gate (same DAG: merge-base --is-ancestor 3e3a7a5d v2.0.1 -> rc=0).
original.when_to_use: When verifying a fix or change landed in a destination reached via file-copy, sync, seed-transplant, or any non-git-merge promotion -- check content/version markers in the destination, never source git SHAs or ancestry (the source DAG does not cross the copy boundary).
original.failure_lesson: git ancestry/SHA identity does not cross a file-copy/sync/seed-transplant boundary; to confirm a change landed past such a boundary, check destination content or a version marker, never a source SHA.

generalized.context: When verifying that a fix or change has successfully landed in a destination system reached via file-copy, sync, seed-transplant, or any non-git-merge promotion mechanism.
approach: Recognize that the source repository's git DAG (commit history) does not cross the file-copy boundary into the destination.
Avoid using source SHA hashes or git ancestry checks (e.g., merge-base) to verify the destination, as these will fail or return false negatives.
Verify the fix in the destination by checking for the presence of specific content (e.g., grep for a unique string) or a version marker (e.g., __version__ >= X.Y.Z).
Reserve git ancestry checks only for the source side to confirm the change reached the staging point before the copy.
generalized.outcome: Prevented false-negative verification failures where a valid fix was rejected because the destination lacked the source's commit history.
generalized.lesson: Git ancestry and SHA identity do not cross a file-copy or sync boundary. When verifying a change in a destination reached via seed-transplant or file-copy, never rely on source SHAs or ancestry checks; instead, verify the fix by checking for specific content or version markers directly within the destination.

original.title: Small-model semantic inducer produces substantive patterns at $0, closing the structural-shell risk; Gate B (retrieval demand) still open
original.content: Lodestar generalization-engine semantic proving run (2026-06-06, omni firsthand): CachingLLMInducer (lib/engine/llm-inducer.ts) routes each trace through qwen2.5:3b via zak-code /complete ($0 local), emitting {context, approach, outcome, lesson, tags} while keeping the pattern SIGNATURE mechanical (computeCoarseSignature) so k-aggregation/quarantine is unchanged. Result on 70 traces (zds-mind 18, ayoai-mind 50, zds-parent 2): 70/70 extracted, ZERO fallbacks; semantic v2 quarantine 8.6% == structural v1 8.6% (mechanical signature retained the 88.6->8.6 win exactly -- the model cannot move patterns across k-groups); utility 0.567->0.657 (structural metric, more merged tags). Patterns carry real domain substance with named entities (Echo, ARC-AGI-3, Charlie, /prime), not 17-step-interaction shells. CONCLUSION: closes the structural-shell half of the single-biggest-risk. Does NOT close the commercial half: traces are the framework own meta-domain sessions, and utility is structural not retrieval-demand. Gate B (downstream-relevance metric) remains the real unproven question. Wire contract validated: /complete returns the object in body.data (not bare/result); model id ollama_chat/qwen2.5:3b.
original.when_to_use: When assessing whether the generalization-engine selective-tier output has commercial value, or choosing the next hardening step for the proving experiment.

generalized.context: When validating a generalization engine that uses a small, local LLM to extract structured knowledge from raw traces, specifically to verify if the extracted patterns contain substantive domain data rather than just structural metadata.
approach: Route each trace through a lightweight local model (e.g., Qwen2.5:3B) via a dedicated API endpoint to generate structured outputs (context, approach, outcome, lesson, tags).
Enforce a mechanical signature generation step (e.g., computeCoarseSignature) to ensure the aggregation and quarantine logic remains unchanged regardless of the model used.
Analyze the output for 'substance' by checking for named entities and domain-specific concepts versus generic interaction shells.
Compare the semantic extraction results against the original structural metrics to verify that the pattern distribution and utility scores remain consistent.
generalized.outcome: 100% successful extraction with zero fallbacks; semantic quarantine rates matched structural baseline exactly, confirming the model cannot artificially shift patterns across aggregation groups; utility scores improved due to more meaningful tag merging.
generalized.lesson: A small, local LLM can successfully extract substantive domain patterns from raw traces at zero cost, effectively closing the risk of 'structural-shell' artifacts (generic metadata without domain meaning). By enforcing a mechanical signature generation step, the aggregation logic remains stable even when switching from structural to semantic extraction. However, this validates the structural integrity of the patterns, not their downstream commercial value or retrieval demand, which remains an open question.

original.title: Small models need explicit next-step hints in tool results to terminate -- success-hint / error-fix in the tool return, not model inference
original.content: zak-code Job-1 (2026-06-06): qwen2.5:3b often failed to STOP after a successful remember tool call -- it kept taking tool-call turns toward the agent-loop iteration cap (~16 calls x ~20s ~= 300s), which looked like a 5-min write latency. Root cause was loop NON-TERMINATION, not I/O (the write was always instant). Fix: a control-flow rail -- the tool RESULT now carries a next-step hint (Memory saved; if nothing else is needed, reply briefly and end the turn); the 3B reads it and terminates. ~300s -> ~2s (~150x), persistence/recall unchanged at 100%. Generalized: tool results carry HINT-on-success / FIX-on-error (e.g. a permission denial names the exact permission_mode that unblocks it). LESSON: small models do not reliably infer that they are done or how to recover -- bake the next action into the tool return string. Parallels the Mind framework own discipline (return-protocol.md: iteration-close.sh prints NEXT ACTION REQUIRED: Call Skill(aspirations); tool/script outputs name the next action) -- same convergent pattern, different runtime.
original.when_to_use: When driving a small/local model through a tool-using agent loop and it over-runs, fails to terminate, or mishandles errors -- bake the next action (success hint or error fix) into the tool result string rather than relying on the model to infer it.

generalized.context: When driving a small or local language model through a tool-using agent loop, the model often fails to terminate after a successful operation or mishandles errors by continuing to generate unnecessary tool calls.
approach: Identify that the model lacks the internal reasoning capacity to infer when a task is complete or how to recover from an error
Modify the tool result schema to explicitly include a 'next-step hint' or 'error-fix' instruction
Ensure the hint directs the model to either end the turn (on success) or take a specific corrective action (on error)
generalized.outcome: The model terminates immediately after the tool call instead of looping until the iteration cap is reached, reducing execution time from minutes to seconds without affecting task accuracy.
generalized.lesson: Small models do not reliably infer that they are done or how to recover from errors; they require explicit guidance. Bake the next action (a success hint to stop or an error fix to proceed) directly into the tool return string rather than relying on the model to infer the correct workflow state.

original.title: Seed-transplant: test-fixture domain tokens ride downstream unscrubbed BY DESIGN -- do not exclude test dirs or add scrub transforms
original.content: Verified firsthand (zds-mind core/scripts/domain-leak-check.sh ~line 76-80): the domain-leak gate SKIPS any file whose basename starts with test_ or test- (test_*.py + test-*.sh) -- test fixtures deliberately use domain tokens to exercise pattern-matching. So Ayoai-specific strings in test fixtures (e.g. the 3 fixtures flagged on PR #2: test_attribution_filter_path_normalize.py, test_daemon_orphan_prevention.py, test_pre_edit_context_gate.py) ride claude-mind->zds-mind unscrubbed and that is CORRECT -- residue never fails preflight. DO NOT exclude test dirs from the seed payload like mind_api/bench/ was excluded (that strips the downstream framework safety net), and DO NOT add inline_edit scrub transforms (the genuine residue roblox-studio.sh / access-roblox-studio / roblox-bridge.py is assertion-coupled, ~30 paired refs in one file; regex-rewriting risks latent downstream test breaks for cosmetic-only benefit). The one production-coupled status string roblox_studio_session_required is already synced code-to-test by transform G12. Source: alpha 2026-06-06, verified firsthand.
original.when_to_use: When assessing whether domain-specific strings in test fixtures block a seed-transplant or need scrubbing -- they do not; the leak gate skips test files by design. Do not exclude test dirs or add scrub transforms.

generalized.context: When assessing whether domain-specific strings in test fixtures block a seed-transplant or require scrubbing, recognize that the domain-leak gate is designed to skip any file whose basename starts with 'test_' or 'test-'.
approach: Identify that test fixtures deliberately use domain tokens to exercise pattern-matching and must remain unscrubbed.
Ensure test directories are included in the seed payload to preserve the downstream framework safety net.
Avoid adding inline scrub transforms (e.g., regex-rewriting) for cosmetic-only benefits, as this risks breaking assertion-coupled references.
Rely on existing code-to-test synchronization (e.g., specific transform rules) for production-coupled status strings rather than manual scrubbing.
generalized.outcome: Domain-specific strings in test fixtures ride the pipeline unscrubbed without failing preflight checks, maintaining the integrity of the downstream test suite.
generalized.lesson: When performing a seed-transplant, do not exclude test directories or apply scrub transforms to test fixtures. The domain-leak gate is designed to skip files matching 'test_*' patterns by design; these files intentionally contain domain tokens to verify pattern matching. Excluding them or scrubbing them removes the downstream safety net and risks breaking assertion-coupled references. Only production-coupled strings should be managed via established code-to-test synchronization rules.

original.title: Auto-merge safety: checks-pass is vacuous without required checks, and for auto-deploy repos merge==deploy (merge-vs-apply separation collapses)
original.content: Adversarial scope-review of the PR-merge-autonomy grant (2026-06-06, omni) surfaced two non-obvious holes in any agent-merges-PR-when-mergeable-CLEAN-plus-checks-pass rule: (1) VACUOUS CHECKS -- all 5 agent-owned repos have zero branch protection / zero required status checks, and 3 have zero CI workflows, so checks-pass was trivially true everywhere; the rule must require at least one PASSING check OR a local-test-suite run, and treat a FAILING check as do-not-merge. (2) MERGE==DEPLOY -- for auto-deploy repos (Amplify web-apps) merging to main triggers a production deploy, so the merge IS the application; the merge-vs-apply separation (safe for git-only repos like zds-mind/Zak-Code) collapses, and a PR renaming live AWS resource refs (lodestar-* to zds-*) would cause an outage if auto-merged. Also: prefer an INCLUSION allow-list of owned repos over an EXCLUSION deny-list (a deny-list silently admits new/sibling repos, e.g. the two Lambda repos under the same org). General lesson: before granting auto-merge, verify (a) checks actually EXIST and pass, (b) whether merge triggers deploy, (c) scope by allow-list not deny-list. Encoded into guard-79 + capability-routing.md PR-merge section.
original.when_to_use: When designing or reviewing any rule that lets an agent or bot auto-merge PRs on a checks-pass condition -- verify checks exist, that merge != deploy for the target repo, and scope by allow-list.

generalized.context: When designing or reviewing rules that grant agents or bots the ability to auto-merge pull requests based solely on a 'checks-pass' condition.
approach: Verify that the target repository has at least one required status check or a local test suite configured; treat a failing check as a hard block.
Determine if merging to the target branch triggers an automatic production deployment (e.g., via CI/CD pipelines), which collapses the distinction between code review and application release.
Scope the auto-merge permission using an inclusion allow-list of specific repositories rather than an exclusion deny-list to prevent silent admission of new or sibling repositories.
generalized.outcome: Prevented vacuous truth where checks pass trivially due to missing configurations, avoided outages caused by auto-deploying unreviewed production changes, and ensured strict control over which repositories are exposed to automated merging.
generalized.lesson: Auto-merge rules relying only on 'checks-pass' are unsafe if checks are missing or if the merge action triggers a production deployment. First, enforce that at least one required check exists and passes (treating failures as blocks). Second, recognize that for auto-deploy repositories, merging IS deploying, so the safety of a 'merge vs. apply' separation collapses. Third, always scope these permissions via an inclusion allow-list of owned repos; exclusion deny-lists silently permit new or sibling repos to be auto-merged.

original.title: Mechanical backstop beats honor-system for diff-reading safety gates
original.content: A safety gate that depends on the LLM noticing a dangerous pattern in a diff (e.g. an AWS resource rename on an auto-deploy repo) is attention-dependent: it fails silently under context loss / autocompact, or when the rename is buried in a large diff. Back any such gate with a mechanical script that greps the diff for the danger pattern and returns a decisive exit code. pr-aws-resource-scan.sh (exit 2=FLAGGED) is the backstop for merge-readiness checklist item 5. Key design choices that held up firsthand: (a) over-flag rather than miss (a safety alert, false positives are cheap, a missed rename on a production auto-deploy is not); (b) FLAGGED is decisive do-not-merge but CLEAN still requires human/agent inspection (a rename behind indirection passes the grep); (c) test the script on positive+negative+error cases before wiring it in. Verify-before-assuming caught a real bug: GNU sed has no lazy quantifier so the repo-slug regex left a trailing .git that would have broken every default-detection call.
original.when_to_use: When a governance/safety checklist item relies on the agent spotting something in a diff or large artifact. Add a mechanical grep-and-exit-code backstop; do not trust attention alone.

generalized.context: When a governance or safety checklist item relies on an agent or human noticing a specific dangerous pattern within a code diff or large artifact (e.g., a critical resource rename in an auto-deploy repository).
approach: Implement a mechanical script that greps the diff for the specific danger pattern and returns a decisive exit code.
Design the script to over-flag rather than miss (prioritize false positives over false negatives).
Configure the script so a FLAGGED status is a hard block preventing merge, while a CLEAN status still requires human/agent inspection.
Test the script rigorously on positive, negative, and error cases before integrating it into the pipeline.
Verify the script's logic against edge cases (e.g., regex trailing characters) before assuming correctness.
generalized.outcome: The mechanical backstop catches dangerous patterns that attention-dependent checks miss due to context loss or buried changes, preventing silent failures in automated deployments.
generalized.lesson: Safety gates relying on attention (LLMs or humans) to spot patterns in diffs are fragile and fail silently under context loss or large diffs. Always back such gates with a mechanical script that greps for the danger pattern and returns a decisive exit code. Design this script to over-flag (false positives are cheap; missed renames in auto-deploy are not), treat a FLAGGED state as a hard block, and verify the script logic against edge cases before deployment.

original.title: Time-boxed sign-off-gated work needs proactive deadline-push, not a pull dashboard
original.content: Two VA Sources-Sought responses (recon-01 telehealth, recon-02 FMBT IV&V) were drafted but lapsed unsubmitted when the 2026-05-28 response windows closed -- the per-send sign-off (guard-12/guard-29, human-only) was never surfaced to user in time. Root cause: deadline tracking existed only as a PULL surface (the /admin/contracts deadline calendar) which requires user to look; nothing PUSHED the approaching deadline to him. Lesson: any deliverable that is BOTH time-boxed (hard external deadline) AND gated on a human sign-off the agent cannot self-provide must be surfaced proactively and escalated as the deadline nears (notify-user/SES push at e.g. T-7/T-3/T-1), never left to a dashboard the human may not check. A draft that expires unsubmitted is wasted work plus a missed opportunity, not a neutral non-event. The push must name the deadline and the specific action needed.
original.when_to_use: When creating or holding a deliverable that is both time-boxed (external deadline) and gated on a human approval the agent cannot give itself (Sources-Sought response, bid, time-limited outreach).

generalized.context: When managing a deliverable that has a hard external deadline and requires a human sign-off that the system cannot generate automatically.
approach: Identify deliverables where the final submission is gated by a human approval the agent cannot provide.
Replace passive 'pull' monitoring (e.g., a calendar the user must check) with active 'push' notifications.
Trigger automated escalation notifications (e.g., email or system alerts) at specific intervals (T-7, T-3, T-1) before the deadline.
Ensure the notification explicitly names the deadline and the specific action required from the human.
generalized.outcome: Prevented drafts from expiring unsubmitted due to missed deadlines, avoiding wasted work and lost opportunities.
generalized.lesson: For any time-boxed deliverable gated by a human sign-off the system cannot provide, never rely on a dashboard the user might miss. Instead, proactively push escalating notifications as the deadline nears. A draft that expires unsubmitted is a failed opportunity, not a neutral event; the system must actively alert the human with the specific deadline and required action.

original.title: WebFetch auto-summary can confidently hallucinate structure; cross-verify before encoding web content
original.content: WebFetch runs a small fast model over the fetched markdown to answer the prompt, and that model can confidently fabricate structure absent from the source. Two confirmed 2026-06 incidents: (1) the Anthropic enterprise PDF auto-summary invented an ACI=Atomic/Composable/Intentional tool framework not in the document; (2) the First Round AI-Powered Isnt a Position article auto-summary invented a tidy 5-step playbook that conflated the real section headings. In both cases a second stricter WebFetch pass asking ONLY for verbatim extraction (exact H1, byline, verbatim section headings, first sentences, paywall status) exposed the discrepancy. This is a DISTINCT failure mode from rb-50/rb-148 (WebFetch returns EMPTY on JS-rendered SPAs) - here the result is non-empty but partly wrong, which is more dangerous because it looks authoritative. Discipline: before encoding any web article/PDF as authoritative tree knowledge, cross-verify the auto-summary with a verbatim-extraction pass; encode only verified content and explicitly flag paraphrase-vs-verbatim in the node (see ai-positioning-playbook + anthropic-agents-enterprise-playbook accuracy notes).
original.when_to_use: Before encoding content fetched via WebFetch (articles, PDFs, whitepapers) into the knowledge tree as authoritative knowledge.

generalized.context: When encoding content fetched via automated web scrapers or PDF processors (articles, whitepapers, reports) into an authoritative knowledge tree.
approach: Recognize that fast inference models used for auto-summarization may confidently fabricate structural elements (headings, frameworks, step-by-step lists) absent from the source.
Execute a second, stricter pass on the raw content requesting ONLY verbatim extraction (exact H1s, bylines, section headings, first sentences) without summarization.
Compare the auto-summary output against the verbatim extraction to identify hallucinated structures or conflated sections.
