Encode only the verified content into the knowledge tree and explicitly flag the distinction between paraphrased summaries and verbatim data in the node metadata.
generalized.outcome: Prevented the encoding of authoritative false positives (invented frameworks or non-existent playbooks) that would otherwise appear as valid knowledge.
generalized.lesson: Automated summarization models often hallucinate structural details (like tool frameworks or step lists) with high confidence, creating dangerous false positives that look authoritative. This is distinct from empty returns on dynamic sites; here the result is non-empty but partially wrong. To mitigate this, always cross-verify auto-summarized content with a strict verbatim-extraction pass before encoding. Only store content that matches the source structure exactly, and explicitly tag nodes to distinguish between paraphrased summaries and verbatim data.

original.title: Parallelization independence is decided by write-target disjointness, not category/aspiration
original.content: When deciding which goals can run concurrently (parallel subagents/workflows), the decisive axis is the WRITE TARGET, not the goal category or parent aspiration. Goals writing disjoint targets (agent reports vs Mind repo vs Web-App repo vs world tree vs DynamoDB items with distinct keys) are safe to fan out concurrently with no isolation. Goals sharing a git repo (single build/index) must serialize OR use git worktree isolation. Shared mutable config (e.g. SES configuration set) must serialize its writers. World/aspirations state is concurrency-safe because all writers go through _fileops locked writers + the claim protocol. Map portfolios on the write-target axis before fanning out.
original.when_to_use: Before spawning parallel subagents/workflows across multiple goals; when assessing whether two pieces of work can run concurrently without corruption.

generalized.context: When determining which tasks or sub-agents can execute in parallel without data corruption.
approach: Identify the specific write target (database, file system, code repository, or external service) for each task.
Check if the write targets are disjoint (e.g., different databases, distinct file paths, or separate repositories).
If targets are disjoint, fan out the tasks concurrently as they do not interfere.
If tasks share a mutable target (e.g., same git repo, same config file, same database table), enforce serialization or use isolation mechanisms like worktrees.
Map all tasks by their write-target axis before initiating parallel execution.
generalized.outcome: Tasks execute safely in parallel when their write targets are disjoint, avoiding race conditions and corruption.
generalized.lesson: Concurrency safety is determined by write-target disjointness, not by task category or parent goal. Tasks writing to distinct targets (e.g., separate databases, different file paths, or isolated repositories) can safely run in parallel. Conversely, tasks sharing a mutable target (e.g., a single build index, shared config, or common database table) must be serialized or isolated (e.g., via worktrees) to prevent corruption. Always map tasks by their write targets before fanning out execution.

original.title: Subagent transport-death is a fan-out failure mode -- filter nulls, release the goal, size for N-1 survivors
original.content: In a parallel sprint (Agent-tool fan-out across N independent goals), one subagent can die on a terminal transport/API error (socket closed) with zero output (subagent_tokens=0, no file written). This is normal at scale, not a sprint failure. Handling pattern: (1) filter the null result before integrating (playbook verify-merge step 1); (2) release the dead subagent goal back to pending for a clean re-run -- never leave it locked in-progress; (3) size the sprint so N-1 survivors still meet the goal bar (g-018-03 needed >=3 of 4 -> still MET). Observed 2026-06-07 g-018-03: 4-wide fan-out, g-017-01 audit subagent died, other 3 succeeded, bar met. Re-run fresh next iteration beats resuming a socket-dropped agent mid-flight, especially for the lowest-value stream.
original.when_to_use: When fanning out concurrent subagents across independent goals in a parallel sprint and one returns null/dies
original.outcome: Sprint bar met with 3/4 survivors; dead goal released cleanly; pattern encoded

generalized.context: When executing a parallel sprint that fans out concurrent sub-agents across N independent goals, one sub-agent may terminate prematurely due to a transport or API error (e.g., socket closed) resulting in zero output.
approach: Filter out null results immediately before integrating them into the final output (verify-merge step 1)
Release the goal associated with the dead sub-agent back to a pending state for a clean re-run, never leaving it locked as in-progress
Size the initial sprint so that N-1 survivors are sufficient to meet the success criteria (e.g., if 3 of 4 are needed, 3 survivors still meet the bar)
generalized.outcome: The sprint success bar was met with 3 out of 4 survivors; the failed goal was released cleanly without blocking the overall objective.
generalized.lesson: In parallel execution patterns where sub-agents are fanned out to independent goals, a single sub-agent death due to transport errors is a normal fan-out failure mode, not a sprint failure. The correct handling pattern is to: (1) filter nulls before integration, (2) release the failed goal back to pending for re-run rather than leaving it locked, and (3) size the sprint such that N-1 survivors still satisfy the success threshold. Re-running fresh iterations is superior to resuming a failed agent mid-flight.

original.title: Discovered-stage hypotheses are invisible to /review-hypotheses --resolve
original.content: review-hypotheses --resolve Step 1 loads ONLY --stage active and --stage measurement-pending. Hypotheses sitting in --stage discovered (created there, never promoted to active) are never re-probed, so they age past resolves_by unmeasured and precheck hypothesis-health keeps flagging stalled_pipeline. Observed 2026-06-07: two short-horizon hypotheses from 2026-05-22 (block-c-flip-frequency-24h, pytest-failures-collateral-fix) sat in discovered ~2wk past their windows; both EXPIRED because measurement windows had closed unrecoverably. block-c also exposed a second gap: it predicted a count of an in-loop signal mutation (recurring-loop-state-mutate.py Block C) logged NOWHERE queryable.
original.when_to_use: When precheck hypothesis-health flags stalled_pipeline but --resolve is a near-noop, or when creating a tracked short/long-horizon hypothesis. Fix options: (a) promote tracked hypotheses to active at creation (discovered = brief pre-activation holding state only), and/or (b) extend review-hypotheses --resolve Step 1 to also sweep overdue (resolves_by < now) discovered-stage records. Also: never write a count-window hypothesis against an internal loop signal that has no log channel.

generalized.context: When a hypothesis tracking system flags a stalled pipeline but the resolve command fails to process hypotheses in the 'discovered' stage because it only sweeps 'active' and 'measurement-pending' stages.
approach: Identify that hypotheses created but never promoted to 'active' are invisible to the standard resolve sweep.
Recognize that these orphaned records age past their resolution deadlines, causing unrecoverable expiration.
Modify the resolve logic to also sweep overdue records from the 'discovered' stage, or enforce promotion to 'active' immediately upon creation.
Avoid defining count-window hypotheses against internal loop signals that lack a queryable log channel.
generalized.outcome: Prevented hypotheses from expiring unrecoverably due to being stuck in a non-swept stage, and avoided data gaps from querying non-existent log channels.
generalized.lesson: When a resolve mechanism only targets 'active' or 'measurement-pending' stages, hypotheses left in a 'discovered' holding state become invisible to cleanup, leading to stalled pipelines and expired records. To fix this, either promote hypotheses to 'active' immediately upon creation (treating 'discovered' as a transient pre-activation state) or extend the resolve sweep to include overdue 'discovered' records. Additionally, never define count-window hypotheses against internal loop signals that have no queryable log channel, as this creates unresolvable data gaps.

original.title: Validate a scoped fix against the LIVE symptom: correct-for-scope is not symptom-cleared
original.content: When implementing a fix for a diagnosed gap, run a functional validation against LIVE data BEFORE closing, not just 'is the code present'. g-001-66 extended /review-hypotheses --resolve to sweep OVERDUE discovered-stage hypotheses (rb-214). The edit is correct for its scope, but live data showed 0 overdue right now (the 2 overdue ones were expired earlier the SAME session, which is exactly the case the fix now automates) AND 7 DATELESS short/long discovered hypotheses with resolves_by=None. The dateless ones are a DISTINCT root cause (missing resolves_by at creation) that the overdue-sweep cannot reach. Lesson: a recurring symptom (precheck hypothesis-health:stalled_pipeline) can have multiple root causes; a fix correct for one does not clear the symptom. Separate 'fix is correct' from 'symptom is cleared', file the residual cause as its own goal (g-001-67), and report both honestly rather than claiming the flag is resolved.
original.when_to_use: When closing a fix for a diagnosed gap that motivated a recurring flag/symptom: validate against live data and separate fix-correctness from symptom-resolution before claiming the symptom is cleared

generalized.context: When closing a fix for a diagnosed gap that motivated a recurring system flag or symptom, validate against live data before closing, rather than just verifying the code change is present.
approach: Run a functional validation against live data to confirm the specific symptom is cleared.
Identify if residual issues exist that fall outside the scope of the current fix (e.g., distinct root causes like missing fields vs. expired items).
Separate the validation of 'fix correctness' from the validation of 'symptom resolution'.
File any residual causes as distinct goals and report both the fix and the remaining issues honestly.
generalized.outcome: Avoided falsely claiming a recurring symptom was resolved when the fix only addressed one specific subset of the problem, while a distinct root cause remained active.
generalized.lesson: A recurring symptom can have multiple root causes; a fix that is correct for its specific scope does not necessarily clear the entire symptom. Do not claim a flag is resolved solely because the code change is present; validate against live data. If the symptom persists due to a distinct root cause (e.g., missing data attributes vs. expired records), file that residual cause as its own goal and report both the fix and the remaining issue honestly.

original.title: Read the implementation, not just the call site, before resolving or acting on a code-behavior hypothesis
original.content: Resolving hypothesis 2026-05-27 (SSR creds) + filing g-008-45, I concluded email.ts bare new SESClient({region}) bypassed persistence.ts buildCredentials() and risked an SSR credential failure - from a SURFACE read of the two CALL SITES. Reading the buildCredentials IMPLEMENTATION (persistence.ts:199) showed it returns undefined by design (g-010-28): both DynamoDB and SES resolve the AMBIENT Amplify SSR compute role via the default chain. The premise (SSR provides no ambient creds) was FALSE; email.ts was correct; the fix would have been a no-op or speculative future-proofing. Verify-before-assuming (reading the code before editing) caught it - but only because I read the impl at execute time, not at hypothesis-resolve time. LESSON: a credential helper returning undefined vs injecting creds is INVISIBLE at the call site; resolve/act on code-behavior claims only after reading the implementation, not the call shape.
original.when_to_use: resolving a hypothesis about how code behaves; about to fix a perceived inconsistency between two call sites; a helper/wrapper sits between the call site and the behavior; framework-architecture

generalized.context: When resolving a hypothesis about code behavior where a helper or wrapper sits between the call site and the actual logic, specifically regarding credential resolution or state injection.
approach: Identify the perceived inconsistency between two call sites (e.g., one using a bare client instantiation vs. one using a helper).
Read the implementation of the helper/wrapper to determine if it returns undefined by design or performs ambient credential resolution.
Verify that the helper's behavior matches the call site's expectations before concluding a fix is needed.
generalized.outcome: Avoided a speculative fix or no-op change caused by a false premise that the helper lacked necessary credentials.
generalized.lesson: A credential helper returning undefined or performing ambient resolution is invisible at the call site; the call shape alone cannot reveal the implementation's behavior. When resolving hypotheses about code behavior, always read the implementation logic before editing. Do not assume a fix is needed based solely on surface-level call site differences.

original.title: When an expected behavior did not happen, check if the capability is WIRED, not just whether it EXISTS
original.content: A capability gap can hide as the script exists but no skill calls it. g-010-43: bids never appeared on /admin/approvals because the OutreachSend-staging script (queue-outreach-draft.sh) existed and worked, but was wired into NO skill -- draft-sources-sought-response said surface the draft for approval with no step that staged it, citing a future goal (g-010-30) that never landed. When researching why an expected/hardwired behavior did not fire, verify the EXISTENCE of the capability AND its WIRING into the process that should invoke it. Missing wiring is a more common gap than missing capability.
original.when_to_use: Diagnosing why an expected automated behavior did not occur; capability-gap research; I thought this was hardwired user reports

generalized.context: When diagnosing why an expected automated behavior or system capability failed to execute despite the underlying script or service appearing functional.
approach: Verify the existence and functionality of the capability (e.g., the script runs successfully in isolation).
Audit the process logic to confirm the capability is explicitly wired into the workflow that should invoke it.
Check for references to future goals or dependencies that were never implemented, which may have blocked the wiring.
generalized.outcome: Identified that the failure was not a missing capability, but a missing integration point where the script was never called by the process.
generalized.lesson: A capability gap often hides as a 'wiring' issue rather than a missing capability. If an expected behavior does not occur, verify not only that the script or service exists and works, but also that it is explicitly wired into the process flow that should invoke it. Missing integration points are a more common root cause than missing capabilities.

original.title: Cross-world daemon aspiration writes: readback is the source of truth, not the curl exit
original.content: When omni files aspirations into another world (ayoai) via its daemon-aware aspirations-add.sh, large multi-goal writes routinely (a) exceed RT_CURL_TIMEOUT=90s and/or (b) trigger an rt_call retry. POST #1 acquires the own-cloud lock and writes ALL goals; a slow response then causes either a curl timeout error OR a retry POST #2 that sees the just-written sibling goals (matched via origin_signal parent_aspiration:asp-NNN) and returns goal_duplication_blocked. BOTH are benign artifacts of POST #1 having succeeded; POST #2 is atomic and writes nothing, so exactly one clean copy exists. NEVER re-file or apply --override-duplication in response to a self-collision block or a timeout. ALWAYS verify by reading the aspiration back: aspirations-read.sh --id asp-NNN. Present with the expected goal count = landed clean (single copy); absent = genuinely blocked-with-no-write. Schema notes: ayoai aspirations-add requires explicit id (format asp-NNN, NOT memorable names), status, and goals; next id = max(NNN across active union archive) + 1. A genuine cross-aspiration false-positive block (incidental token overlap such as experience.jsonl or the word valid) is the only case where --override-duplication is correct, and only after verifying the matched goal is genuinely different work.
original.when_to_use: Filing or re-filing aspirations/goals into a remote world via daemon-aware scripts; interpreting a timeout or goal_duplication_blocked from aspirations-add.sh

generalized.context: When writing large multi-goal payloads to a remote system via a daemon-aware script, where the operation may trigger a timeout or a 'goal duplication blocked' error due to a retry mechanism seeing the initial write.
approach: Recognize that a timeout or 'duplication blocked' error often indicates a benign race condition where a retry saw the first successful write, not a failure.
Never re-file the payload or apply an override flag in response to these self-collision artifacts.
Always verify the state by reading the resource back using the canonical read script with the specific ID.
Confirm the write succeeded if the readback shows the expected goal count; treat absence of data as a genuine failure.
generalized.outcome: Avoided false-positive re-filing attempts and unnecessary overrides; ensured exactly one clean copy of the payload exists.
generalized.lesson: When a daemon-aware write operation fails with a timeout or a 'duplication blocked' error, assume the initial write succeeded and a retry caused the conflict. Do not re-file or override. Always verify by reading the resource back: if the readback contains the expected data, the write was successful; if absent, the write genuinely failed.

original.title: Direct aws-exec DynamoDB writes are invisible to world/changelog.jsonl + pipeline.jsonl -- query the live table to verify a record exists
original.content: g-010-43: a research sub-agent concluded no DynamoDB records exist for recon-05/06 by checking world/changelog.jsonl + pipeline.jsonl and finding nothing -- but the Contract rows DID exist at stage=qualifying (confirmed by a live aws-exec dynamodb get-item). Direct DynamoDB writes via world/scripts/*-write.sh (aws-exec.sh) do NOT pass through the world changelog or the hypothesis pipeline -- those track world-FILE writes only. To verify whether a Contract/OutreachSend/Prospect record exists, query the live zds-reachout table; never infer presence/absence from changelog or pipeline.jsonl. (verify-before-assuming: the schema/live probe is signal 2, not the changelog absence.)
original.when_to_use: Auditing whether a DynamoDB outreach/contract record exists; verifying a staging claim; any negative conclusion about zds-reachout records

generalized.context: When auditing whether a record exists in a cloud database (e.g., DynamoDB) after a script has performed a direct write operation.
approach: Check the local changelog or pipeline JSONL files to see if a write was logged
Observe that the record is missing from these files despite the write having occurred
Execute a live database query (e.g., get-item) against the target table to verify actual data presence
generalized.outcome: Confirmed that direct database writes bypass the local file-based changelog and pipeline tracking systems, leading to false negatives if relying solely on file logs.
generalized.lesson: Direct writes to cloud databases (via CLI or SDK) do not automatically populate local changelog or pipeline tracking files. Relying on these files to verify the existence or absence of records leads to false negatives. Always query the live database table directly to confirm record presence before concluding that a write failed or never happened.

original.title: Parallel-research-for-root-cause: fan out N subagents on DISJOINT READ targets, then triangulate + cross-check
original.content: g-010-43 root-cause research used 3 concurrent subagents on disjoint read targets (web-app approval flow / bid artifacts / agent bid-prep process). Benefits observed: (1) ~2x faster than serial; (2) triangulation -- 3 independent angles converged on one root cause, raising confidence; (3) cross-check caught an error -- subagent-2 concluded no DynamoDB records from changelog/pipeline.jsonl, but a live-table probe (informed by subagent-1s flow map) corrected it. The research analogue of Operating Principle 7 / rb-211 (parallel EXECUTION on disjoint WRITE targets): here the disjointness test is READ-target separation, and the synthesis step is triangulate-and-reconcile. Use when a root-cause question has a large/multi-surface search space (code + state + process). Always reconcile subagent claims against live ground truth before acting -- subagents can reach confident-but-wrong negatives (rb-219).
original.when_to_use: Root-cause research with a large multi-surface search space (code, external state, process); diagnosing why an expected behavior did not happen; any deep investigation where independent angles can triangulate

generalized.context: When conducting root-cause research across a large, multi-surface search space involving code, external state, and process flows.
approach: Spawn N concurrent subagents to investigate disjoint read targets (e.g., approval flows, artifact logs, process steps) simultaneously
Triangulate findings by converging independent angles to identify a single root cause
Cross-check subagent conclusions against live ground truth probes to catch confident-but-wrong negatives
Reconcile all subagent claims before taking action
generalized.outcome: Achieved ~2x faster investigation than serial execution; increased confidence through triangulation; detected and corrected errors where a subagent missed data that a live probe revealed
generalized.lesson: For deep investigations with a large multi-surface search space, fan out N subagents on disjoint read targets to enable parallel execution and triangulation. This approach accelerates discovery and raises confidence by converging independent angles. Crucially, always reconcile subagent claims against live ground truth before acting, as subagents can confidently reach incorrect negative conclusions that a direct probe can correct.

original.title: Chronic structural-heuristic false positives: record an exemption field, do not re-triage or blind-execute
original.content: When a structural/size heuristic chronically over-flags in a domain whose true criterion is semantic, three responses exist, one durable. Blind-execute=HARM (fragmenting coherent long-form nodes destroys retrieval, rb-94). Re-triage every cycle=WASTE (same false positives re-surface; rb-94 sat times_helpful=0 for 10 days because its judgment had nowhere to live). DURABLE FIX: add a per-item exemption field the heuristic honors (decompose_exempt:true) so a one-time semantic judgment is recorded and never re-surfaces. The structural gate cannot judge semantics; give the judgment a home. g-001-03 2026-06-07: get_decompose_candidates skips decompose_exempt nodes (5 lines), /tree SKILL.md gates the judgment before clustering, 18 coherent intelligence/consulting nodes exempted in one pass (candidate count 18 to 0). Generalizes to any over-flagging gate: lint false positives, audit zero-counts, pricing-anomaly flags.
original.when_to_use: When a structural/size gate keeps surfacing the same items as candidates every cycle but domain judgment says they are fine; long-form/heterogeneous knowledge bases where size is a poor proxy for the true split criterion.

generalized.context: When a structural or size-based heuristic chronically over-flags items in a domain where the true split criterion is semantic (e.g., long-form knowledge bases where document length is a poor proxy for content type), and re-triage cycles fail to resolve the issue.
approach: Identify that the structural gate cannot judge semantic content and is generating false positives.
Audit the candidate list to find items with zero-counts or consistent false flags.
Add a per-item exemption field (e.g., decompose_exempt:true) that the heuristic explicitly honors.
Record a one-time semantic judgment in this field to prevent the item from surfacing as a candidate in future cycles.
generalized.outcome: The structural gate stops flagging valid items, reducing noise from N to 0 in a single pass and preventing the same false positives from re-surfacing in subsequent cycles.
generalized.lesson: When a structural or size gate keeps surfacing the same items as candidates despite domain judgment saying they are fine, do not rely on re-triage or blind execution. Instead, add a per-item exemption field that the heuristic honors. This gives the semantic judgment a permanent home, allowing the structural gate to skip these nodes entirely and avoiding the waste of repeated false positives.

original.title: CONFIRMED-on-observation is not CONFIRMED-on-mechanism (unreflected-pool replay)
original.content: Replay (g-001-05, 2026-06-07) of CONFIRMED hypothesis 2026-05-23_g-001-08-empty-unreflected-pattern (conf 0.85) surfaced a mechanism mis-attribution. The OBSERVATION held: the unreflected-hypothesis pool is usually empty across ~9 g-001-08 closures. But the stated MECHANISM (resolutions self-mark reflected=true at resolve-time) is contradicted by 2 independent signals: (1) review-hypotheses --resolve explicitly sets reflected=false on each record (skill doc); (2) g-001-02 (computeRole, CONFIRMED 2026-06-07) currently sits with reflected=false, excluded from replay candidates, awaiting g-001-08 --learn. The pool is kept near-empty by the g-001-08/--learn CADENCE reflecting records shortly after resolve, NOT by resolve-time self-marking. The hypothesis was confirmed on the right observable for the wrong reason.
original.when_to_use: When a CONFIRMED hypothesis also encodes a causal mechanism; before treating a confirmed observation as proof of its stated cause, re-probe the mechanism independently.
original.failure_lesson: Mechanism self-marks-reflected-true was wrong; --resolve sets reflected=false and the g-001-08 cadence empties the pool. Do not bind a confirmed observation to an unverified cause (verify-before-assuming, Causal Attribution Claims).
original.description: A confirmed prediction can carry a wrong mechanism; observation-confirmation does not validate the causal story.

generalized.context: When a CONFIRMED hypothesis includes a specific causal mechanism explanation, and subsequent replay or observation confirms the observable effect but contradicts the stated cause.
approach: Separate the validation of the observable outcome (e.g., the pool is empty) from the validation of the proposed mechanism (e.g., self-marking at resolve-time).
Cross-reference independent signals or documentation to verify the actual mechanism (e.g., check if the resolve step explicitly sets a flag to false).
Identify the true causal agent by tracing the lifecycle (e.g., determine if a subsequent cadence or external process is responsible for the state change).
Reconcile the confirmed observation with the corrected mechanism to update the hypothesis without discarding the valid observation.
generalized.outcome: Identified that the hypothesis was confirmed on the correct observable (empty pool) but attributed the cause incorrectly (self-marking vs. external cadence).
generalized.lesson: A confirmed observation does not automatically validate the stated causal mechanism of a hypothesis. If an observation (like an empty pool) is confirmed, you must independently verify the mechanism (e.g., by checking if the resolve step actually sets the flag or if a subsequent process handles it). Do not bind a confirmed effect to an unverified cause; instead, re-probe the mechanism using independent signals or documentation to ensure the causal chain is accurate before finalizing the hypothesis.

original.title: vitest 4 / vite 8 transforms with OXC; enable .tsx tests via oxc.jsx.runtime not esbuild.jsx
original.content: The ZDS web app runs vitest 4.1.7 / vite 8.0.14, which transform with OXC, not esbuild. A .tsx test importing a component (e.g. a renderToStaticMarkup render test of a server component) fails vite import-analysis with: content contains invalid JS syntax / do not set jsx to preserve, because tsconfig sets jsx preserve for the Next build. Fix: add oxc: { jsx: { runtime: automatic } } to vitest.config.ts. The esbuild jsx option is IGNORED (vitest warns: oxc options will be used and esbuild options will be ignored). Inert for existing .ts tests; never touches the Next swc build. renderToStaticMarkup from react-dom/server renders async server components in the node test env without jsdom: call renderToStaticMarkup(await PageComponent()) and assert on the returned HTML string.

generalized.context: When running unit tests for a web application using Vitest 4+ and Vite 8+ with the OXC transformer (instead of esbuild), specifically when testing React Server Components that use renderToStaticMarkup.
approach: Configure the test runner to use OXC's automatic JSX runtime via oxc: { jsx: { runtime: 'automatic' } } in the config file.
Ensure the test imports the server component and calls renderToStaticMarkup(await Component()) to render it in the Node environment without jsdom.
Assert the resulting HTML string directly.
generalized.outcome: Resolved 'invalid JS syntax' import errors caused by the mismatch between the project's 'jsx: preserve' TypeScript setting and the default OXC behavior, while correctly rendering server components in the Node test environment.
generalized.lesson: When using Vitest 4+ with Vite 8+ and the OXC transformer, you must explicitly set 'runtime: automatic' in the OXC config to handle JSX correctly, as the esbuild options are ignored and OXC defaults to 'preserve' which conflicts with standard test setups. Additionally, render server components in Node tests by awaiting the component and passing it to renderToStaticMarkup, as jsdom is not available in this environment.

original.title: Stale goal premise + forged-tooling claim drift: verify actual behavior before implementing
original.content: g-008-38 was filed weeks before execution claiming 'NO app/sitemap.ts exists (dead mechanism)' and asking to wire sitemap.ts to consume public/.sitemap-registry.jsonl. By execution time the premise was stale: app/sitemap.ts EXISTED (a hand-maintained curated array), the registry was a DEAD write (add-page.sh wrote it, nothing read it), and the /lp/:slug rewrite the manage-website SKILL.md claimed add-page ensures was never implemented. The correct fix was the OPPOSITE of the goal title: remove the dead registry-write (not wire sitemap.ts to consume it), add the rewrite once to next.config.js, reconcile the SKILL.md claims. Two drift sources compounded: an aged goal premise, plus forged-tooling that writes artifacts nothing consumes and a SKILL.md documenting behavior the companion script never implements.
original.when_to_use: executing an aged or Idea goal, or any goal whose premise references tooling behavior or file state. Read the actual companion script AND the actual target file before implementing; do not trust the goal text or the SKILL.md claim. The right fix may be the inverse of the goal title.

generalized.context: When executing an aged goal or any task where the premise relies on the existence of specific files, tooling behavior, or configuration states.
approach: Read the actual companion script and the actual target file to verify current state
Check if the referenced tooling writes artifacts that are actually consumed by other parts of the system
Verify if documentation (e.g., SKILL.md) claims match the actual implementation in the codebase
Identify if the goal's proposed fix is the inverse of the actual problem (e.g., removing dead code instead of wiring new connections)
generalized.outcome: Avoided implementing unnecessary wiring for dead mechanisms and corrected the system by removing unused write operations and implementing the missing rewrite logic.
generalized.lesson: When a goal premise references file existence or tooling behavior, verify the actual state of the codebase before implementing. Aged goals often contain stale premises where the described state no longer exists. Additionally, be wary of 'forged tooling' (scripts that write artifacts nothing consumes) and documentation that claims features the code does not implement. The correct fix may be the inverse of the goal title: instead of wiring a new consumer, you may need to remove a dead producer or implement a missing feature.

original.title: Tree distill-candidate metric: verify distilled-flag + strategic value before re-distilling
original.content: The /tree maintain DISTILL metric (low_utility / large_mediocre triggers from tree-read.sh --distill-candidates) produces false positives. Observed 2026-06-08 (g-001-03): dow-contracting-startups-101 flagged worst (utility 0.2, times_helpful 0, times_noise 7) but is ALREADY distilled (distilled:true, 2026-05-29) AND user-reemphasized (user re-fed the a16z DoW primer, engraved into asp-014); re-distilling would strip the preserved decision-kernel. 4 of 5 candidates showed times_helpful=0 despite 6-10 retrievals each, indicating times_helpful is under-incremented system-wide, so low utility_ratio is a soft signal not a distill mandate. times_noise is more reliable but can be stale (accrued before a prior distillation). Correct action: apply nothing, document skips in the run-record, do not damage already-distilled or strategic-core nodes.
original.when_to_use: Running /tree maintain and evaluating DISTILL candidates: before re-distilling a flagged node, (1) check its distilled front-matter flag, (2) check whether it is strategic-core or user-reemphasized, (3) weight times_noise over times_helpful (under-counted).

generalized.context: When running a knowledge maintenance pipeline that flags nodes for re-distillation based on low utility or high noise metrics.
approach: Verify the node's 'already distilled' status flag before initiating any re-distillation process.
Check if the node is marked as strategic-core or user-reemphasized to identify preserved decision-kernels.
Prioritize 'times_noise' over 'times_helpful' when evaluating utility, as the latter is often under-incremented system-wide and thus a soft signal.
Recognize that low utility ratios may be stale artifacts from prior distillations rather than indicators of current irrelevance.
generalized.outcome: Prevented the accidental stripping of preserved decision-kernels from already-distilled or strategically important nodes.
generalized.lesson: Before re-distilling a flagged knowledge node, strictly verify its 'already distilled' status and strategic importance. Do not trust 'times_helpful' metrics as a primary distillation trigger, as they are frequently under-incremented system-wide; instead, rely more heavily on 'times_noise' which is a more reliable indicator of actual degradation. Re-distilling nodes that are already processed or strategically emphasized risks destroying preserved decision-kernels.

original.title: Re-scope and correct node forward-references when a goal delivers narrower than its prior encoding assumed
original.content: A tree node encoded for goal G2 often forward-attributes future work to a later goal G3. When the actual scope of G3 turns out narrower than the G2 encoding assumed, closing G3 MUST (a) re-scope each orphaned piece to an explicit new goal and (b) correct the forward-reference in the node. Never silently absorb the extra work (scope creep, violates implementation-discipline.md) nor silently drop it (lost signal). Canonical: g-019-03 was scoped to submissionClass intake classification (document-found-opportunity + advance-contract-stage). The g-019-02 encoding in reachout-data-model.md had attributed BOTH Contract-draft inheritance AND the rfi_response state-machine transition to g-019-03. At close: re-scoped inheritance to g-019-07 (Idea), rfi transition to g-019-08 (Investigate), and corrected the two node forward-references + Cross-References + front-matter trigger.
original.when_to_use: When closing a goal whose target tree node forward-references this goal for work: verify the actual delivered scope against what the node claims this goal does, and re-scope or correct any mismatch.

generalized.context: When closing a goal whose target node in the knowledge tree forward-references future work to that goal, verify the actual delivered scope against what the node claims.
approach: Identify the forward-references and cross-references in the target node that attribute work to the current goal
Compare the actual scope of work delivered in the current goal against the assumptions made in the node's encoding
For any orphaned pieces of work that were not delivered: re-scope them to explicit new goals
Update the target node to correct the forward-references, cross-references, and front-matter triggers to reflect the new goal assignments
generalized.outcome: Prevented scope creep by not silently absorbing undelivered work and avoided lost signals by not silently dropping work; ensured the knowledge tree accurately reflects the current state of implementation.
generalized.lesson: When a goal node forward-references work to a future goal, and the actual delivery scope is narrower than assumed, you must explicitly re-scope the orphaned work to new goals and correct the forward-references in the node. Never silently absorb the extra work (which violates implementation discipline) nor silently drop it (which loses critical signal). The canonical process involves updating the node's forward-references, cross-references, and front-matter triggers to align with the re-scoped goals.

original.title: Local build-check must mirror CI (vitest+tsc), not just build - build-pass != test-pass
original.content: g-012-18-a added an OPTIONAL prospectToken field to OutreachEmail + a pass-through in outreach-dispatch.ts. npm run build PASSED (optional TS field is type-valid) but npx vitest run FAILED: three exact-match toHaveBeenCalledWith({to,subject,body}) dispatch-test assertions (outreach-dispatch.test.ts x2 + outreach-dispatch-ddb-fallback.test.ts) broke because the send mock now received an extra prospectToken key. The OLD build-check.sh ran ONLY npm run build, so the failure shipped to PR #3 unseen and CI (ci.yml: npx vitest run + npx tsc --noEmit) caught it post-push - user fixed the assertions himself (commits 0b0cb27, b754222). Also: the pull_request CI event tests the MERGE-with-main result, which surfaced a THIRD stale assertion (ddb-fallback) the branch-tip push run did not hit. FIX: build-check.sh now runs vitest + tsc + build in CI order (g-012-39). build-pass is necessary but NOT sufficient - an exact-match assertion (toHaveBeenCalledWith vs objectContaining) breaks on ANY new payload field even when types are valid.
original.when_to_use: Before pushing any web-app change that adds/removes a field on a payload asserted by toHaveBeenCalledWith; whenever validating a producer-side change locally. Run build-check.sh (now vitest+tsc+build), never just npm run build.
original.failure_lesson: A green local build is not a green CI. Mirror the CI gate locally or the gap ships.

generalized.context: When adding or removing fields in a payload that is asserted using exact-match matchers (e.g., toHaveBeenCalledWith) in unit tests.
approach: Run the full CI gate locally (unit tests + type checking + build) instead of only running the build command.
Ensure local validation mirrors the CI pipeline order and scope to catch assertion failures caused by new payload keys.
Avoid relying solely on type validity, as exact-match assertions break on any new field even if the type is correct.
generalized.outcome: Prevented a regression where a local build passed but CI failed due to broken test assertions, ensuring the fix was caught before the merge.
generalized.lesson: A passing local build is not sufficient to guarantee a passing CI pipeline. When modifying payload structures, exact-match assertions (like toHaveBeenCalledWith) will fail if new fields are added, even if the code is type-valid. You must mirror the full CI gate (tests + type checking + build) locally before pushing, as the build step alone cannot detect assertion mismatches caused by schema evolution.

original.title: Read the canonical mechanism before assuming an Apply goal is agent-executable
original.content: Some Apply goals are human-gated by security design. g-016-43 (Apply AGENT_WRITE_PATH change) looked agent-executable (participants [agent], user-approved), but the canonical mechanism (grant-agent-write-paths.py) documented that omni MUST NOT run it: AGENT_WRITE_PATH is the security membrane and no agent may modify its own or another agents write scope. Two reinforcing reasons it is human-only: (1) self.md forbids editing Ayoai-Mind directly; (2) granting write-scope is a credential grant (capability-before-user human-only class). KEY MECHANISM INSIGHT: Python open() inside a Bash-run script bypasses the Write/Edit tool hooks, so the membrane is enforced by convention + the script docstring, NOT by a hook - which is exactly why it must be human-run. Lesson: before executing an Apply/grant goal, read the canonical script/mechanism docs; some applies are human-gated even WITH approval of the change. verify-before-assuming (read actual state) also confirmed the change was already applied - the goal was complete on arrival.

generalized.context: When an Apply goal requests a security-sensitive configuration change (e.g., modifying an agent's write scope or path) that appears agent-executable based on approval status.
approach: Read the canonical script or mechanism documentation to verify execution constraints.
Identify if the operation bypasses standard tool hooks (e.g., using raw file I/O like Python open() inside a shell script instead of the managed tool interface).
Confirm if the operation is human-gated due to security membranes (credential grants) or self-modification prohibitions.
Verify the current system state to check if the change was already applied prior to execution.
generalized.outcome: Prevented an unauthorized agent execution of a security-critical operation and avoided redundant work by confirming the state was already updated.
generalized.lesson: Before executing an Apply goal that modifies security boundaries or agent capabilities, read the canonical mechanism documentation. Some operations are human-gated by design (e.g., credential grants, self-modification prohibitions) even if they have approval. If the canonical script uses raw system calls (like Python open() in Bash) to bypass managed tool hooks, the operation must be human-run. Always verify the current state before assuming the goal is pending.

original.title: New Lambda S3-write prefix needs an IAM PutObject grant for that prefix
original.content: When an S3-triggered Lambda gains a NEW write prefix (e.g. adding outreach-replies/ alongside the existing agent-inbox/), the execution role IAM policy almost always scopes s3:PutObject to the OLD prefix only - so the new write fails AccessDenied at runtime even though the code is correct. Verified on ForwardEmailReceivedAtZacharyKysarDotCom (g-012-18-b): ForwardEmailLambdaPerms granted PutObject on zacharykysaremail/agent-inbox/* only. Two-part fix: (1) check the role inline policy (aws iam get-role-policy) BEFORE assuming the write works; (2) make the manifest/PutObject step non-fatal so the primary action (forwarding the reply) still happens if the grant is missing - never let a missing IAM grant swallow the high-value payload.
original.when_to_use: adding a new S3 write prefix to an existing Lambda; AccessDenied on s3:PutObject from a Lambda; Lambda code correct but write fails at runtime; email-infrastructure

generalized.context: When an S3-triggered Lambda function gains a new write prefix (e.g., adding a new folder path alongside an existing one), the execution role's IAM policy often scopes s3:PutObject to the old prefix only.
approach: Check the role's inline IAM policy (using get-role-policy) BEFORE assuming the write will work
Make the manifest/PutObject step non-fatal so the primary action still executes if the grant is missing
generalized.outcome: Prevents the high-value payload from being swallowed by a silent AccessDenied error caused by a missing IAM grant for the new path.
generalized.lesson: When an S3-triggered Lambda gains a new write prefix, the execution role's IAM policy almost always scopes s3:PutObject to the old prefix only. You must verify the inline policy before assuming the write works. Crucially, make the manifest/PutObject step non-fatal so the primary action still happens if the grant is missing; never let a missing IAM grant swallow the high-value payload.

original.title: Grep the consumer codebase for a field before estimating a UI goal that depends on it
original.content: g-019-04 (build Action-Required admin page filtering on submissionClass) looked like a clone-an-existing-page goal, but a grep of the web-app lib/+app/ for submissionClass returned NOTHING -- the runner had been writing the attribute onto DynamoDB rows since g-019-02 but the web-app OutreachSend type never read it. The UI was blind to a field the backend had been writing for days (invisible plumbing debt). That hidden data-layer prerequisite plus two embedded data-model decisions made the goal compound; decomposing it (g-019-09 plumbing -> g-019-10 page -> g-019-11 filter) was the right call. LESSON: when a UI/consumer goal depends on a field, grep the CONSUMER codebase for that field BEFORE estimating scope -- a producer-written attribute the consumer does not read is silent plumbing debt that turns a clone into a multi-part feature.

generalized.context: When estimating the scope of a UI or consumer feature that depends on a specific data field, verify whether the consumer codebase actually reads that field.
approach: Perform a grep or search for the target field name within the consumer application's source code before committing to a 'clone existing page' strategy.
Identify if the field exists only in the producer's data layer (e.g., database rows) but is absent from the consumer's data model or type definitions.
Decompose the goal into distinct phases: first resolve the missing data plumbing (adding the field to the consumer model), then implement the UI logic.
generalized.outcome: Avoided underestimating scope by recognizing that a 'clone' was actually a multi-part feature requiring hidden data-layer plumbing and model updates.
generalized.lesson: When a UI or consumer goal depends on a specific field, grep the consumer codebase for that field BEFORE estimating scope. A field written by a producer but never read by the consumer represents silent plumbing debt; assuming it exists leads to underestimating the effort required to bridge the gap between data storage and application logic.

original.title: Fail-closed by type-distinctness: a new non-acting terminal state should be a distinct enum the existing gate already excludes
original.content: When a new terminal state must NOT trigger a gated/guarded action, give it a DISTINCT enum value that the existing gate already excludes - do not add a new boolean/flag that the action path must remember to check. The gate then enforces the invariant STRUCTURALLY with zero new guard code, and a one-line test proves it. Canonical (g-019-10): the manual_submit mark-done needed to never dispatch. Instead of a 'do not dispatch' flag, markDone records SendDecision='submitted', a value distinct from 'approved'. isSendApproved already requires 'approved', so assertDispatchAllowed stays fail-closed for any submitted item automatically. Corollary: a new enum member is a cross-file obligation - grep every consumer (.decision===, .status===, Record<Enum>) before shipping; g-019-10 found exactly one binary assumption to fix (a dashboard 'Approved':'Rejected' label that would have mislabeled submitted as Rejected). Also: when an enum field couples two types (here recordSignOff does send.status=decision so SendDecision must be a subset of SendApprovalStatus), add the new member to BOTH or typecheck breaks.

generalized.context: When designing a state machine where a new terminal state must strictly prevent a specific guarded action from executing.
approach: Assign the new terminal state a distinct enum value that the existing action gate already excludes (e.g., if the gate checks for 'approved', use 'submitted' instead of a new 'do_not_dispatch' flag).
Ensure the existing gate logic remains unchanged, relying on the structural exclusion of the new enum value to enforce the invariant.
Perform a cross-file grep for all consumers of the enum (switch statements, type checks, status mappings) to identify and fix any binary assumptions that might misinterpret the new state.
If the enum field couples two types (e.g., a status field that must be a subset of an approval status), add the new member to both type definitions to prevent type-checking failures.
generalized.outcome: The system enforces the 'fail-closed' invariant structurally with zero new guard code, and a single-line test confirms the action is blocked for the new state.
generalized.lesson: To ensure a new terminal state never triggers a specific guarded action, assign it a distinct enum value that the existing gate already excludes, rather than adding a new boolean flag that the action path must explicitly check. This approach enforces the invariant structurally with zero new guard code. Additionally, because enum changes are cross-file obligations, you must grep all consumers (switch statements, type checks, status mappings) before shipping to fix any binary assumptions. If the enum field couples two types, ensure the new member is added to both type definitions to avoid breaking type checks.

original.title: Stale .next/types fails typecheck after web-app branch switch
original.content: First npm run typecheck after git checkout of a different branch in Zak-Data-Solutions-Web-App failed TS2307 Cannot-find-module for .next/types/app/admin/action-required/page.ts -- a generated type left over from a build on the PREVIOUS branch (which had that route). Next.js writes .next/types and tsconfig includes them, so tsc validates stale generated types for routes the current branch does not have. rm -rf .next then typecheck exited 0.
original.when_to_use: Before web-app typecheck/build right after a git branch switch, or when typecheck fails on a .next/types file referencing a route you did not touch.
original.failure_lesson: After switching web-app branches whose route sets diverge, run rm -rf .next before npm run typecheck or npm run build. The generated-types cache is per-branch and tsconfig-included; a stale entry produces a false TS2307 unrelated to your change (incident g-019-12).

generalized.context: When performing a typecheck or build immediately after switching git branches in a Next.js application where the new branch lacks routes that existed in the previous branch.
approach: Identify that the typecheck fails with TS2307 Cannot-find-module for a file in .next/types corresponding to a route from the previous branch
Recognize that Next.js generates .next/types per-branch and the tsconfig includes these generated types, causing validation against stale data
Execute rm -rf .next to clear the generated type cache before running the typecheck or build
generalized.outcome: The typecheck exits successfully (0) without false-positive errors regarding missing modules.
generalized.lesson: In Next.js applications, the .next/types directory contains generated type definitions specific to the current branch's route structure. When switching branches, stale entries from the previous branch remain in .next/types and are included via tsconfig, causing TS2307 Cannot-find-module errors for routes that no longer exist. To prevent false-positive build failures, always clear the .next directory (rm -rf .next) before running typecheck or build after a branch switch.

original.title: Routing-field feature: plumb -> build-branch-with-safe-terminal -> wire-consumers-through-shared-SSOT-complement
original.content: When introducing a routing field that splits one flow into N branches, decompose into three ordered goals: (1) PLUMB the field through the type + EVERY write path -- interface, persistence, AND every in-memory factory/constructor (a declared-but-undropped field is invisible plumbing debt, rb-232 mirror; caught in g-019-10 where registerOutreachSend silently dropped submissionClass). (2) BUILD the new branch with a structurally-safe terminal state -- give the new terminal a DISTINCT enum value the existing safety gate already EXCLUDES, so the invariant holds with zero new guard code (rb-233 fail-closed-by-type-distinctness; SendDecision=submitted is not approved, so assertDispatchAllowed stays fail-closed). (3) WIRE the consumers through a SINGLE shared helper that encodes the default/back-compat rule, so the per-branch filters are EXACT COMPLEMENTS -- an item can never land in two branches or none. The shared helper at the wire step is load-bearing: inlining the default at each consumer lets the filters drift into overlap/gap. Verified end-to-end on asp-019: g-019-09 plumb submissionClass, g-019-10 build manual_submit queue + submitted terminal, g-019-11 wire approvals/action-required via effectiveSubmissionClass.
original.when_to_use: Before estimating or starting any goal that adds a classification/routing/mode field to an existing flow with multiple downstream consumers. Use the 3-goal decomposition; put the back-compat default in one exported helper consumed by all branches.

generalized.context: When introducing a routing field that splits a single data flow into multiple downstream branches (e.g., adding a classification or mode field to an existing pipeline with multiple consumers).
approach: PLUMB the new field through every write path: update the data type definition, persistence layer, and critically, every in-memory factory or constructor to ensure the field is never silently dropped.

BUILD the new branch with a structurally-safe terminal state by assigning it a distinct enum value that existing safety gates already exclude, ensuring the system remains fail-closed without adding new guard code.

WIRE all consumers through a SINGLE shared helper function that encodes the default/back-compat rule, ensuring per-branch filters act as exact complements so an item cannot land in two branches or none.
generalized.outcome: Prevented invisible plumbing debt where fields are dropped in factories, avoided introducing new safety gate logic by leveraging existing distinctness, and ensured mutually exclusive routing branches via a centralized default rule.
generalized.lesson: When adding a routing field to a multi-branch flow, decompose the work into three ordered steps: (1) PLUMB the field through every write path, including in-memory factories and constructors, to prevent silent data loss; (2) BUILD the new branch with a terminal state using a distinct enum value that existing safety gates already exclude, maintaining the fail-closed invariant without new guards; (3) WIRE consumers through a single shared helper that encodes the default rule, ensuring branch filters are exact complements to prevent overlap or gaps.

original.title: Gotcha: a code/template merge does NOT re-seed already-stored DynamoDB outreach drafts
original.content: g-020-03: PR#9 (g-019-13) rewrote the 6 federal OSDBU email bodies and added standard-signature + capability-statement-PDF in the web-app code, but the 6 pending OutreachSend drafts in zds-reachout were created 2026-06-02..06-07 with their bodies STORED at creation time. Merging the code does not propagate to stored drafts -- the live draft queue lags the merged code by one quality pass. Signature + PDF attachment are DISPATCH-time additions (apply to any draft at send via lib/email.ts/outreach-dispatch.ts), but the email BODY is frozen at draft-creation. To make queued drafts reflect code-side template changes, regenerate/re-seed them into DynamoDB; a fresh `git merge` is not enough.
original.when_to_use: after merging outreach email-template/quality changes, before telling the user that queued drafts reflect those changes

generalized.context: When merging code changes that update email templates or body content, but the draft records in the database were created prior to the merge.
approach: Identify that the email body is frozen at the moment of draft creation in the database
Recognize that signature and attachment logic are applied dynamically at dispatch time, not at creation
Understand that a standard code merge does not retroactively update the frozen body text in existing draft records
generalized.outcome: The live draft queue continues to serve outdated email bodies despite the codebase reflecting the latest templates, creating a lag between code quality and user-facing content.
generalized.lesson: When email draft bodies are stored at creation time, a code merge does not automatically update queued drafts. Changes to templates or body content only apply to new drafts or are appended at dispatch time (for signatures/attachments). To reflect code-side template changes in existing queued drafts, you must explicitly regenerate or re-seed the draft records in the database; a git merge alone is insufficient.

original.title: Empty stdout is a confounded signal: check rc AND stderr before concluding a read returned nothing
original.content: Measuring whether a wrapper/daemon read returns empty must distinguish two failure modes: (a) malformed or mode-flagless request -> structured error on STDERR, rc=1, empty STDOUT; (b) genuine empty-from-contention -> empty STDOUT, rc=0. Piping 2>/dev/null collapses (a) into a fake (b). Incident 2026-06-09 (g-001-08, hypothesis 2026-05-24_daemon-read-wrapper-empty-during-background-write): the hypothesis predicted aspirations-read.sh returns empty under a background-write lock. Two probe attempts produced 30 of 30 empty -- both malformed. aspirations-read.sh --id with a goal id looks up a nonexistent ASPIRATION (--id takes asp-NNN, not g-NNN-NN), and a bare --source agent omits the REQUIRED mode flag (one of --active / --id / --summary / --meta / --archive / --blocked / --stepping_stones / --active_compact). The daemon returned clean not_found and missing_flag JSON on stderr throughout. The corrected probe (aspirations-read.sh --active --source agent, capturing rc AND stderr): baseline rc=0 len=132011; under 15 lock-holding background writes, 30 of 30 concurrent reads non-empty rc=0. Hypothesis CORRECTED -- the daemon serializes and returns the last-committed snapshot; it never empty-reads under contention.
original.when_to_use: Before concluding any wrapper or daemon read returned empty (under contention, lock, or restart), and when designing any concurrency or contention probe. If your probe pipes 2>/dev/null, you are measuring nothing -- capture rc and stderr separately first.
original.failure_lesson: A read returning empty STDOUT with rc != 0 has told you nothing about contention; it most likely failed to parse the request. Never 2>/dev/null the very channel whose emptiness you are measuring. aspirations-read.sh requires a mode flag, and --id resolves an aspiration id, not a goal id.

generalized.context: When measuring whether a wrapper or daemon read returns empty data under contention, lock, or restart conditions.
approach: Distinguish between two failure modes: (a) malformed requests causing structured errors on STDERR with rc=1, and (b) genuine empty content due to contention with rc=0.
Never pipe STDERR to /dev/null (e.g., 2>/dev/null) when measuring output emptiness, as this collapses error signals into false positives.
Verify that the probe command includes all required mode flags and uses correct identifier formats before assuming the daemon is unresponsive.
Capture both the return code (rc) and STDERR output separately to validate the request was parsed correctly.
generalized.outcome: Corrected probes that included required mode flags and captured STDERR showed that the daemon consistently returned non-empty data (rc=0) even under background write contention, disproving the hypothesis that it returns empty reads during locks.
generalized.lesson: A read returning empty STDOUT with a non-zero return code (rc != 0) indicates a request parsing failure, not contention. If your probe pipes STDERR to /dev/null, you are measuring nothing because you are hiding the error signal. Always capture rc and STDERR separately to distinguish between 'no data available' and 'invalid request.' Additionally, ensure your probe includes all mandatory mode flags and uses the correct identifier format (e.g., distinguishing between aspiration IDs and goal IDs) to avoid triggering 'not found' or 'missing flag' errors that manifest as empty output.

original.title: Rebase WIP onto a moved main without reverting merged PRs: additive re-apply
original.content: When a feature branch was based on a stale commit and other PRs merged onto main meanwhile, committing the whole working tree DELETES the merged PRs changes (a revert of merged work). Safe procedure: (1) commit WIP to a temp branch so nothing is lost; (2) branch fresh off origin/main; (3) for files NOT touched by the merged PRs (prove with git diff stale-base origin/main -- file), take your edited versions directly - edits apply cleanly because the base is identical; (4) for files the merged PRs ALSO touched, re-apply ONLY your additive changes onto origin/main version, recovering exact text from the temp WIP commit via git show temp:path; (5) verify both the merged-PR symbols AND your new symbols survive via grep. Result: zero merged work reverted. Used in g-019-13 to layer the email-quality build onto already-merged PRs 6/7/8.
original.when_to_use: Committing a feature branch whose base is older than current origin/main, especially after stacked PRs merged; any time git diff shows your branch would delete files you did not author.

generalized.context: When a feature branch is based on a stale commit and other pull requests have merged onto the main branch, committing the entire working tree directly would delete the changes from those merged PRs.
approach: Commit the current WIP to a temporary branch to preserve the work without applying it yet.
Create a fresh branch directly from origin/main.
For files not touched by the merged PRs, copy the edited versions directly from the temp branch (edits apply cleanly as the base is identical).
For files touched by the merged PRs, re-apply only the additive changes by extracting the exact text from the temp WIP commit and overlaying it onto the origin/main version.
Verify that both the merged PR symbols and the new symbols survive using a text search (e.g., grep).
generalized.outcome: Zero merged work was reverted; the new changes were successfully layered onto the existing merged PRs.
generalized.lesson: When integrating a feature branch onto a main branch that has diverged due to merged PRs, never commit the entire working tree directly, as this acts as a revert of merged changes. Instead, isolate the WIP in a temp branch, then selectively re-apply changes: copy untouched edits directly and re-apply only additive modifications to touched files by extracting them from the temp commit. This ensures zero loss of merged work while cleanly layering new changes.

original.title: gh pr merge --delete-branch leaves local main stale; do not fix the stale working-tree files
original.content: After gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch, gh switches your local checkout to local main and tries to fast-forward it. If local main diverged (e.g. an orphan pre-squash duplicate of an earlier PR) the ff fails (Not possible to fast-forward, aborting) and the working tree now shows STALE local-main content. This is a LOCAL-checkout artifact ONLY: origin/main (the deploy source, e.g. Amplify auto-deploy) is correct. DO NOT edit or fix the stale files - that would be a wrong-direction change. Verify origin/main has your merged work via git show origin/main:file, then optionally reset local main to origin/main. Observed g-019-13: local main was 1 ahead (orphan dup of PR 1) and 9 behind since the first squash-merge; benign because all work branches off origin/main.
original.when_to_use: Right after gh pr merge --delete-branch, if the working tree suddenly shows old content or git reports local main diverged.

generalized.context: After merging a pull request with a command that deletes the remote branch (e.g., `git pull --rebase origin/main` or `gh pr merge --delete-branch`), if the local main branch diverged due to an orphan duplicate or local drift, the fast-forward may fail, leaving the working tree with stale content.
approach: Recognize that the stale working tree is a local artifact only; the remote origin/main (the deployment source) contains the correct merged state.
Verify the remote state is correct by inspecting the file content via `git show origin/main:filename`.
Reset the local main branch to match the remote (`git reset --hard origin/main`) instead of manually editing the stale files.
generalized.outcome: Avoided introducing wrong-direction changes to the working tree while restoring the local branch to the correct remote state.
generalized.lesson: When a pull request merge that deletes the remote branch fails due to local divergence, the resulting stale working tree files are artifacts of the failed fast-forward. Do not manually edit these files to fix them, as this introduces incorrect changes. Instead, verify the remote branch holds the correct merged state and reset the local branch to match the remote.

original.title: SES attachments require SendRawEmail + multipart/mixed MIME (SendEmail cannot attach)
original.content: AWS SES SendEmailCommand has NO attachment support. To send an email with a file attachment (e.g. a capability-statement PDF) hand-build a multipart/mixed MIME message and send via SendRawEmailCommand with Source, Destinations, RawMessage.Data. The raw builder must: set a multipart/mixed boundary; put the text body as the first part; base64-encode each attachment wrapped at 76 cols with Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding base64, Content-Disposition attachment; RFC2047-encode non-ASCII subjects; and sanitize header values (strip CR/LF) to neutralize header injection. IAM needs ses:SendRawEmail (distinct from ses:SendEmail). Built in lib/email.ts buildRawMimeMessage for g-019-13.
original.when_to_use: Any outreach or transactional email that must carry a file attachment via SES in the Zak-Data-Solutions web-app or any SES integration.

generalized.context: When sending emails via AWS SES (or similar transactional email services) that require file attachments, note that the standard SendEmail API often lacks native attachment support.
approach: Identify that the standard SendEmail command cannot handle attachments
Manually construct a multipart/mixed MIME message structure
Place the text body as the first part of the MIME message
Base64-encode each attachment and wrap it with Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, and Content-Disposition headers
Apply RFC2047 encoding to non-ASCII subjects and sanitize header values (strip CR/LF) to prevent header injection
Ensure the IAM role has the specific 'SendRawEmail' permission (distinct from 'SendEmail')
generalized.outcome: Successfully transmitted emails with file attachments without relying on unsupported API features or workarounds.
generalized.lesson: When a transactional email service's standard SendEmail API does not support attachments, you must bypass it by hand-building a multipart/mixed MIME message. This involves encoding the body and attachments as base64 parts within a raw message payload. Crucially, you must sanitize all header values (stripping CR/LF) to neutralize header injection attacks and ensure the IAM role explicitly permits 'SendRawEmail', as this permission is distinct from the standard 'SendEmail' permission.

original.title: Scope a terse user directive against live system state BEFORE filing the aspiration
original.content: When an inbound user directive is terse (e.g. a four-word commit-and-merge ask), do NOT file a vague aspiration from prose alone. First read the relevant live state (git status of each affected repo, infra-health, DynamoDB rows), THEN file. On 2026-06-09 the terse directive became two precise verifiable goals only because git status revealed the exact divergences first: web-app ahead 1 / behind 9 vs origin/main, Mind repo 40 commits ahead unpushed. The intake quality came from reading real state, not parsing prose harder. Corollary: a new directive often subsumes already-queued work (g-019-13 was folded into g-021-01) - cross-check the queue and supersede rather than duplicate.
original.when_to_use: inbound user directive is terse or high-level; directive maps to concrete system or repo state the agent can read; about to file via create-aspiration from-user; operational

generalized.context: When an inbound user directive is terse or high-level (e.g., a four-word request to commit and merge) and maps to concrete system state the agent can read.
approach: Do not file a vague aspiration based solely on parsing the prose of the directive.
First read the relevant live system state (e.g., git status of affected repositories, infrastructure health, database rows) to identify exact divergences or current queue status.
File the aspiration only after grounding it in this verified state, which transforms the directive into precise, verifiable goals.
Cross-check existing work queues to see if the new directive subsumes already-queued tasks, and supersede duplicates rather than creating redundant work.
generalized.outcome: The intake quality improved because the directive became two precise, verifiable goals only after reading the real system state (revealing exact divergences) rather than parsing the prose harder.
generalized.lesson: When an inbound user directive is terse or high-level, do not file a vague aspiration from prose alone. First read the relevant live system state (repository status, infrastructure health, database rows) to identify exact divergences. This grounds the directive in reality, transforming it into precise, verifiable goals. Additionally, always cross-check the work queue, as a new directive often subsumes already-queued tasks; supersede duplicates rather than creating redundant work.

original.title: Patch-id-compare local-ahead commits against upstream before reconciling a diverged branch via PR
original.content: When a branch is ahead N / behind M and you intend to reconcile by rebasing-then-pushing or opening a PR, FIRST compare each local-ahead commit against the upstream log. If the upstream already contains a commit with the same git patch-id --stable, the local commit is redundant (the user or another path already merged identical work) and the correct reconcile is a local-only git rebase onto the upstream, which auto-skips the already-applied commit. Opening a PR for a redundant commit creates a duplicate or empty PR and, for a deploy-on-merge repo, triggers a needless production deploy. Incident 2026-06-09 g-021-01: local 3ca0d6f (g-012-37 tests) had the same patch-id as upstream 90d2dc8 (the user merged it as PR #1); rebase auto-dropped it and synced local main with zero remote mutation, honoring branch-protection.
original.when_to_use: a git branch is ahead N / behind M of its upstream; about to reconcile by rebasing+pushing or opening a PR; the repo deploys on merge to the protected branch; operational

generalized.context: When a feature branch is ahead N and behind M of its upstream, and you intend to reconcile it via rebase-then-push or by opening a pull request.
approach: Compare each local-ahead commit against the upstream log using the stable patch identifier (e.g., git patch-id --stable)
Identify if the upstream already contains a commit with the same patch-id, indicating the work was already merged by another path
If a match is found, perform a local-only rebase onto upstream to auto-skip the redundant commit instead of pushing or opening a PR
generalized.outcome: Avoided creating a duplicate or empty pull request and prevented a needless production deployment for a repository configured to deploy on merge.
generalized.lesson: When reconciling a diverged branch, always verify local-ahead commits against the upstream log using stable patch identifiers before pushing or opening a PR. If the upstream already contains a commit with the same patch-id, the local work is redundant; a local-only rebase will auto-skip it. Opening a PR for such redundant commits creates noise and, in deployment-on-merge workflows, triggers unnecessary production changes.

original.title: Gate B negative fold is structural-collapse variance, NOT K_NULL null-side noise
original.content: Gate B Step-1 on 173 raw Claude-session traces (hybrid sig, k=1, K_NULL=15) returned INCONCLUSIVE: patterns/fold 7/11/13 (floor=50), aggregate null_lift 0.092, and fold-1 null_lift -0.224. K_NULL=15 (the gate-owner variance fix, applied for exactly this) did NOT eliminate the negative fold (zeta RANK-1 hypothesis predicted it would). FALSIFIED: the negative fold is not null-side sampling noise; it is small-pattern-pool variance on the ENGINE side (median_engine swung 0.345 vs 0.706/0.715 across folds). Root cause = structural-signature collapse: raw Claude sessions are structurally near-identical ({user,assistant,tool}) so the signature collapses 115 train traces into ~10 distinct patterns. K_NULL only smooths the null estimator; it cannot fix engine-side small-sample variance. Both the negative fold AND the floor failure share ONE root cause and resolve only when the pattern pool clears the floor.
original.when_to_use: When interpreting Gate B fold variance or proposing K_NULL/null-side fixes for negative folds; when deciding whether more raw traces will help (they will not past the ~32-40 structural ceiling).

generalized.context: When analyzing fold variance in a validation pipeline where raw input traces are structurally near-identical (e.g., fixed user/assistant/tool roles), and a null-side variance fix (K_NULL) fails to eliminate negative folds.
approach: Verify if the negative fold persists despite applying a null-side variance fix (K_NULL) to the estimator
Check if the root cause is small-pattern-pool variance on the engine side by observing if the median signature swings significantly across folds
Identify that raw traces with identical structural signatures collapse into a limited number of distinct patterns regardless of sample size
generalized.outcome: Confirmed that the negative fold is not null-side sampling noise but structural-signature collapse; increasing raw trace count beyond the structural ceiling (~32-40) will not resolve the issue.
generalized.lesson: When a negative fold persists despite applying a null-side variance fix (like K_NULL), the root cause is likely structural-signature collapse on the engine side, not sampling noise. This occurs when raw input traces are structurally near-identical, causing them to collapse into a small pool of distinct patterns. Consequently, increasing the number of raw traces beyond the structural ceiling provides no benefit; the issue resolves only when the pattern pool diversity increases.

original.title: Gate B corpus: use proprietary CURATED artifacts (rb/guardrails), not raw Claude session traces -- and it is a PIVOT
original.content: Principal redirect (2026-06-09): Gate B was eating raw ~/.claude session transcripts (collect-projects.ts), which structurally collapse to 7-13 patterns/fold. The fix is to feed the PROPRIETARY CURATED ARTIFACTS - reasoning banks + guardrails - which are already-generalized, semantically distinct, and do NOT collapse. Inventory: 3778 curated units across 4 distinct domains (ayoai 1486rb+543guard, zds 242+87, prediction-markets, gov-contracting). Best cross-world test: ayoai patterns to zds gov-contracting goal-queries, clears the 50-floor 40x. METHODOLOGY VALID with 3 mitigations: (1) queries from GOAL STATEMENTS (aspirations.jsonl) NOT held-out rb; (2) stratify framework-category vs domain-specific patterns; (3) report absolute median_null + strip curator metadata from query text. STRATEGIC: this is a PIVOT not an engine validation. The pearl centers a mechanical generalization ENGINE; rb/guardrails are curated by the cognitive layer and bypass the engine. Testing them validates a curated-knowledge commons, not the engine thesis. The engine shrinks to a privacy-gate; the cognitive layer becomes the differentiator. Surface as a deliberate strategic pivot.
original.when_to_use: When defining the Gate B corpus, the commons product, or the value-spine thesis.

generalized.context: When constructing a knowledge corpus for a system that ingests reasoning artifacts, avoid feeding raw, uncurated session transcripts (e.g., raw chat logs) which structurally collapse into a small number of generic patterns.
approach: Feed the system PROPRIETARY CURATED ARTIFACTS (reasoning banks and guardrails) instead of raw logs.
Ensure curated artifacts are already generalized and semantically distinct to prevent pattern collapse.
Validate the corpus by querying from GOAL STATEMENTS (aspirations) rather than held-out reasoning data.
Stratify the framework category from domain-specific patterns during ingestion.
Report absolute median null values and strip curator metadata from query text to ensure clean evaluation.
generalized.outcome: The corpus successfully cleared a high-difficulty cross-domain test (applying patterns from one domain to a completely different domain like government contracting) without collapsing into generic patterns.
generalized.lesson: When building a knowledge commons, raw session transcripts collapse into a few generic patterns (7-13/fold) and fail to generalize. You must use PROPRIETARY CURATED ARTIFACTS (reasoning banks/guardrails) which are pre-generalized and semantically distinct. This is a strategic pivot: the engine becomes a privacy gate, while the cognitive layer (the curated knowledge) becomes the differentiator. To validate this, query from GOAL STATEMENTS (aspirations) rather than held-out reasoning data, and stratify framework categories from domain-specific patterns.

original.title: Forge-validation goals requiring N clean invocations need a usage-counter substrate
original.content: ABC chain. Antecedent: g-012-19 required confirming 3 forged contract-pipeline skills (advance-contract-stage, document-found-opportunity, draft-sources-sought-response) were each invoked successfully by their parent at least 3 times in real use. Behavior: audited every plausible substrate -- forged-skills.yaml has no usage_count/last_used field on any skill; agent-activity-log.sh is write-only (no per-skill read); world changelog has 0 mentions of the skill names (forged skills do not self-log to changelog); no local sources-sought draft artifacts exist. Consequence: the validation goal cannot be mechanically verified -- there is no counter to read.
