Verification falls back to manual tally or inferential artifact-counting (DORMANT Contract rows / draft files). Lesson: when forging a skill whose forge-validation will count real-use invocations, ALSO provision a countable substrate -- e.g. have the forged skill self-increment usage_count + stamp last_used in forged-skills.yaml on each clean invocation, or emit a greppable invocation marker. Without the substrate, the forge-validation goal is structurally unverifiable and idles pending forever.
original.when_to_use: When forging a skill, or writing/auditing a forge-validation goal that counts real-use invocations of a skill.

generalized.context: When defining validation goals for a synthetic skill that requires counting real-world invocations, ensure a dedicated counter mechanism exists.
approach: Audit all potential data sources (configuration files, activity logs, changelogs, local artifacts) for existing usage counters or invocation markers.
Identify if the validation goal relies on a metric that is currently untrackable (e.g., no field in the skill definition, write-only logs, or missing artifacts).
Provision a countable substrate by having the skill self-increment a usage counter and timestamp the last use on each successful invocation, or emit a greppable marker.
generalized.outcome: The validation goal becomes mechanically verifiable via a direct read of the counter, rather than relying on manual tallying or inferential artifact counting.
generalized.lesson: When a validation goal requires counting real-use invocations of a synthetic skill, the system must provision a countable substrate (e.g., a usage counter and timestamp in the skill definition). Without this explicit counter, the goal is structurally unverifiable because standard logs or artifacts may not capture the specific invocation count, forcing reliance on manual auditing or indirect inference.

original.title: Gate B first GO: cross-world transfer is real but stratified by QUERY work-type, not pattern domain
original.content: Raw (non-generalized) curated corpus, semantic retrieval, KNULL=10, 3659 judge calls, 0 fallbacks: 40 zds FRAMEWORK-goal queries x 1839 ayoai rb/guardrail patterns = null_lift 0.301 ALL / 0.237 framework-patterns / 0.346 domain-patterns, median_engine 0.797 -- GO (bar: 0.15 lift, 0.30 median). Same corpus with mostly-DOMAIN zds queries scored 0.003 = NO-GO. Conclusion: the commons value concentrates where the CONSUMER QUERY is shared-cognitive-infrastructure work; cross-DOMAIN transfer of raw curated knowledge is absent. Counterintuitive sub-result: domain-stratum patterns showed the HIGHEST lift (0.346) for framework queries because their random-draw null baseline is low (0.434 vs 0.555 for framework patterns whose shared vocabulary inflates the null); lift = engine minus null, so high-null strata are handicapped. Run: gate-b-curated-crossworld.test.ts, GATE_B_QUERY_STRATUM=framework, seed 6976613, 92.7 min.
original.when_to_use: When interpreting Gate B / commons retrieval results, designing the generalization A/B comparison arms, or deciding what knowledge classes a cross-world commons should carry

generalized.context: When evaluating cross-project knowledge transfer, specifically comparing how well 'shared-cognitive-infrastructure' queries (framework goals) versus 'domain-specific' queries (application patterns) retrieve raw curated knowledge from a common pool.
approach: Run a stratified retrieval test separating queries into 'framework-goal' (shared infrastructure) and 'domain-pattern' (specific application logic) categories
Calculate the lift score (engine score minus null baseline) for each category
Compare the null baselines: note that framework queries often have a lower null baseline due to less shared vocabulary, while domain queries have a higher null baseline due to inflated shared terms
generalized.outcome: Cross-project transfer succeeds only for 'framework-goal' queries (lift ~0.30), while 'domain-pattern' queries show near-zero lift (~0.003). Crucially, domain patterns showed the highest raw lift for framework queries because their high null baseline handicapped the framework patterns' lift calculation.
generalized.lesson: Cross-project knowledge transfer is real but strictly stratified by query intent: it works for 'shared-cognitive-infrastructure' work (framework goals) but fails for 'domain-specific' work (application patterns). Do not assume raw curated knowledge transfers across domains; the value concentrates where the consumer query targets shared infrastructure. Additionally, be aware that lift metrics can be misleading: a category with a high null baseline (due to shared vocabulary) will artificially suppress its lift score, potentially hiding high absolute performance.

original.content: Before pursuing any contract opportunity, verify scale matches sole-proprietor SDVOSB capacity: single-period value under $500K is comfortable, sole-source path supports $25K-$5M services or $25K-$7.5M manufacturing (FAR 19.1406), but anything requiring bonding, multi-year IDIQ holding, large past-performance citations, or team-size demonstrations is structurally out of reach. If the RFP requires those, file as pass stage with reason scale-out-of-reach.
original.trigger_condition: opportunity-evaluation, sizing-check before pursuit decision
original.rule: Before pursuing any contract opportunity, verify scale matches sole-proprietor SDVOSB capacity: single-period value under $500K is comfortable, sole-source path supports $25K-$5M services or $25K-$7.5M manufacturing (FAR 19.1406), but anything requiring bonding, multi-year IDIQ holding, large past-performance citations, or team-size demonstrations is structurally out of reach. approach: Verify the single-period contract value is under $500K for a comfortable fit.

If the RFP mandates these, file as 'pass' with the reason 'scale-out-of-reach' to avoid wasted effort.

original.content: FORWARD_TO_EMAILS in any SES-based email forwarder must point to an address OUTSIDE the SES-captured domain. Forwarding to an in-domain address creates infinite Lambda recursion.
original.trigger_condition: Setting up or modifying environment variables for an SES-driven Lambda forwarder, OR designing a new email pipeline with SES inbound receipt + Lambda transformation.
original.rule: FORWARD_TO_EMAILS in any SES-based email forwarder must point to an address OUTSIDE the SES-captured domain. Forwarding to an in-domain address creates infinite Lambda recursion.

generalized.context: When configuring an email forwarder that uses a cloud email service (like SES) to trigger a serverless function (like Lambda) for processing.
approach: Identify the domain of the email service provider (the 'captured domain')
Ensure the FORWARD_TO_EMAILS destination address is explicitly OUTSIDE this provider's domain
Verify the destination does not resolve to an alias or subdomain owned by the same provider
generalized.outcome: Prevents infinite recursion loops where the function triggers itself by forwarding the email back to its own domain.
generalized.lesson: In any serverless email forwarder architecture where the email service provider triggers a function, the FORWARD_TO_EMAILS destination must point to an address OUTSIDE the provider's own domain. Forwarding to an in-domain address (or an alias within the same provider's namespace) causes the function to re-trigger itself, creating an infinite recursion loop that exhausts resources.

original.title: Large RFI Q&A signals integrator competition
original.content: When RFI has Q&A attachment with >20 industry questions: large Q&A count signals established competitive field of large integrators (Deloitte/Booz/Accenture class). Read Q&A to assess competitor class before drafting any response.

original.rule: When RFI has Q&A attachment with >20 industry questions: large Q&A count signals established competitive field of large integrators (Deloitte/Booz/Accenture class). Read Q&A to assess competitor class before drafting any response.

approach: Count the total number of industry questions in the Q&A attachment.
If the count exceeds 20, interpret this as a signal of an established competitive field involving large-scale system integrators.

generalized.lesson: A high volume of industry-specific questions (specifically >20) in an RFI Q&A attachment signals that the opportunity is being pursued by established, large-scale system integrators. original.content: When designing rule-based routing/filtering chains, place inclusion checks (route X to special handler) BEFORE exclusion checks (drop Y from echo). The reverse order silently drops legitimate inclusion cases that also match exclusion criteria.
original.trigger_condition: Writing or reviewing any routing/filtering code (Lambda routers, middleware chains, message dispatchers, firewall rules, request handlers) with both inclusion and exclusion paths.
original.rule: When designing rule-based routing/filtering chains, place inclusion checks (route X to special handler) BEFORE exclusion checks (drop Y from echo). The reverse order silently drops legitimate inclusion cases that also match exclusion criteria.

generalized.context: When designing rule-based routing or filtering chains that contain both inclusion rules (route X to special handler) and exclusion rules (drop Y from echo).
approach: Place inclusion checks (positive matches) before exclusion checks (negative matches) in the evaluation order
Ensure that if a request matches an inclusion criteria, it is processed immediately without reaching subsequent exclusion filters
generalized.outcome: Prevents legitimate inclusion cases from being silently dropped if they also match an exclusion criterion defined later in the chain
generalized.lesson: In rule-based routing or filtering chains, always evaluate inclusion rules before exclusion rules. If the order is reversed, a request matching an inclusion criteria may be incorrectly dropped by a subsequent exclusion rule, causing silent failures for valid traffic.

original.content: Use ASCII hyphens (-) not em-dashes in any JSON payload piped to mind_api daemon scripts (aspirations-add, aspirations-add-goal, reasoning-bank-add, guardrails-add, etc). The daemons utf-8 parser rejects byte 0x97 with invalid_body error.
original.trigger_condition: Composing JSON for any *-add.sh script in core/scripts/. Pre-flight: grep for em-dashes before piping.
original.rule: Use ASCII hyphens (-) not em-dashes in any JSON payload piped to mind_api daemon scripts (aspirations-add, aspirations-add-goal, reasoning-bank-add, guardrails-add, etc). The daemons utf-8 parser rejects byte 0x97 with invalid_body error.

generalized.context: When composing JSON payloads to be piped into daemon scripts (e.g., aspiration or guardrail update scripts) that parse UTF-8 input.
approach: Replace all em-dashes (byte 0x97) with standard ASCII hyphens (-) within the JSON string values
Perform a pre-flight grep or regex check for em-dashes before piping the payload to the daemon script
generalized.outcome: Prevents the daemon's UTF-8 parser from rejecting the payload with an 'invalid_body' error.
generalized.lesson: Daemon scripts that parse UTF-8 input often reject payloads containing em-dashes (byte 0x97) as invalid. Always sanitize JSON payloads by replacing em-dashes with ASCII hyphens before piping them to daemon update scripts to avoid 'invalid_body' parsing errors.

original.content: Single-quote any string containing literal $LATEST (or $ followed by uppercase word) in bash. Specifically for CloudWatch log stream names: aws logs get-log-events --log-stream-name 2026/05/22/[$LATEST]abc REQUIRES single quotes. Double-quotes expand $LATEST to empty.
original.trigger_condition: Invoking aws logs * commands with stream names from describe-log-streams output, or any bash string containing a literal $ followed by an identifier that is NOT a variable.
original.rule: Single-quote any string containing literal $LATEST (or $ followed by uppercase word) in bash. Specifically for CloudWatch log stream names: aws logs get-log-events --log-stream-name 2026/05/22/[$LATEST]abc REQUIRES single quotes. Double-quotes expand $LATEST to empty.

generalized.context: When invoking AWS CLI commands (or similar tools) with arguments containing literal strings like $LATEST or any $ followed by an uppercase identifier, specifically when retrieving log events or stream names.
approach: Identify if the argument string contains a literal $ followed by an uppercase word (e.g., $LATEST) rather than a shell variable.
Wrap the entire argument string in single quotes (e.g., '[$LATEST]') to prevent shell expansion.
Avoid using double quotes, as they will expand the $LATEST sequence to an empty string, causing the command to fail.
generalized.outcome: The command executes successfully and retrieves the correct log stream data without expanding the literal string to empty.
generalized.lesson: When passing arguments containing literal $ followed by uppercase identifiers (like $LATEST) to CLI tools, always use single quotes. Double quotes trigger shell variable expansion, which turns $LATEST into an empty string, breaking the command. Single quotes preserve the literal text exactly as intended.

original.content: Export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in the same Bash invocation before any aws CLI call that takes an argument starting with / and representing an AWS resource path (CloudWatch log groups /aws/lambda/X, IAM ARN paths, S3 keys with leading /). Without this, Git Bash MSYS converts the path to C:/Program Files/Git/... and the command fails with InvalidParameterException.
original.trigger_condition: Running aws CLI from Git Bash on Windows with any argument starting with /. Symptoms: InvalidParameterException with C:/Program Files/Git/ prefix in the value.
original.rule: Export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in the same Bash invocation before any aws CLI call that takes an argument starting with / and representing an AWS resource path (CloudWatch log groups /aws/lambda/X, IAM ARN paths, S3 keys with leading /). Without this, Git Bash MSYS converts the path to C:/Program Files/Git/... and the command fails with InvalidParameterException.

generalized.context: When executing CLI tools from Git Bash on Windows with arguments that represent resource paths starting with a forward slash (e.g., S3 keys, IAM ARNs, log group paths).
approach: Identify that Git Bash's MSYS layer may incorrectly convert forward-slash resource paths into local Windows file paths (e.g., C:/Program Files/Git/...)
Prepend the environment variable export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 to the same Bash invocation before calling the CLI tool
Ensure the CLI tool receives the original resource path string without the Windows file system prefix
generalized.outcome: Prevents InvalidParameterException errors caused by the CLI tool receiving a local file path instead of the intended resource identifier.
generalized.lesson: When running CLI tools from Git Bash on Windows with arguments that are resource paths starting with /, the MSYS layer may corrupt them into local Windows file paths. To prevent this, always export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in the same Bash invocation before the command. This ensures the tool receives the correct resource path rather than a malformed local file path, avoiding InvalidParameterException errors.

original.content: Scripts calling core/scripts/env-read.sh to retrieve a credential value MUST use the value subcommand: env-read.sh value <KEY>. Bare positional form (env-read.sh <KEY>) triggers an argparse error printed to stderr; with 2>/dev/null, the variable resolves to empty string and the script silently misbehaves.
original.trigger_condition: Authoring or auditing any shell wrapper that loads a credential from .env.local via env-read.sh. Mostly relevant for forged skills, world/scripts/, and heritage-port wrappers from predecessors whose env-read.sh CLI predated the sub-command structure.
original.rule: Scripts calling core/scripts/env-read.sh to retrieve a credential value MUST use the value subcommand: env-read.sh value <KEY>. Bare positional form (env-read.sh <KEY>) triggers an argparse error printed to stderr; with 2>/dev/null, the variable resolves to empty string and the script silently misbehaves.

generalized.context: When authoring or auditing shell wrapper scripts that retrieve credential values from a .env file using a dedicated utility script.
approach: Identify the utility script used for credential retrieval (e.g., env-read.sh).
Ensure the script is invoked with the explicit value subcommand: utility value <KEY>.
Avoid invoking the script with the bare positional form: utility <KEY>.
generalized.outcome: Prevents argparse errors from being suppressed by stderr redirection (2>/dev/null), which would otherwise cause the variable to resolve to an empty string and lead to silent script failures.
generalized.lesson: When retrieving credentials via a utility script, always use the explicit value subcommand (utility value <KEY>). Invoking the script with the bare positional form (utility <KEY>) triggers an argparse error; if this error is suppressed via stderr redirection, the script receives an empty string instead of the credential, causing silent misbehavior.

original.content: Before invoking any outreach-send skill, action, or dispatch path, a per-send approval from the principal (user) MUST exist for the specific (prospect, template/variant) pair. CANONICAL CHANNEL (g-010-29, user 2026-05-27): the authenticated Approve-and-Send click on the website /admin/outreach surface -- one admin click records the per-send sign-off AND dispatches the email (after a confirmation step). The former multi-channel model (email reply, terminal sign-off) is RETIRED: the website click is the SINGLE approval channel. CORE INVARIANT UNCHANGED: no prospect send without the principal's explicit authenticated approval (fail-closed on zero), and the AGENT CANNOT self-approve or self-send -- only an admin-authenticated browser session can drive the send; the agent only drafts and renders the approve control. Web-app enforcement: app/admin/outreach/actions.ts approveAndSend re-verifies the Cognito admin group, then lib/outreach-dispatch.ts records the guard-29 sign-off and calls assertDispatchAllowed (fail-closed) immediately before the SES send, resolving the recipient from the prospect (fail-closed if the prospect has no email). DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH: the shell dispatch gate (world/scripts/outreach-send.sh -> outreach-signoff-verify.sh) remains fail-closed for any CLI-initiated send (guard-40; live-verified exit 1 on no sign-off, 2026-05-27) but is no longer a user-facing approval channel. Web-app enforcement: app/admin/outreach/actions.ts approveAndSend re-verifies the Cognito admin group, then lib/outreach-dispatch.ts records the guard-29 sign-off and calls assertDispatchAllowed (fail-closed) immediately before the SES send, resolving the recipient from the prospect (fail-closed if the prospect has no email). approach: Enforce a single canonical approval channel (e.g., an authenticated 'Approve-and-Send' UI action) that records the sign-off and triggers dispatch in one step.
Retire legacy multi-channel models (e.g., email replies, terminal sign-offs) to ensure the website click is the ONLY approval source.
Implement a fail-closed invariant where no prospect message is sent without explicit principal approval, preventing the agent from self-approving or self-sending.
Add defense-in-depth by maintaining a shell dispatch gate that blocks any CLI-initiated sends if no sign-off exists, even if the UI channel is retired.
Verify the admin group and assert dispatch allowed immediately before the email service call, failing closed if the prospect lacks a valid email address.
generalized.outcome: Ensured that no prospect-facing message is dispatched without explicit, authenticated principal approval, eliminating unauthorized or accidental sends.

Consolidate this into a single canonical channel (e.g., a UI action) that both records the sign-off and triggers dispatch, retiring legacy methods like email replies or CLI flags. original.content: Before assuming AI/agent-behind-the-scenes delivery is permissible on a government contract, verify the solicitation key-personnel/who-performs terms, subcontracting-disclosure requirements, and data-handling rules (controlled/CUI data must NOT flow into arbitrary AI services). original.rule: Before assuming AI/agent-behind-the-scenes delivery is permissible on a government contract, verify the solicitation key-personnel/who-performs terms, subcontracting-disclosure requirements, and data-handling rules (controlled/CUI data must NOT flow into arbitrary AI services). approach: Verify the solicitation's 'who-performs' or key-personnel terms to ensure AI delivery aligns with staffing requirements.

original.content: When a command exit code drives control flow (gate checks, loop control), do NOT pipe the command through grep before reading the exit status. The shell exit-status reflects the LAST pipeline stage (grep), not the command. Capture rc immediately (run the command alone, read rc on the next line) or redirect output to a file and filter for display separately. Misreading greps exit status as the commands nearly caused a false runner-identity loop-ejection (rc=1 was greps no-match, not the scripts).
original.trigger_condition: Reading a script or command exit status that gates a decision while filtering its output through a pipe
original.rule: When a command exit code drives control flow (gate checks, loop control), do NOT pipe the command through grep before reading the exit status. The shell exit-status reflects the LAST pipeline stage (grep), not the command. Capture rc immediately (run the command alone, read rc on the next line) or redirect output to a file and filter for display separately. Misreading greps exit status as the commands nearly caused a false runner-identity loop-ejection (rc=1 was greps no-match, not the scripts).

generalized.context: When a script's exit code drives critical control flow (gate checks, loop termination) and the command output is filtered through a pipe (e.g., grep) for display.
approach: Avoid piping the command directly into the shell variable capturing the exit status.
Run the command standalone to capture its immediate exit code, or redirect output to a file and filter separately.
Ensure the exit status variable reflects the primary command's result, not the final pipeline stage's result.
generalized.outcome: Prevented false-positive control flow failures where a 'no-match' filter exit code (1) was incorrectly interpreted as the primary command's failure.
generalized.lesson: When a command's exit code drives control flow, never pipe it through a filter (like grep) before capturing the status. The shell exit status reflects the LAST stage of the pipeline (the filter), not the original command. If the filter fails to match output, it returns 1, which will incorrectly trigger a failure state in your logic. Capture the exit code immediately after the command runs alone, or redirect output to a file and filter that file separately for display.

original.title: MSYS path conversion mangles bare-slash CLI args on Windows Git Bash
original.content: On Windows Git Bash (MSYS), prefix external-CLI commands that pass a bare slash argument (e.g. aws s3api --delimiter "/") with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1. Without it MSYS silently rewrites the bare "/" into a Windows path, the argument changes meaning, and the command misbehaves with no error. Canonical incident: agent-inbox-list.sh --delimiter "/" never matched, so the agent-inbox/processed/ sub-prefix leaked into Contents and every hourly poll would re-file duplicate aspirations from already-handled emails.
original.trigger_condition: Authoring or invoking a world/scripts (or core/scripts) shell script on Windows Git Bash that passes a bare slash or other Unix-path-shaped literal as an argument to an external CLI (aws, gcloud, curl, etc.).
original.rule: On Windows Git Bash (MSYS), prefix external-CLI commands that pass a bare slash argument (e.g. aws s3api --delimiter "/") with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1. Without it MSYS silently rewrites the bare "/" into a Windows path, the argument changes meaning, and the command misbehaves with no error. Canonical incident: agent-inbox-list.sh --delimiter "/" never matched, so the agent-inbox/processed/ sub-prefix leaked into Contents and every hourly poll would re-file duplicate aspirations from already-handled emails.

generalized.context: When invoking external CLI tools (e.g., AWS CLI, gcloud, curl) from shell scripts on Windows Git Bash (MSYS) with arguments containing bare forward slashes (e.g., --delimiter "/")
approach: Identify if the command passes a Unix-style literal path or delimiter as an argument
Prefix the command with the environment variable MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 to disable automatic path conversion
Ensure the script runs in Git Bash on Windows, not standard CMD or PowerShell
generalized.outcome: Prevents MSYS from silently rewriting the bare slash into a Windows path, avoiding silent argument mangling and logic errors
generalized.lesson: On Windows Git Bash (MSYS), the environment automatically converts bare forward slashes into Windows paths. When passing Unix-style literals (like delimiters or flags) to external CLIs, prefix the command with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1. Without this, the argument changes meaning silently, causing the command to misbehave without throwing an error.

original.content: Do NOT put a leading MIND_AGENT=<name> prefix on a PIPELINE whose right-hand wrapper resolves AGENT_DIR. Shell semantics: in `MIND_AGENT=name producer | wrapper` the var binds ONLY to producer, so the wrapper runs with MIND_AGENT unset -> AGENT_DIR=None -> NoneType os.PathLike error (observed: experience-add.sh during g-001-08, line 360 read_jsonl(ARCHIVE_PATH=None)). The bash-agent-inject PreToolUse hook auto-injects MIND_AGENT on its own (verified: unprefixed wm-read.sh resolves AGENT_DIR fine) and per CLAUDE.md respects an explicit MIND_AGENT override, so a manual leading prefix is both unnecessary and, on a pipeline, harmful. FIX: omit the manual prefix (let the hook inject), OR place it on the wrapper side: `producer | MIND_AGENT=name bash wrapper`. WORLD_DIR/META_DIR-scoped wrappers (pipeline-move, reasoning-bank-add, guardrails-add) mask the missing var via the first-available-conf fallback; only AGENT_DIR-scoped wrappers (experience-add, wm-set/append, journal-add, session-*, agent-source aspirations-*) fail.
original.trigger_condition: Piping stdin into an AGENT_DIR-scoped core/scripts wrapper while manually setting MIND_AGENT as a leading pipeline prefix

The bash-agent-inject PreToolUse hook auto-injects MIND_AGENT on its own (verified: unprefixed wm-read.sh resolves AGENT_DIR fine) and per CLAUDE.md respects an explicit MIND_AGENT override, so a manual leading prefix is both unnecessary and, on a pipeline, harmful. FIX: omit the manual prefix (let the hook inject), OR place it on the wrapper side: `producer | MIND_AGENT=name bash wrapper`. WORLD_DIR/META_DIR-scoped wrappers (pipeline-move, reasoning-bank-add, guardrails-add) mask the missing var via the first-available-conf fallback; only AGENT_DIR-scoped wrappers (experience-add, wm-set/append, journal-add, session-*, agent-source aspirations-*) fail.

generalized.context: When piping a producer command into a shell wrapper script that resolves a directory path based on an environment variable (e.g., AGENT_DIR derived from MIND_AGENT).
approach: Identify if the right-hand wrapper script relies on an environment variable to determine its working directory or configuration path
Avoid setting the environment variable as a leading prefix on the producer side of the pipe (e.g., `VAR=val producer | wrapper`)
Instead, either let the upstream hook inject the variable automatically, or explicitly set the variable on the wrapper side of the pipe (e.g., `producer | VAR=val bash wrapper`)
Verify that the wrapper script does not fail with a NoneType or missing path error when the variable is unset in its execution context
generalized.outcome: Prevented a runtime error where the wrapper script failed to resolve its configuration directory because the environment variable was only bound to the producer process, not the wrapper process.
generalized.lesson: In shell pipelines, environment variables set as a leading prefix on the producer command (e.g., `VAR=val cmd1 | cmd2`) bind only to the producer. The downstream wrapper runs with the variable unset, causing it to fail if it relies on that variable to resolve paths. To fix this, either omit the manual prefix and rely on upstream injection, or explicitly set the variable on the wrapper side of the pipe (e.g., `cmd1 | VAR=val bash cmd2`).

original.title: AWS CLI on Windows Git Bash: convert mktemp paths via cygpath; never inline file:// in CLI shorthand
original.content: When passing a file to the native Windows AWS CLI from Git Bash, convert the path with cygpath -m FIRST. mktemp returns an MSYS /tmp path the native CLI cannot load (fails with: Unable to load paramfile file:///tmp/...: No such file or directory). AND never inline file:// inside AWS CLI shorthand structure syntax like Body={Text={Data=file://FILE}} - file:// is expanded ONLY for a top-level parameter value; inside shorthand the literal path string silently becomes the value (the body became file:///tmp/... instead of text). Correct pattern: build the whole structure as JSON to one temp file, convert its path via cygpath -m, and pass --message file://WINPATH as a top-level arg. Complements guard-21 (MSYS bare-slash pathconv) - same Windows-native-CLI-from-Git-Bash theme, different failure mode.
original.trigger_condition: Authoring or invoking a shell script on Windows Git Bash that calls the AWS CLI (aws ses send-email, any --cli-input-json or --message structure param) passing a file:// paramfile or a temp file created by mktemp.
original.rule: When passing a file to the native Windows AWS CLI from Git Bash, convert the path with cygpath -m FIRST. mktemp returns an MSYS /tmp path the native CLI cannot load (fails with: Unable to load paramfile file:///tmp/...: No such file or directory). AND never inline file:// inside AWS CLI shorthand structure syntax like Body={Text={Data=file://FILE}} - file:// is expanded ONLY for a top-level parameter value; inside shorthand the literal path string silently becomes the value (the body became file:///tmp/... instead of text). Correct pattern: build the whole structure as JSON to one temp file, convert its path via cygpath -m, and pass --message file://WINPATH as a top-level arg. Complements guard-21 (MSYS bare-slash pathconv) - same Windows-native-CLI-from-Git-Bash theme, different failure mode.

generalized.context: When invoking a native Windows CLI tool from a Git Bash shell that requires a file path argument (e.g., passing a temp file created by mktemp or a JSON structure containing file references).
approach: Convert MSYS-style paths (returned by mktemp) to Windows-native paths using cygpath -m before passing them to the native CLI.
Never inline file:// URIs inside shorthand syntax structures (e.g., Body={Text={Data=file://...}}) because the URI expansion only works for top-level parameters.
Instead, construct the full JSON structure in a temporary file, convert the file path via cygpath -m, and pass the file:// URI as a top-level argument pointing to that converted path.
generalized.outcome: Prevents 'No such file or directory' errors caused by path format mismatches and avoids silent data corruption where literal path strings are treated as content values.
generalized.lesson: When bridging Git Bash and native Windows CLI tools, two distinct path handling rules apply: First, always convert MSYS paths to Windows-native paths using cygpath -m before passing them to the native binary, as the native tool cannot interpret MSYS paths. Second, never embed file:// URIs inside shorthand syntax structures (like nested JSON objects); the URI expansion mechanism only functions for top-level parameters. If you need to pass a file's content via shorthand, write the full structure to a temp file, convert its path, and pass the file:// URI as a top-level argument pointing to that converted file.

original.content: When Glob returns empty for a file the user has explicitly named: try Bash find <plausible-parent> -maxdepth 4 -iname *pattern* 2>/dev/null BEFORE concluding the file does not exist. Glob honors .gitignore (ripgrep backend); personal docs, OneDrive content, and ignored artifacts will not surface via Glob.
original.trigger_condition: Glob (or Read with absolute path) returns no-match for a file path the user typed or referenced. Especially likely for resumes, profile docs, OneDrive content, credentials, build artifacts.
original.rule: When Glob returns empty for a file the user has explicitly named: try Bash find <plausible-parent> -maxdepth 4 -iname *pattern* 2>/dev/null BEFORE concluding the file does not exist. Glob honors .gitignore (ripgrep backend); personal docs, OneDrive content, and ignored artifacts will not surface via Glob.

generalized.context: When a file search (Glob) returns no results for a file path explicitly provided by the user, especially for personal documents, cloud-synced content, or build artifacts.
approach: Recognize that the search backend (e.g., ripgrep) respects .gitignore rules, causing personal docs and ignored artifacts to be hidden.
Execute a Bash find command against a plausible parent directory with a limited depth (-maxdepth 4) and case-insensitive matching (-iname) before concluding the file is missing.

original.title: Standalone test runners must not expose test* names to pytest
original.content: In core/scripts/tests/, a standalone runner (has main(), invoked via py -3 <file>.py, NOT meant for pytest) MUST NOT name any module-level function or decorator test or test_* -- pytest collects names matching test* and ERRORs on them (e.g. a def test(fn) registration decorator errors on missing fixture fn), which makes the ENTIRE pytest core/scripts/tests suite exit 1 and masks real pass/fail signal. Fix: name such helpers non-test* (sibling convention: @with_sandbox) OR set <fn>.__test__ = False after the def. Verify with: pytest <file> --collect-only -q (must show 0 errors).

Fix: name such helpers non-test* (sibling convention: @with_sandbox) OR set <fn>.__test__ = False after the def. Verify with: pytest <file> --collect-only -q (must show 0 errors).

generalized.context: When authoring or editing a standalone test runner script (invoked via `python <file>.py` with a `main()` function) that is not intended to be executed by the test framework.
approach: Ensure no module-level functions or decorators are named `test` or `test_*`
Rename such helpers using a sibling convention (e.g., `@with_sandbox`) or explicitly disable collection by setting `__test__ = False` on the function
Verify the fix by running the framework's collection command with `--collect-only -q` to confirm zero errors
generalized.lesson: Standalone test runner scripts must not expose names matching the test framework's collection pattern (e.g., `test*`). If such functions exist, the framework will attempt to collect them as tests, fail due to missing fixtures or invalid definitions, and cause the entire test suite to exit with an error code. This masks the actual pass/fail signal of the intended tests. To prevent this, either rename helper functions to non-test patterns or explicitly set `__test__ = False` on them.

Ensure the test environment explicitly unsets these production variables or mocks the cloud SDK to prevent accidental writes.
Never run test suites within the production deployment pipeline if there is any risk of those production variables being inherited or set.
generalized.outcome: Prevents test fixtures from being written to production tables, avoiding data contamination and potential service disruption.
generalized.lesson: A 'no-op when unset' gate in database code is latent protection, not active isolation. If tests run in an environment where production credentials or table names are set (even accidentally), the code will execute and write data. You must actively neutralize production paths in tests by unsetting env vars, mocking the SDK, or using isolated test databases. Never assume the absence of a write operation in the code implies safety in the environment.

generalized.context: When tests run inside a CI/CD deployment pipeline (e.g., running `vitest` or similar before the build step), every test MUST be portable across all CI agents.
approach: Eliminate platform-specific launchers (e.g., `python -3`) and hard-coded external/absolute paths (e.g., `C:/`, `OneDrive`, `world/`) from shell commands.
Gate any such non-portable dependencies behind `existsSync()` checks combined with `it.skipIf()` to ensure tests SKIP rather than FAIL on unsupported environments.
Ensure the test suite does not block the entire deployment pipeline if a specific environment constraint is missing.
generalized.outcome: Prevents non-portable test failures from blocking the entire deployment pipeline, even when the subsequent build step succeeds.
generalized.lesson: In CI/CD pipelines where tests run before the build, ensure all tests are cross-platform portable. Avoid platform-specific launchers and hard-coded absolute paths. Instead, gate these dependencies using `existsSync()` checks with `it.skipIf()` so that tests skip gracefully on unsupported environments rather than failing and blocking the deployment. This separates CI portability concerns from production write-safety concerns.

original.content: On Windows, do NOT use a bare /tmp path for a file handed between Git Bash (MSYS) and Windows Python (py -3): MSYS bash writes /tmp under the Git-Bash install, but py -3 resolves /tmp to C:	mp (drive-root-relative), so the file is not found. Prefer building JSON/payloads inline (printf piped to the script) per the encode-session JSON Construction Policy; when a temp file is genuinely needed for a bash-to-py-3 handoff, use an absolute Windows temp path both runtimes agree on (e.g. C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/<file>).
original.trigger_condition: Writing a temp file in Git Bash that a Windows Python (py -3) process will read in the same task, on this Windows deployment.
original.rule: On Windows, do NOT use a bare /tmp path for a file handed between Git Bash (MSYS) and Windows Python (py -3): MSYS bash writes /tmp under the Git-Bash install, but py -3 resolves /tmp to C:	mp (drive-root-relative), so the file is not found. Prefer building JSON/payloads inline (printf piped to the script) per the encode-session JSON Construction Policy; when a temp file is genuinely needed for a bash-to-py-3 handoff, use an absolute Windows temp path both runtimes agree on (e.g. C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/<file>).

generalized.context: When writing a temporary file in a Unix-like shell environment (e.g., Git Bash/MSYS) that must be read by a native Windows process (e.g., Python on Windows) within the same session.
approach: Avoid using bare /tmp paths, as the shell resolves them to the Git-Bash installation directory while the Windows process resolves them to the Windows drive root.
Prefer building payloads inline using pipes (e.g., printf piped to the script) to eliminate the need for intermediate files.
If a temporary file is strictly required, use an absolute Windows path (e.g., C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/<file>) that both runtimes can access.
generalized.outcome: Prevents file-not-found errors caused by path resolution mismatches between the shell environment and the native OS.
generalized.lesson: When passing data between a Unix-like shell environment and a native Windows process, do not use bare /tmp paths because they resolve to different directories in each runtime. Instead, prefer inline piping to avoid file I/O entirely, or explicitly use an absolute Windows path that is valid for both environments.

Gate rejections and validation errors are emitted as JSON on stdout/stderr; suppressing them turns a blocked write into a silent no-op, producing partial failure that reads as success. Run state mutations with full output visible and verify each result before claiming completion.

Use one compound Bash call (sequential commands) or issue dependent calls in separate messages.

original.title: Raw data is never the product (Lodestar / Generalization Engine)
original.content: Only Generalization-Engine output (de-identified, k-aggregated patterns) may cross the membrane into the Lodestar commons or any shared/licensed artifact. Raw customer or work traces are NEVER shared, sold, or published verbatim. The training-data product is privacy-budget-gated and opt-in per contributor, and NEVER includes government or Private-Vault (Tier-2) data by default. An LLM review that merely flags content as sensitive-or-not is a heuristic, not a guarantee; the guarantee is k-aggregation plus two-sided leakage tests (fail-closed), with the privacy budget a hard emit-count cap in v0 (formal epsilon/delta DP is a v1 goal). Architectural privacy, not contractual.
original.trigger_condition: Any design or action that shares, publishes, licenses, or trains on agent traces, knowledge, or patterns; any Lodestar commons contribution path; any training-data product work.

An LLM review that merely flags content as sensitive-or-not is a heuristic, not a guarantee; the guarantee is k-aggregation plus two-sided leakage tests (fail-closed), with the privacy budget a hard emit-count cap in v0 (formal epsilon/delta DP is a v1 goal). Architectural privacy, not contractual.

generalized.context: When designing or executing any workflow that shares, publishes, licenses, or trains on user traces, system logs, or behavioral patterns.
approach: Restrict data crossing organizational boundaries to only de-identified, k-aggregated patterns generated by a dedicated generalization engine
Enforce a hard emit-count cap as the primary privacy budget mechanism, treating LLM sensitivity flags only as heuristics rather than guarantees
Implement fail-closed two-sided leakage tests to verify no raw data or identifiable traces are exposed
Exclude high-sensitivity categories (e.g., government records or private vault data) by default in the training dataset
generalized.outcome: Ensures that only anonymized, aggregated insights leave the system while raw traces remain strictly contained, preventing privacy breaches regardless of heuristic review failures.
generalized.lesson: Architectural privacy must rely on hard technical constraints rather than contractual promises or heuristic reviews. Only de-identified, k-aggregated patterns should ever cross the boundary into shared artifacts or training sets. The system must enforce a hard cap on data emission counts and use fail-closed leakage tests to guarantee that raw traces never leave the secure environment, even if an LLM review incorrectly flags content as safe.

generalized.context: When testing local LLM recovery on a deployment where the inference server is supervised by a system tray application (e.g., Windows tray) and relies on GPU acceleration
approach: Identify that the standard chat endpoint (/api/chat) triggers a specific GPU-level wedge when used with certain models (e.g., qwen2.5:3b)
Route all diagnostic probes and judge calls exclusively to the completion endpoint (/api/generate) instead of the chat endpoint
Ensure the inference server process is restarted via the system tray application, not just the serve command, as the latter does not clear the GPU wedge
Understand that a simple process restart or model unload is insufficient; a machine reboot or GPU driver reset is required to clear the corruption caused by the chat endpoint
generalized.outcome: Prevented a self-inflicted wedge that corrupts the inference server, ensuring that subsequent recovery attempts via /api/generate remain functional without requiring a full machine reboot
generalized.lesson: When testing local LLM recovery on a GPU-accelerated deployment supervised by a system tray application, avoid using the /api/chat endpoint for diagnostics. A single call to /api/chat can trigger a GPU-level wedge that corrupts the server's generation capabilities, surviving process kills, model unloads, and service restarts. Only a machine reboot or GPU driver reset clears this state. Route all probes to the /api/generate completion path to avoid self-inflicting this failure mode.

Pivot strategy to either micro-purchase routes or non-set-aside positioning for these specific agencies.
Continue focusing set-aside research efforts only on agencies with confirmed, active IT set-aside records.
generalized.outcome: Avoided wasting research cycles on agencies that do not actually offer IT set-asides despite having general set-aside pressure.
generalized.lesson: When targeting agencies for minority-owned business set-aside contracts, verify the specific NAICS code alignment before investing research time. Many agencies (e.g., HHS, NASA, SSA) may have pressure to meet set-aside goals but route them entirely to non-IT categories or other sectors, resulting in zero IT set-asides on record. Pursuing IT set-asides in these agencies is futile; instead, use micro-purchase routes or non-set-aside positioning. Only allocate deep research resources to agencies with confirmed, active IT set-aside records.
