original.title: SAM.gov + DLA CAGE entity pages are JS-rendered SPAs -- WebFetch returns no data
original.content: Tried to verify CAGE 78DL6 + UEI HADPGKG7GN26 active status via WebFetch on (1) sam.gov/entity/HADPGKG7GN26/coreData -- returned only the SAM.gov header, no entity data (SPA requires login + JS rendering); (2) cage.dla.mil/Search/Results?cage=78DL6 -- returned the CAGE program navigation UI, no search results (interactive search form, not URL-driven). Also tried WebSearch for the UEI string -- no indexed records (entity profiles are not indexed by search engines for privacy). Conclusion: cannot independently verify USG registration data (CAGE, UEI, SAM registration status, SDVOSB status) via web tools. Either rely on user confirmation (they have SAM.gov login + the SBA VetCert portal) or use FPDS (https://www.fpds.gov) for HISTORICAL contract data which IS publicly searchable.
original.when_to_use: Verifying any USG entity registration status (CAGE, UEI, SAM active status, SDVOSB cert) for the consultancy itself or any third-party entity.

generalized.context: When attempting to verify US government entity registration status (CAGE, UEI, SAM active status, SDVOSB certification) via automated web tools like WebFetch or WebSearch.
approach: Recognize that government entity portals (e.g., SAM.gov, DLA CAGE) render data as JavaScript Single Page Applications (SPAs) requiring authentication and client-side rendering.
Observe that direct URL parameter queries (e.g., appending a CAGE code to a search URL) often return only navigation UIs or headers without the actual entity data.
Note that these entity profiles are frequently excluded from public search engine indexes for privacy reasons.
Conclude that automated web scraping cannot independently verify current registration status for these specific entities.
generalized.outcome: Automated verification attempts return empty data or UI shells; no indexed records are found via search engines.
generalized.lesson: Do not rely on automated web tools (WebFetch, WebSearch) to verify current US government entity registration status (CAGE, UEI, SAM, SDVOSB) because these portals are JavaScript-rendered SPAs requiring login and are not indexed by search engines. Instead, rely on user confirmation (who possesses login credentials) or query the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) for historical contract data, which remains publicly searchable.

original.title: Amplify Authenticator post-login redirect must live in the authenticated child, not a Hub signedIn listener
original.content: In the Next.js + @aws-amplify/ui-react app, /login wired its post-login redirect to Hub.listen(auth, signedIn). That event fires ONLY on the sign-in transition. A visitor who arrives already-authenticated (valid existing session) renders the Authenticator authenticated child (Signed in ... Redirecting) but no signedIn event fires, so the redirect never runs and the page hangs forever. Fix: move the redirect into the authenticated child component (a PostLogin component with useEffect calling router.replace), which mounts whenever authStatus is authenticated (fresh sign-in OR existing session). Verified by build 16/16 and matches the reported stuck-on-Redirecting symptom for an already-signed-in user.
original.when_to_use: any post-auth redirect in this Next.js+Amplify app, or any Amplify Authenticator-gated route that must redirect both fresh sign-ins and returning authenticated users

generalized.context: When implementing post-login redirects in a Next.js application using an AWS Amplify-style UI library where the authentication state is managed via a child component rather than a global event listener.
approach: Identify that the global authentication event (e.g., Hub.listen for 'signedIn') only fires during the active sign-in transition and does not trigger for users who arrive with an existing valid session.
Move the redirect logic from the global event listener into the authenticated child component itself.
Implement the redirect using a client-side hook (e.g., useEffect) that triggers whenever the local auth status changes to 'authenticated', covering both fresh logins and returning users.
Ensure the component mounts and executes the redirect immediately upon rendering for pre-authenticated visitors.
generalized.outcome: Resolved the issue where returning authenticated users were stuck on a 'Redirecting' screen because the global event listener never fired for their existing session.
generalized.lesson: When using an Amplify-style UI library in Next.js, do not rely solely on global authentication events (like 'signedIn') for post-login redirects, as these events only fire during the active sign-in transition and miss users with existing sessions. Instead, place the redirect logic inside the authenticated child component using a state listener (e.g., useEffect watching authStatus). This ensures the redirect executes for both fresh sign-ins and returning users who already possess a valid session.

original.title: build-landing-page + hallmark validated end-to-end; local build needs no AWS
original.content:
First real landing page (lp-zds-home, 2 copy-variants a/b) validated the full /build-landing-page -> /hallmark -> page-register.sh -> audit -> serve-local.sh chain end-to-end, locally, with ZERO AWS dependency.

Established facts:
1. The chain is local-only at BUILD time. /build-landing-page emits self-contained HTML+CSS into AGENT_WRITE_PATH/public/lp/<id>/. The AWS deploy goals (g-008-10 AWS mode, g-008-11 Amplify, g-008-12 Route 53) are DEPLOY-time deps, not build-time -- SKILL.md L176-179: 'local integration works without the remote; only commit-push requires it.' g-008-08's blocked_by listing those three was over-broad relative to its documented local-validation scope (verification outcomes are all local).
2. /hallmark is an LLM-driven design skill: invoked as a Skill in this framework, the AGENT is the generation engine (follows the anti-slop disciplines, emits HTML+CSS). No external Together-AI/API call, no credential boundary.
3. variant_axis=copy = same macrostructure + theme, different headline/proof framing. This deliberately overrides Hallmark's per-output diversification rule -- correct for an A/B copy test (isolate the copy var).
4. brief.value_prop_node should reference the decomposed child where the thesis lives (intelligence/value-proposition/elevator-pitches), not the umbrella value-proposition node (an index after the 2026-05-24 decompose).
5. public/lp pages are self-contained STATIC HTML, not Tailwind components -- even though the web-app is Next.js+Tailwind. Hallmark's 'always emit tokens.css at project root' is less applicable; inline per-page tokens are right for standalone static pages.

Self-audit (hallmark audit): 0 HIGH, 1 LOW -- gate 58 (token improvisation): 3 inline OKLCH values in button-state styles; lifted to named tokens (--color-on-accent/-success/-error) inline as own-mess cleanup.

Gaps surfaced -> filed as follow-up Idea goals under asp-008: (a) no page-update companion script (the `audit` sub-command's documented registry audit_summary write and Step 2.7 draft->live status promotion have no script; page-register.sh only appends); (b) the /manage-website add-page Next.js integration chain (Step 2.4b) was not exercised -- scoped out, this goal validated build-landing-page + hallmark per its title.
original.when_to_use: Building or validating landing pages via /build-landing-page + /hallmark; deciding whether landing-page work is blocked by AWS deploy infra; authoring landing-page briefs (value_prop_node target, variant axes).

generalized.context: When building or validating static landing pages via a local generation pipeline that produces self-contained HTML/CSS files.
approach: Separate build-time dependencies from deploy-time dependencies: ensure the build script generates static assets locally without requiring cloud infrastructure.
Treat the generation engine (LLM or script) as a local skill that emits complete HTML+CSS files, avoiding external API calls or credential boundaries during the build phase.
When testing copy variants (A/B tests), explicitly override the engine's default diversification rules to isolate only the headline and proof framing while keeping the macrostructure constant.
Reference the specific child node containing the thesis or value proposition in the brief, rather than the parent umbrella node, to ensure the generated content targets the correct argument.
Ensure generated pages are standalone static files, not framework components, to guarantee they render correctly in any environment.
generalized.outcome: Validated the full end-to-end chain (build -> generation -> registration -> audit -> serve) locally with zero dependency on cloud deployment infrastructure.
generalized.lesson: When validating a landing page generation pipeline, decouple the build process from deployment infrastructure. The build should generate self-contained static HTML/CSS files locally using a local generation engine, treating cloud deployment (hosting, routing, domain) as a separate, post-build dependency. This allows full end-to-end validation of the content generation and assembly logic without needing access to cloud services. Additionally, when testing specific copy variants, explicitly constrain the generation engine to vary only the targeted elements (e.g., headlines) while preserving the overall structure, overriding any default diversification behaviors.

original.title: AppSync allow.authenticated() cannot serve public routes; use direct server-side DynamoDB
original.content: Amplify Data with allow.authenticated() (Cognito userPool) FAILS auth on unauthenticated PUBLIC routes (contact form -> Lead, /api/track beacon -> AnalyticsEvent). A persistence layer written BY public API routes must use IAM/public auth, not userPool. Clean fix: direct server-side DynamoDB (DynamoDBDocumentClient via @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb) using either the SSR compute role (most secure) or fromCognitoIdentityPool creds (Ayoai AnalyticsService pattern). Discovered g-010-20 2026-05-26 when user redirected the g-010-16 AppSync layer to the Ayoai direct-DynamoDB pattern; committed amplify_outputs.json was also a placeholder stub (no real data.url) so the AppSync layer was a production no-op anyway.
original.when_to_use: designing a persistence/data layer written by public (unauthenticated) Next.js routes on Amplify

generalized.context: When designing a persistence layer for public (unauthenticated) API routes on a serverless platform that relies on Cognito for user authentication.
approach: Identify that standard authenticated data access methods (e.g., Cognito User Pool) will fail for unauthenticated public requests.
Replace the authenticated persistence layer with a direct server-side database client (e.g., DynamoDB Document Client) invoked via the SSR compute role or Cognito Identity Pool credentials.
Ensure the data access logic bypasses the user-specific authentication flow entirely for these public endpoints.
generalized.outcome: Public routes successfully write to the database without triggering authentication failures; avoided production no-ops caused by placeholder configuration files.
generalized.lesson: When a persistence layer is required by public (unauthenticated) routes on a platform using Cognito for auth, standard authenticated access methods will fail. You must use a direct server-side database client (e.g., DynamoDB Document Client) configured with either the SSR compute role or Cognito Identity Pool credentials. This bypasses the user-specific auth flow required for private routes, ensuring public endpoints can function correctly.

original.title: Validate the access model against the full consumer surface before committing to an architecture
original.content: Replay of the asp-010 persistence arc (g-010-16 -> g-010-20 -> g-010-22) surfaced an avoidable build-then-rebuild churn of ~3 goals. g-010-16 built the persistence layer on Amplify Data/AppSync with allow.authenticated() (Cognito userPool). g-010-20 discovered AT DEPLOY that the PUBLIC routes (contact-form->Lead, /api/track->AnalyticsEvent) cannot authenticate against a userPool (rb-79). g-010-22 then rewrote the entire layer to direct server-side DynamoDB SDK. Root cause: the access/auth model was chosen BEFORE enumerating that unauthenticated (public) writers shared the same persistence surface as authenticated ones. Lesson: before selecting a persistence/auth/foundational architecture, enumerate EVERY consumer type (public, authenticated, server-side/cron) and verify the chosen access-control model serves all of them. A five-minute surface enumeration prevents a full build-then-rebuild cycle. Instance fact lives in rb-79; this is the generalizable design discipline. Transfers to consultancy solution design: validate a proposed architecture against the FULL stakeholder/requirement surface before committing the design.
original.when_to_use: Before selecting a persistence, auth, or other foundational architecture that will serve more than one consumer type (public + authenticated + server-side). Also when designing a client solution architecture against a requirements/stakeholder surface.

generalized.context: When designing a persistence or authentication architecture that must serve multiple consumer types simultaneously (e.g., public web users, authenticated users, and server-side cron jobs),
approach: Enumerate every distinct consumer type that will write to or read from the system before selecting an access-control model
Verify that the chosen model (e.g., Cognito user pools, API keys, or direct SDK access) can technically support all enumerated consumer types
Identify conflicts where public or server-side consumers cannot authenticate against a user-centric model intended for human users
generalized.outcome: Avoided a full build-then-rebuild cycle caused by discovering incompatible access requirements after the persistence layer was already implemented
generalized.lesson: Before committing to a foundational architecture (persistence, auth, or data layer), explicitly enumerate every consumer type (public, authenticated, server-side) and verify the chosen access-control model serves all of them. Selecting a model based on only one consumer type (e.g., authenticated users) often leads to costly rewrites when unauthenticated or automated consumers are added later.

original.title: Match the sourcing instrument to the time horizon; a multi-signal root-cause-framed negative scout is a success
original.content: SAM.gov Opportunities shows only POSTED/current solicitations; forecast tools (GSA Forecast of Contracting Opportunities, VA OSDBU forecast, Acquisition Gateway) show PLANNED/forward pipeline before it posts. A 'what is up for renewal LATER' question is a forward-horizon question SAM.gov structurally cannot answer - use the forecast tools for that horizon. Separately: a scouting goal that returns 'nothing new' is a SUCCESS, not a failure, when backed by multi-signal search (multiple NAICS x set-aside postures, Sources-Sought + all-types) AND a root-cause frame explaining the thin result (e.g. rb-004: DOGE killed 650+ VA contracts Q4-2025, restoration awards land 2026-2027). Bare 'nothing found' from one search is under-reporting; the multi-signal scan + frame is the real answer.
original.when_to_use: sourcing/scouting goals, especially forward-pipeline questions (later, renewal, upcoming) where SAM.gov posted-only data is insufficient and forecast tools are the right instrument

generalized.context: When conducting sourcing or scouting for opportunities that are in the forward pipeline (planned, upcoming, or renewal) rather than currently posted, standard procurement portals that only display active solicitations are structurally insufficient.
approach: Identify the time horizon of the inquiry: if the goal is 'what is up for renewal later' or 'upcoming pipeline', standard portals cannot answer this.
Switch to specialized forecast tools or forward-pipeline instruments designed to show planned opportunities before they are officially posted.
Frame the search using a multi-signal approach (combining multiple industry codes, set-aside postures, and source types) rather than a single query.

Interpret a 'nothing new' result as a successful negative scout when backed by the multi-signal scan and a root-cause explanation for the thin results (e.g., budget cuts, policy changes, or delayed restoration).
generalized.outcome: Avoided false negatives by using the correct instrument for the time horizon and correctly identified a lack of opportunities as a valid, data-backed success state rather than a search failure.
generalized.lesson: When answering forward-horizon questions (planned or renewal opportunities), do not rely on standard procurement portals that only show posted solicitations; use forecast tools instead. Furthermore, a 'nothing found' result is a success, not a failure, if it is derived from a multi-signal search strategy combined with a root-cause frame explaining the absence of data (e.g., budget cuts or policy shifts). Relying on a single search yielding 'nothing' constitutes under-reporting.

original.title: World companion scripts need $WORLD_DIR resolution when run directly from Bash
original.content: When invoking a world/ companion script directly from a Bash tool call (e.g. world/scripts/email-send.sh from notify-user Step 3, or agent-inbox-*.sh / sam-gov-search.sh), the literal 'world/scripts/X.sh' path fails rc=127 (No such file or directory) because world/ is an external user-supplied path (WORLD_PATH = <USER_HOME>/OneDrive/Zak-Data-Solutions/Agents-World), NOT a PROJECT_ROOT subdir. Resolve it: source core/scripts/_paths.sh then bash "$WORLD_DIR/scripts/X.sh". The notify-user SKILL.md Step 3 shows the unresolved literal form (ported from Ayoai-Mind where world/ may have been a local dir) - a recurrence trap. Confirmed 2026-05-27: literal form rc=127; resolved $WORLD_DIR form sent the email OK (SES MessageId returned).
original.when_to_use: Before running any world/ companion script directly from a Bash tool call; or when a 'world/scripts/...: No such file or directory' rc=127 error appears. Future fix candidate: correct the notify-user SKILL.md Step 3 examples to the resolved form.

generalized.context: When invoking a companion script directly from a Bash tool call where the script resides in a user-supplied external directory (e.g., ~/Documents/Projects/World/scripts/) rather than the project root.
approach: Identify that the literal relative path (e.g., 'world/scripts/X.sh') fails with rc=127 because the directory is not a fixed project subdirectory.
Source the project's path resolution script (e.g., 'source core/scripts/_paths.sh') to load the dynamic environment variable pointing to the external directory.
Execute the script using the resolved variable (e.g., 'bash "$WORLD_DIR/scripts/X.sh"') instead of the literal path.
generalized.outcome: The script executed successfully (rc=0) and performed its intended action (e.g., sending an email via SES), whereas the literal path invocation returned 'No such file or directory'.
generalized.lesson: When running companion scripts from an external user-supplied directory via Bash, never use a literal relative path like 'world/scripts/X.sh'. Instead, source the project's path resolution script to load the dynamic directory variable (e.g., $WORLD_DIR) and invoke the script using that variable. This prevents 'No such file or directory' errors caused by the external directory not being a fixed subdirectory of the project root.

original.title: Unauthenticated Cognito identity-pool role is publicly assumable - never grant it DynamoDB access to sensitive data
original.content: A web app's unauthenticated Cognito identity-pool role is assumable by anyone who reads the public client bundle (the identity pool ID ships in amplify_outputs.json / page source). Any IAM grant on that role is effectively public. In g-010-28 the ZDS site's unauth role had a DynamoDB PutItem/Query grant on the outreach table (lead PII + prospect list), readable by anyone who pulled the public key. Fix pattern: (1) route all DynamoDB access through the SSR server compute role (Zak_first_test_role), assumed in authenticated server context via buildCredentials() returning undefined -> ambient AWS provider chain; (2) give the unauth role ZERO DynamoDB policies; (3) split sensitive data (outreach=zds-reachout) from low-sensitivity data (analytics=zds-analytics, server-side via /api/track) into separate tables so even server-side grants stay scoped. Verified closed by fresh IAM probe: live app appId d1v8dip61c1yp0 (Zak-Data-Solutions-Web-App), unauth role amplify-d1v8dip61c1yp0-ma-amplifyAuthunauthenticate-9yTl9ImT3ViB has empty inline AND attached policy lists. Identify which unauth role belongs to which app via the amplify-<appId>- role-name prefix.
original.when_to_use: When designing or reviewing data persistence for an Amplify/Cognito web app, choosing which IAM role writes to DynamoDB, or auditing identity-pool roles for public exposure of sensitive data.
original.failure_lesson: An unauthenticated identity-pool DynamoDB grant exposed lead PII + the prospect list publicly until g-010-28 closed it; the public identity-pool ID makes the unauth role's grants reachable by anyone.
original.description: Route web-app DynamoDB writes through the SSR server compute role, not the publicly-assumable unauthenticated Cognito identity-pool role; split sensitive from low-sensitivity data into separate tables.

generalized.context: When designing or reviewing data persistence for a web application using an unauthenticated identity provider, or auditing identity-pool roles for public exposure of sensitive data.
approach: Recognize that the identity pool ID is embedded in the public client bundle (e.g., build output files or page source), making the unauthenticated role assumable by anyone.
Ensure the unauthenticated role has ZERO direct IAM policies granting access to data stores (e.g., DynamoDB, S3).
Route all data access through the server-side compute role (assumed in an authenticated server context) rather than the client-side unauthenticated role.
Split sensitive data (e.g., user PII, lead lists) from low-sensitivity data (e.g., analytics, server-side tracking) into separate tables to minimize blast radius.
Verify the fix by probing the live application's unauthenticated role to confirm it has no attached or inline policies.
generalized.outcome: The unauthenticated role was confirmed to have empty inline and attached policy lists, preventing public access to sensitive data.
generalized.lesson: An unauthenticated identity-pool role is effectively public because its ID is exposed in the client bundle; any IAM grant on that role is immediately accessible to attackers. Never grant this role direct access to sensitive data stores. Instead, route all data operations through the server-side compute role (assumed in an authenticated context) and segregate sensitive data into dedicated tables to ensure even server-side grants remain scoped correctly.

original.title: Next.js 'use server' modules export only server actions -- extract auth-gated flows to a plain lib module for a unit-testable seam
original.content: g-010-29 needed a test proving an unauthenticated click cannot dispatch outreach. The server action (app/admin/outreach/actions.ts approveAndSend) lives in a Next.js 'use server' module, where EVERY export must be an async server action -- you cannot export a plain testable helper, and the auth check (requireAdminEmail) wraps runWithAmplifyServerContext + fetchAuthSession, which is brittle to mock. Fix: extract the flow approveAndDispatch(adminEmail, sendId, note) into a plain lib module (lib/outreach-dispatch.ts). The server action becomes a thin wrapper: resolve auth via requireAdminEmail, then call the flow. Because the flow takes adminEmail as a PARAMETER (null/empty = unauthenticated), the test passes null and asserts it throws AND the SES transport mock is never called -- no Amplify server context to mock. Two real call sites (the production server action + the test) justify the extraction, so it is not a single-use abstraction (implementation-discipline rule 3). Second reusable lesson: in a dispatch/send gate, run the fail-closed authorization assert (assertDispatchAllowed) BEFORE resolving the recipient or making the network call, so an unapproved send can never reach the transport even on a later code edit. The client-side confirmation widget is UX friction against a mis-click, NOT a security gate -- security is the server-side gate chain (requireAdminEmail -> approveAndDispatch null-refusal -> assertDispatchAllowed), tested independently of the UI.
original.when_to_use: When a Next.js server action needs unit-testable business logic, or when building any fail-closed dispatch/send gate where you must prove an unauthorized caller cannot trigger the side effect.
original.failure_lesson: Leaving auth-gated logic inside a 'use server' module makes the 'unauth cannot act' invariant effectively untestable (Amplify server context mock is brittle); the invariant then rests on inspection alone.
original.description: To unit-test 'an unauthenticated caller cannot send', extract the auth-gated business logic out of the 'use server' module into a plain lib module that takes the auth identity as a parameter; order fail-closed gates so the authorization assert runs before any recipient resolution or network call.

generalized.context: When a server-side action requires unit testing to prove that unauthenticated callers cannot trigger side effects, and the auth logic relies on brittle cloud context mocks.
approach: Extract the core business flow (e.g., dispatch/send logic) into a plain library module that accepts authentication state as a parameter.
Refactor the server action to become a thin wrapper that resolves auth via the parameter and delegates to the library function.
Implement a fail-closed authorization assertion BEFORE resolving recipients or making network calls.
Verify the test passes by injecting null/empty auth parameters, causing the flow to throw without invoking the transport layer.
generalized.outcome: The 'unauthorized cannot act' invariant became unit-testable without mocking brittle cloud contexts; the SES transport mock was never called during the failure case.
generalized.lesson: When a server-side action needs to prove that unauthenticated callers cannot trigger side effects, do not keep auth-gated logic inside the action module. Instead, extract the flow into a plain library module that accepts auth state as a parameter. This allows tests to pass null/empty auth, triggering a fail-closed assertion before any network calls are made. This avoids brittle mocks of cloud contexts and ensures the security gate is tested independently of the UI.

original.title: Amplify SSR (WEB_COMPUTE) SES send needs a compute role; set computeRoleArn via boto3 not aws-cli 2.15.7
original.content: Symptom: website approve-to-send (and any server-side SES SendEmail) failed in production. Root cause: Amplify Hosting WEB_COMPUTE (Next.js SSR) app d1v8dip61c1yp0 had computeRoleArn=None. lib/email.ts builds new SESClient({region}) with NO explicit credentials, so the AWS SDK default credential chain resolves to the SSR compute role; with no role attached, there are no creds and every send throws. Fix: (1) create IAM role amplify-d1v8dip61c1yp0-ssr-compute, trust principal amplify.amazonaws.com (sts:AssumeRole), inline policy ses:SendEmail+ses:SendRawEmail scoped to arn:aws:ses:us-east-2:891377285145:identity/zacharykysar.com; (2) set it as the app compute role; (3) redeploy so the SSR runtime binds it. GOTCHA: aws-cli 2.15.7 has no --compute-role-arn on amplify update-app (only --iam-service-role-arn, which is the BUILD role, a different thing). Use boto3: botocore 1.42.66 supports update_app(appId, computeRoleArn). iamServiceRoleArn (Zak_first_test_role) is the build role and is NOT the compute role; independent.
original.when_to_use: Diagnosing server-side AWS-SDK failures on Amplify SSR, or setting an Amplify compute role from this machine

generalized.context: When diagnosing server-side AWS SDK failures in a serverless compute environment (e.g., Next.js SSR) where SES SendEmail operations fail due to missing credentials.
approach: Verify that the compute role attached to the serverless function includes the necessary SES permissions (SendEmail, SendRawEmail).
Ensure the role's trust policy allows the compute service (e.g., amplify.amazonaws.com) to assume it.
Use the SDK client library (boto3) to update the application's compute role, as the CLI tool version 2.15.7 lacks the --compute-role-arn flag.
Distinguish between the build service role (iamServiceRoleArn) and the runtime compute role, as they are independent and serve different purposes.
generalized.outcome: The serverless function successfully assumed the compute role, resolved the missing credentials error, and SES email sends succeeded.
generalized.lesson: When server-side AWS SDK calls fail with missing credentials in a serverless environment, the root cause is often a missing or misconfigured compute role. Crucially, if using AWS CLI version 2.15.7, you cannot set the compute role via the --compute-role-arn flag; this flag does not exist. Instead, you must use the SDK client library (boto3) to update the compute role. Always distinguish the build service role (iamServiceRoleArn) from the runtime compute role, as they are independent entities.

original.title: Amplify Gen2 SSR runtime identity != app service role; computeRoleArn=None means no DynamoDB grant at runtime
original.content: Amplify Gen2 WEB_COMPUTE (Next.js SSR) apps have TWO IAM identities: iamServiceRoleArn (build/deploy) and computeRoleArn (the SSR RUNTIME). They are NOT the same. If computeRoleArn is None/empty, the SSR runtime has no grants to custom (non-Amplify-managed) DynamoDB tables EVEN IF the service role has AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess. Symptom: prod writes silently fail (persistence.ts is best-effort, catch->return false) while writes via root creds / local CLI succeed, and env vars + service-role perms all look correct. Diagnostic: aws amplify get-app --app-id <id> -> check computeRoleArn. Fix: attach a compute role with dynamodb perms on the custom tables, then redeploy. Verified 2026-05-29 (g-012-01): zds-reachout had 0 rows from prod despite OUTREACH_TABLE_NAME set on main branch AND Zak_first_test_role having DynamoDBFullAccess; computeRoleArn was None.
original.when_to_use: prod DynamoDB writes silently fail but local/root writes work; Amplify SSR app not persisting despite env vars set; service role has perms but runtime cannot write; go-to-market

generalized.context: When deploying a serverless SSR application (e.g., Next.js) where the build/deployment role differs from the runtime execution role, and the application attempts to write to custom-managed database tables.
approach: Identify that the platform creates two distinct IAM identities: one for the build/deployment pipeline and a separate one for the runtime execution.
Verify that the runtime execution role (often exposed as a specific attribute in the app configuration) is explicitly attached to the custom database tables.
Check if the runtime role is missing or empty, which causes the runtime to lack permissions even if the build/deployment role has full access.
Attach a dedicated compute role with the necessary database permissions to the application and redeploy.
generalized.outcome: Resolved silent production write failures where local/root credentials worked but the live runtime could not persist data to custom tables.
generalized.lesson: In serverless SSR architectures, the build/deployment IAM role and the runtime execution role are distinct entities. If the runtime role is missing or empty, the application cannot access custom-managed resources (like non-platform database tables) even if the build role has full permissions. This results in silent write failures in production while local or root-credential operations succeed. Always ensure the specific runtime execution role is explicitly granted access to custom resources.

original.title: The a16z DoW startup playbook, reduced to SDVOSB sole-prop scale
original.content: user re-fed the a16z 'DoW Contracting for Startups 101' primer on 2026-05-29 and asked to engrave it into plans (-> asp-014). The article is a VC/product-company playbook: SBIR -> STRATFI/TACFI -> Other Transactions -> program-of-record, illustrated at Anduril/Palantir scale. Applied through the rb-001 scale lens (formal $1M+ IDIQs/BPAs structurally gate out a one-person SDVOSB via bonding, past-performance, and team-size requirements), the ACTIONABLE reduction for Zak-Data-Solutions is three sole-prop-sized lanes: (1) SBIR Phase I / D2P2 ($50K-$225K) is the one article pathway sized for a sole prop -- non-dilutive, feasibility/prototype scope, deliverable solo; (2) SDVOSB sole-source services (FAR 19.1406, $5M services cap) remains the primary revenue lane per rb-001..rb-004; (3) DoW-entry advisory + CMMC/FedRAMP readiness offerings monetize the knowledge as Track-1 services without needing scale. The cheap, concrete GATE that unblocks the SBIR lane is CMMC L1 self-assessment (15 FAR 52.204-21 practices, near-zero cost) + SBIR.gov/DSIP registration. Do NOT chase programs-of-record, prime teaming for scale, or $1M+ IDIQs -- that is the guard-002 scale trap. The Pentagon org map (DIU/CDAO/USW(R&E)/service innovation hubs/OSDBU + CCMD demand signals) is most useful as an OUTREACH target list (-> asp-010), not a procurement ladder to climb. Full knowledge: intelligence/government-contracting-heritage/dow-contracting-startups-101 + 274-line archive.
original.when_to_use: When evaluating any DoW/defense opportunity or routing a prospect through the DoW playbook -- decide which of the three sole-prop-sized lanes applies (SBIR Phase I/D2P2, SDVOSB sole-source services, or DoW-entry advisory offering) and reject venture-scale pathways.

generalized.context: When evaluating any government or defense contracting opportunity for a sole proprietorship or small team, route the prospect through a scaled-down version of the venture-scale playbook.
approach: Identify three viable lanes sized for a single operator: (1) Phase I/Proof-of-Concept grants ($50K-$225K) for non-dilutive feasibility work, (2) Sole-source service contracts (up to $5M) leveraging small-business set-asides, and (3) Advisory/Readiness services (e.g., compliance certification prep) that monetize existing knowledge.
Execute the low-cost gate required to unlock the grant lane (e.g., a self-assessment for compliance standards) and register on the official grant portal.

Explicitly reject venture-scale pathways such as prime teaming for large IDIQs, programs-of-record, or multi-million dollar BPAs, as these are structurally gated out by bonding, past-performance, and team-size requirements.
Use the client organization's internal org map (innovation hubs, R&E divisions) as a target list for direct outreach rather than attempting to climb a complex procurement ladder.
generalized.outcome: Avoided the 'scale trap' of pursuing unattainable large contracts and focused resources on three executable revenue streams appropriate for a sole proprietor.
generalized.lesson: When a sole proprietor or small team evaluates government contracting opportunities, apply a 'scale lens' to filter out venture-scale pathways (large IDIQs, prime teaming) that are structurally gated by bonding and team-size requirements. Instead, focus on three specific lanes: (1) Phase I/Proof-of-Concept grants for non-dilutive feasibility, (2) Sole-source service contracts under the small-business cap, and (3) Advisory services that monetize existing expertise. The critical gate to unlock the grant lane is often a low-cost compliance self-assessment and portal registration. Treat the client's internal org map as a direct outreach target list rather than a procurement ladder to climb.

original.title: Cognito group membership overrides the default authenticated Identity-Pool role - fence per-user data policies onto the group role too
original.content: Admin login to lodestar.wiki threw AccessDeniedException on dynamodb:Query for amplifyAuthadminGroupRole even though the default authenticated role had the per-user partition policy. Root cause: adding a Cognito user to a group switches their Identity-Pool credentials to the GROUP role (group precedence), so IAM grants attached only to backend.auth.resources.authenticatedUserIamRole never apply to group members. Fix: attach the fenced policy (dynamodb LeadingKeys = cognito sub) to BOTH backend.auth.resources.authenticatedUserIamRole AND every backend.auth.resources.groups[<name>].role. Distinct from rb-88 (unauthenticated role is publicly assumable) - this is the authenticated-to-group override path.
original.when_to_use: Any Amplify/Cognito app that adds users to Identity-Pool groups (admin, etc.) AND fences DynamoDB or other IAM access per-user. Grant on the authenticated role alone is not enough - mirror onto each group role.

generalized.context: When an application uses an Identity Provider (like Cognito) to manage user groups and fences IAM access (e.g., DynamoDB policies) based on the authenticated user's partition key, adding a user to a group causes their credentials to assume the GROUP role instead of the default authenticated user role.
approach: Identify that group membership triggers a role switch from the default authenticated role to the specific group role.
Verify that IAM grants attached only to the default authenticated role do not automatically apply to group members.
Attach the required resource-based policies (e.g., DynamoDB policies with user-specific partition keys) to BOTH the default authenticated role AND every specific group role.
generalized.outcome: Resolved AccessDeniedException errors when group members attempted to access resources protected by user-specific IAM policies.
generalized.lesson: When an Identity Provider supports user groups, adding a user to a group switches their assumed role from the default authenticated role to the group role. Consequently, IAM grants attached only to the default authenticated role will not apply to group members. To secure resources with user-specific policies (e.g., partition keys), you must explicitly attach those policies to both the default authenticated role AND every individual group role.

original.title: Cognito DEVELOPER email SourceArn must be the verified DOMAIN identity ARN, not the email-address ARN
original.content: Deploy rolled back with Email address is not verified (.../identity/no-reply@lodestar.wiki). Amplify Gen2 native senders.email (auth/resource.ts) derives the SES SourceArn from the from EMAIL ADDRESS, producing an email-address identity ARN that is not verified - only the lodestar.wiki DOMAIN identity is. Fix: drop senders.email and set the Cognito email config via a CDK escape hatch in backend.ts: cfnUserPool.emailConfiguration = { emailSendingAccount: DEVELOPER, sourceArn: arn:aws:ses:<region>:<acct>:identity/<DOMAIN>, from: ... , replyToEmailAddress: ... }. The domain identity covers every address @ that domain.
original.when_to_use: Switching Cognito from default (verificationemail.com, spam-prone) to SES DEVELOPER mode for a domain you own. Point SourceArn at the domain identity; the native senders.email API points it at the email-address identity and fails verification.

generalized.context: When configuring a user pool to send emails via SES in DEVELOPER mode for a domain you own, ensure the SourceArn points to the verified domain identity, not the individual email address identity.
approach: Identify that the native senders.email configuration derives the SourceArn from the 'from' email address, creating an unverified email-address identity ARN.
Remove the native senders.email configuration to avoid the mismatch.

Manually set the email configuration via a CDK escape hatch, explicitly setting sourceArn to the verified domain identity ARN (e.g., arn:aws:ses:<region>:<account>:identity/<domain>) instead of the email address ARN.
Ensure the 'from' address and reply-to address are set within this manual configuration.
generalized.outcome: Email delivery succeeded because the SES identity used for signing (the domain) was verified, whereas the native API attempted to use an unverified email-address identity.
generalized.lesson: When switching a user pool to SES DEVELOPER mode for a custom domain, the native senders.email API incorrectly derives the SourceArn from the sender's email address, resulting in an unverified identity error. To fix this, bypass the native API and manually configure the email settings via a CDK escape hatch. Explicitly set the sourceArn to the verified domain identity ARN (covering all addresses @ that domain) rather than the specific email address ARN.

original.title: When the Amplify SSR compute role is unreachable from the CDK tree, capture SSR/client errors via a tagged log line + CloudWatch subscription filter -> Lambda -> SES
original.content: Wanted error-to-email alerting on lodestar.wiki like the zak-data-solutions setup. The clean approach (grant the SSR runtime role ses:SendEmail and send inline) is blocked: per rb-118 the Amplify Gen2 WEB_COMPUTE compute role is a managed role NOT present in the CDK construct tree, so backend.<x>.resources cannot reach it to attach a policy. Working pattern instead: client error boundaries (global-error.tsx, error.tsx) POST {digest,message,url,...} to /api/report-error; the route console.errors a single TAGGED line (LODESTAR_CLIENT_ERROR + JSON). A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter on /aws/amplify/<appId> (pattern matches the tag + AccessDeniedException + TypeError + $fault) invokes a tiny standalone Lambda (own role) that formats and sends via SES. Decouples alerting from the un-grantable compute role.
original.when_to_use: Adding error->email (or any side-effecting alert) to an Amplify Gen2 SSR app when you cannot attach IAM to the managed compute role. Route through a tagged console.error + CloudWatch Logs subscription filter + a separate Lambda you DO control.

generalized.context: When adding error-to-email (or any side-effecting alert) to an SSR application where the compute role is a managed service role not present in the infrastructure-as-code construct tree, preventing direct IAM policy attachment.
approach: Implement client-side error boundaries to POST structured error digests to a dedicated reporting endpoint.
Configure the server route to log errors as a single tagged console.error line (e.g., 'SERVICE_TAG + JSON') instead of standard logs.
Create a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter matching the specific tag and error patterns (e.g., AccessDeniedException, TypeError) to trigger a standalone Lambda.
Ensure the standalone Lambda has its own IAM role with permissions to send emails via SES, decoupling alerting from the un-grantable compute role.
generalized.outcome: Successfully implemented error-to-email alerting without requiring direct IAM access to the managed compute role.
generalized.lesson: When you cannot attach IAM policies to a managed compute role (e.g., in serverless environments where the role is external to your CDK tree), decouple side-effecting alerts from the application runtime. Instead, have the client POST error digests to a server endpoint that logs them with a unique tag. Use a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to match that tag and invoke a standalone Lambda with its own IAM role to handle the alerting. This bypasses the permission restriction on the managed role while maintaining observability.

original.title: SDVOSB opportunity sourcing: 541519 is the richest NAICS vein by count but fit-filtering is mandatory
original.content: When sourcing federal opportunities for Zak-Data-Solutions (SDVOSB data-engineering / applied-AI), query capability NAICS 541511 / 541512 / 541519 filtered to SDVOSBC + VSA set-asides. NAICS 541519 (Other Computer Related Services) under SDVOSBC is by far the richest vein by COUNT (20 of 27 eligible notices in the 2026-05-31 first-post-activation sweep), but most are VA software-license / maintenance / equipment buys with low services fit. Count is not opportunity -- fit-filter every result by fetching the full description before recommending pursuit. The 2 genuinely high-fit notices in the first sweep were both applied-AI / data-engineering SERVICES procurements, not the license/maintenance bulk.
original.when_to_use: running a SAM.gov opportunity sweep for Zak-Data-Solutions; triaging which NAICS/set-aside vein to prioritize; opportunity-sourcing
original.failure_lesson: Treating high NAICS notice count as high opportunity density. The 541519 SDVOSBC count (20) is inflated by low-fit VA license/maintenance buys; without fit-filtering, the richest-count vein masquerades as the richest-opportunity vein and wastes evaluation effort.

generalized.context: When sourcing opportunities for a specialized vendor (e.g., data-engineering or applied-AI) within a federal contracting system, query capability NAICS codes filtered to the specific veteran-owned set-aside.
approach: Identify that the highest-count NAICS code in the set-aside (e.g., Other Computer Related Services) often contains a bulk of low-fit procurements like software licenses, maintenance, or equipment.
Do not treat high notice count as high opportunity density; recognize that volume is inflated by non-service-based buys.
Mandatory fit-filter every result by fetching the full description before recommending pursuit to ensure alignment with core service capabilities.
generalized.outcome: Avoided wasting evaluation effort on low-fit license/maintenance buys; identified the genuinely high-fit opportunities as specific applied-AI/data-engineering services rather than the bulk volume.
generalized.lesson: When sourcing for a specialized vendor within a set-aside, the NAICS code with the highest notice count is often inflated by low-fit procurements (licenses, maintenance, equipment) that do not match your core service capabilities. Do not prioritize based on count alone; always fetch and filter the full description to distinguish between high-volume noise and genuine high-fit service opportunities.

original.title: Filter SAM searches by --ptype k/o to isolate biddable solicitations (Evaluate-gate at query layer)
original.content: SAM v2 search --ptype: o=Solicitation and k=Combined Synopsis/Solicitation are BIDDABLE instruments; r=Sources Sought and s=Special Notice/sole-source-intent are NOT biddable. The g-007-12 sweep inferred biddability from titles and mislabeled a sole-source Special Notice as PURSUE (rb-145). Filtering --ptype k/o at the QUERY layer eliminates that error class before any record reaches evaluation. Combine with --ncode (NAICS) and an open-only filter (responseDeadLine >= today) for a multi-NAICS biddable sweep in ~7-14 calls returning only actionable candidates. Empirical 2026-05-31: SDVOSBC biddable across 541519/541512/541511/518210 yielded ~0 capability-fit open bids (only off-domain: a Hologic AI license resale and medical coding services), confirming the solo-SDVOSB win path is VA sole-source + radar-building (rb-001), not open competition.

generalized.context: When sourcing opportunities via a government procurement portal where instrument types vary (e.g., Solicitations vs. Sources Sought) and biddability is not explicitly labeled in titles.
approach: Filter the search query at the query layer using the specific instrument type code for biddable solicitations (e.g., k/o for Combined Synopsis/Solicitation).
Explicitly exclude non-biddable instrument types (e.g., Sources Sought, Special Notices) to prevent misclassification errors.
Combine this filter with NAICS code constraints and an open-status filter (response deadline >= today) to narrow results to actionable candidates.
generalized.outcome: Eliminated the error class of mislabeling sole-source notices as pursuable opportunities before any record reached the evaluation stage, reducing API calls to only relevant candidates.
generalized.lesson: When sourcing opportunities via a procurement portal, filter by instrument type at the query layer to isolate biddable solicitations. Do not rely on title analysis or post-retrieval evaluation to determine biddability, as non-biddable instruments (like Sources Sought) are often mislabeled in titles. This pre-filtering step prevents false positives and ensures only actionable open bids enter the evaluation pipeline.

original.title: zds-reachout is single-table-design: verify a SPECIFIC pk-partition, not table ItemCount, before concluding a write-path works/fails
original.content: The web-app DynamoDB tables are single-table-design with pk-typed record classes. zds-reachout pk taxonomy: AgentActivity, Lead, OutreachTouch, Prospect, OutreachSend, SendSignOff, OutreachDispatch, Suppression, Contract, ContractTransition. zds-analytics: AnalyticsEvent. LESSON (rb-245 applied to DynamoDB, 2026-05-31, g-010-41): ItemCount=25 / scan COUNT=25 looked like outreach persistence works, but the 25 were ALL AgentActivity feed records (pk=AgentActivity, written by world/scripts/agent-activity-log.sh) -- a false positive. Querying the specific partitions (aws dynamodb query --key-condition-expression pk=:pk --select COUNT) revealed OutreachSend=5, SendSignOff=7, OutreachDispatch=7 -- THAT is the proof the sign-off/dispatch path persists. Always query the specific pk before concluding a particular write-path works or no-ops.

generalized.context: When debugging write-path failures in a single-table-design database where records share a common partition key prefix but differ by record type.
approach: Check the global table ItemCount to see if any new records were written
Identify that the total count matches records from a different, unrelated record type (e.g., system logs or feed data) sharing the same partition key
Execute a query specifically targeting the intended record type's partition key (e.g., pk=OutreachSend) rather than scanning the whole table
Verify the count of the specific record type to confirm persistence
generalized.outcome: Avoided a false positive conclusion that the write-path failed; confirmed the path works by isolating the specific record type count from unrelated data sharing the same partition key.
generalized.lesson: In single-table-design databases, a global ItemCount or scan count is insufficient to verify a specific write-path because unrelated record types often share the same partition key. Always query the specific partition key for the intended record type to distinguish valid writes from noise generated by other entities.

original.title: A frontend-only Amplify app consuming another product Cognito pool inherits that pool email sender
original.content: Vinheim was wired to share Lodestar deployed Cognito pool (us-east-2_hn0tffYPP) for one-account-across-products. Consequence: Cognito signup/verification emails for vinheim.com signups are sent as the pool EmailConfiguration From = Lodestar <no-reply@lodestar.wiki>, ReplyTo support@lodestar.wiki -- not a Vinheim address. Shared pool = one sender identity. Per-product sender branding requires either genericizing the shared pool From, or a Cognito custom-message Lambda trigger, or separate pools (which breaks shared accounts).
original.when_to_use: Sharing a Cognito user pool across products/domains for unified sign-in; the verification-email sender is shared and will brand as the pool owner.

generalized.context: When a frontend application shares a Cognito user pool with another product to enable unified sign-in across domains.
approach: Recognize that the shared user pool's EmailConfiguration defines a single 'From' address and 'Reply-To' address for all verification emails.
Identify that signups from the secondary product will inherit the primary product's sender branding (e.g., 'no-reply@lodestar.wiki') instead of the secondary product's own domain.
Select a mitigation strategy: either genericize the shared pool's sender address, implement a Cognito custom-message Lambda trigger to override the email template, or accept the branding limitation.
generalized.outcome: Verified that verification emails for the secondary product are sent from the primary product's identity, confirming the shared pool constraint.
generalized.lesson: When sharing a Cognito user pool across multiple products for unified authentication, remember that the pool's EmailConfiguration enforces a single sender identity for all verification emails. Signups from any product in the pool will inherit the pool owner's 'From' and 'Reply-To' addresses. To maintain distinct branding per product without creating separate pools (which breaks shared accounts), you must either genericize the shared pool's sender address or implement a Cognito custom-message Lambda trigger to dynamically override the email template.

original.title: Windows Python open() cannot resolve MSYS /c/ paths from _paths.sh AGENT_DIR -- read via stdin
original.content: deploy-status.sh built CONFIG="${AGENT_DIR}/web-app-config.yaml" then read it with py -3 -c "yaml.safe_load(open(r'$CONFIG'))". It silently returned empty ('app_id not set') for an EXISTING, correct config. Root cause (probed, not assumed): _paths.sh yields AGENT_DIR in MSYS form (/c/<WORKSPACE>/...), and Windows Python open() raises FileNotFoundError on a /c/... path even though bash [ -f ] sees the file. py -3 HAS PyYAML (6.0.3) so the import was never the problem; the path format was. The 2>/dev/null swallowed the FileNotFoundError, masking the bug. Sneaky asymmetry: WORLD_DIR/META_DIR come from local-paths.conf in Windows form (C:/Users/...) so Python open() works on them; AGENT_DIR is computed from PROJECT_ROOT (bash pwd, MSYS /c/) so it does NOT. FIX: pipe the file via stdin (cat "$CONFIG" | py -3 -c 'import yaml,sys; yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin)') so bash resolves /c/ and Python reads stdin with zero path-format dependency.
original.when_to_use: Authoring or reviewing any .sh that sources _paths.sh and passes an AGENT_DIR-derived (or PROJECT_ROOT-derived) path to a Windows Python open()/file API via -c. Prefer reading contents over stdin, or convert with cygpath -w, or use the canonical mind-read.sh reader. Also never let 2>/dev/null mask a file read whose emptiness changes control flow.

generalized.context: When a deployment script sources a path configuration file (like _paths.sh) on Windows and passes the resulting path to a Python subprocess via command-line arguments.
approach: Identify that the path configuration script outputs paths in MSYS format (e.g., /c/...) while Windows Python's open() function expects native Windows format (e.g., C:/...)
Recognize that standard file existence checks (like bash [ -f ]) may pass on MSYS paths even if Python cannot resolve them, leading to silent failures
Avoid suppressing errors with 2>/dev/null when the failure mode is a missing file, as this masks the root cause
Pipe the file contents to the Python process via stdin (cat file | python -c '...sys.stdin...') instead of passing the file path as an argument
generalized.outcome: Eliminated silent failures where Python returned empty results or raised FileNotFoundError for existing configuration files due to path format mismatch.
generalized.lesson: On Windows, when invoking Python from a bash script to read a file whose path is derived from a shell environment variable (potentially in MSYS format), never pass the path as a command-line argument to Python. Instead, pipe the file contents via stdin. This bypasses the OS-level path resolution differences between bash (MSYS) and the Windows Python interpreter, preventing silent failures where the file exists but cannot be opened.

original.title: N4 own-cloud migration is OBSERVED COMPLETE (2026-06-06), not a pending cutover
original.content: N4 (the ayoai-mind own-cloud rename onto operator-prefixed names) is already done as of 2026-06-06 - it is NOT a pending scary cutover that must be fired before starting the 6 ayoai agents. Firsthand evidence from live AWS us-east-2: (1) zds-own-cloud-data is live + authoritative - last write 2026-06-06 22:52, holds agent execution temp files (alpha/temp/rb1472.json @ 18:06 = an agent is actively executing against it), and shared files (reasoning-bank, guardrails) are a full day fresher than the lodestar-data copies. (2) lodestar-data is frozen at the 2026-06-06 06:31 pre-cutover state and serves as the de-facto pre-migration snapshot/rollback (3930 objects, ~211MB). (3) The 5 lodestar-* DynamoDB tables are empty (1 row total). Implication: the agents can start without firing any migration; their backend already exists. original.when_to_use: When deciding whether N4 / the lodestar-data -> zds-own-cloud-data own-cloud migration must run before starting the ayoai agents, or when asked about live AWS migration state, or before deleting lodestar-data.

generalized.context: When verifying the status of a database migration from a legacy source (e.g., lodestar-data) to a new target (e.g., zds-own-cloud-data) in a live cloud environment before starting dependent services.
approach: Inspect the target storage bucket for recent write timestamps and active execution artifacts (e.g., temp files) to confirm the migration is live and authoritative.
Compare the freshness of shared data files in the target against the source to ensure the target is current.
Query the associated database tables in the source to check for residual data or active records.
Determine if the source is frozen at a pre-migration state and serves only as a rollback snapshot.
generalized.outcome: Confirmed the migration is complete and the target is authoritative; the source is frozen and empty, meaning dependent agents can start immediately without triggering a cutover script.
generalized.lesson: Do not assume a database migration is pending or requires a manual cutover script before starting dependent services. Verify the live state by checking for recent writes and active execution artifacts in the target storage. If the target holds active data and the source is frozen/empty, the migration is complete, and services can start immediately. However, retain the frozen source data as the only rollback artifact until a stable period of operation is confirmed, as cloud object storage often lacks native rollback capabilities.

original.title: Sources Sought responses are the ideal first move for a new SDVOSB (capability statement, not priced proposal)
original.content: For a brand-new SDVOSB with no past performance, leading with Sources Sought responses beats cold RFP bids against incumbents. A Sources Sought is market research: (a) a strong response directly shapes whether the agency sets the follow-on aside for SDVOSB; (b) low risk (no binding price, no protest exposure); (c) builds the agency relationship before the RFP. First applied 2026-06-07 (g-007-13): DHS/FEMA EDAMI Data Quality Sources Sought (Notice 70FA3126I00000003, NAICS 541512, ~1.5-5M follow-on within SDVOSB sole-source threshold). Qualifying filters: no single locked incumbent (prior awards to different firms), consultative scope at sole-proprietor scale, genuine published need (FEMA 2023-2027 Data Strategy). Pair with honesty discipline: never fabricate a Notice ID/deadline/requirement; separate agent-verified from user-must-confirm.
original.when_to_use: Selecting how a new SDVOSB with thin past performance should enter a federal agency -- prefer Sources Sought over cold RFP bids
original.outcome: First bid staged via Sources Sought entry path

generalized.context: When a new vendor with no past performance enters a federal agency procurement cycle where a specific capability is needed but no formal RFP exists yet.
approach: Identify 'Sources Sought' opportunities (market research notices) rather than waiting for formal Requests for Proposals (RFPs).
Submit a strong capability statement response to influence the agency's decision to set aside the subsequent contract for small/disadvantaged businesses.
Ensure the scope matches a sole-proprietor scale and verify there is no single locked incumbent before engaging.
Maintain strict honesty discipline: never fabricate notice IDs, deadlines, or requirements; clearly separate agent-verified facts from user-confirmed details.
generalized.outcome: Successfully staged the first bid via the Sources Sought entry path, shaping the agency's future contracting strategy.
generalized.lesson: For new vendors with thin past performance, responding to 'Sources Sought' notices is superior to cold RFP bidding against incumbents. A Sources Sought response serves as market research: a strong submission directly influences whether the agency sets aside the follow-on contract for small/disadvantaged businesses. This approach carries low risk (no binding price, no protest exposure) and builds the agency relationship before the formal RFP. Success requires matching the scope to a sole-proprietor scale, ensuring no single locked incumbent exists, and maintaining strict honesty by never fabricating notice details.

original.title: Two reach-out surfaces: /admin/contracts (Contract row) tracks the pipeline; /admin/approvals (OutreachSend row) is the approve-and-act queue -- a bid needs BOTH
original.content: The zds-reachout table holds distinct record types per surface. A Contract row (pk=Contract, written by document-found-opportunity / contract-pipeline-write.sh, runner stages identified|qualifying) makes a bid appear on /admin/contracts (tracking only, NO approval). An OutreachSend row (pk=OutreachSend status=pending, written by queue-outreach-draft.sh) makes the draft appear on /admin/approvals for the principals website Approve & Send. g-010-43 gap: recon-05/06 had the Contract row but not the OutreachSend row, so they were tracked but not approvable. Every bid the principal must approve on the website needs the OutreachSend row -- writing only the Contract row is the silent half-staging.
original.when_to_use: Staging a bid/outreach for website approval; explaining the contracts-vs-approvals distinction; debugging why a bid is not approvable

generalized.context: When staging a bid or outreach item for website approval, distinguish between the tracking record and the approval queue record.
approach: Write a 'Contract' row (primary key: Contract) to the main table to track the pipeline status (identified/qualifying stages).
Write a separate 'OutreachSend' row (primary key: OutreachSend, status: pending) to the same table to create the item in the approval queue.
Ensure both rows exist before expecting the item to appear in the 'Approve & Send' interface.
generalized.outcome: Avoided a 'silent half-staging' error where items were tracked in the pipeline but invisible to the approval workflow because the approval queue record was missing.
generalized.lesson: When an item requires both pipeline tracking and user approval, it must generate two distinct record types in the staging table: a 'Contract' row for tracking lifecycle stages and an 'OutreachSend' row (with status=pending) to populate the approval queue. Relying solely on the tracking row results in the item being visible to the system but invisible to the approval interface, causing false negatives in the approval workflow.

original.title: vitest module-factory mocks do not intercept intra-module calls
original.content: When you extract a shared helper into a module and a caller lives in the SAME module (e.g. resolveProspect calls fetchProspects, both in lib/persistence.ts), a vi.mock('@/lib/persistence', importOriginal-spread) that overrides fetchProspects does NOT change what resolveProspect calls -- the intra-module reference binds to the real sibling, not the mocked export. Symptom (g-012-35): the g-012-36 dispatch test mocked fetchProspects to drive the fallback, but after dispatch was rewired through resolveProspect the test exercised the REAL fetchProspects (no-ops to [] in test env), so the fallback branch never ran and the test failed. Fix: test the composition at a seam the mock CAN reach -- either mock the consumer's imported dependency at ITS import site (mock resolveProspect where dispatch imports it), or mock the underlying dependency the real function uses (mock @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb send() so the real fetchProspects returns rows). The split: a unit test of the COMPOSED function mocks the SDK; a unit test of a CONSUMER mocks the composed function. Caught by run-full-suite-after-deep-code; a targeted-test-only close would have shipped the broken mock.
original.when_to_use: extracting a shared helper that calls a sibling export in the same module, then writing or updating vitest/jest module-factory mocks for it or its consumers

generalized.context: When extracting a shared helper function into a module and a caller resides in the SAME module, attempting to mock the helper via a module-level factory (e.g., vi.mock) fails because the intra-module reference binds to the real sibling function, not the mocked export.
approach: Identify that the caller and the helper share the same module scope, causing the caller to bypass the mock.
Shift the mock target to the consumer's import site (mock the composed function where it is imported) OR mock the underlying external dependency (e.g., the SDK send method) that the real helper uses.
Ensure the test exercises the composition at a seam the mock can actually intercept.
generalized.outcome: The test correctly exercised the fallback branch by forcing the mocked behavior, rather than accidentally running the real function which returned empty results.
generalized.lesson: When a caller and a helper function reside in the same module, a module-level mock (vi.mock) applied to the helper will not intercept calls made by the caller. The caller's internal reference binds to the real function. To test this composition, either mock the composed function at the consumer's import site or mock the underlying external dependency (like an SDK call) that the helper uses. A targeted test failing to hit the fallback logic often indicates the mock was applied at the wrong scope.

original.title: agent-inbox --body-clean strips forwarded threads; use --with-body to read a forwarded email's substance
original.content: world/scripts/agent-inbox-fetch.sh --body-clean strips quoted reply-chains AND forwarded-message blocks (it treats a forwarded thread as a quoted chain). When user forwards an email thread for review (e.g. 'Did i do this right?!' over a forwarded GSA reply to Michelle), --body-clean returns ONLY his short cover note -- the forwarded substance (the reply being reviewed, the original inbound) is gone. The manifest body_preview also truncates at 500 chars, so it only shows the start of the forward. To read the forwarded content, fetch --with-body (raw MIME) and read the text/plain part below the cover note. Detection pattern: a cover-note-only --body-clean result + a 'Fwd:' / 'Forwarded message' subject => re-fetch --with-body to recover the thread. Still run the Step 2.25 self-escalation parser on the clean cover note first (protocol order), then use --with-body for the human-review substance.

generalized.context: When an automated email ingestion script strips quoted reply chains and forwarded message blocks (treating them as noise), a forwarded thread appears as only a short cover note.
approach: Detect the pattern: a cover-note-only result from the standard fetch combined with a subject line containing 'Fwd:' or 'Forwarded message'.
Re-fetch the specific email using the raw MIME flag (e.g., --with-body) to bypass the stripping logic.
Parse the raw response to extract the text/plain content located below the cover note.
Execute the standard self-escalation parser on the clean cover note first to maintain protocol order, then process the recovered thread content for human review.
generalized.outcome: Recovered the full substance of the forwarded thread (the original inbound message or reply being reviewed) that was otherwise lost due to aggressive body cleaning.
generalized.lesson: When an email ingestion pipeline strips quoted chains and forwarded blocks, a forwarded thread will appear as only a short cover note. To recover the actual content, detect the 'Fwd:' subject pattern and re-fetch the message using the raw MIME flag. Always run the standard protocol parser on the clean cover note first, then parse the raw body for the substantive thread content.

original.title: Generalization A/B clean pair PROVES the bet: LLM generalization causally unlocks cross-domain commons retrieval (+0.19 lift delta, only variable)
original.content: Perfectly controlled pair on identical 40 stratified zds DOMAIN-goal queries, same seed/judge/retrieval/KNULL, floor met, 0 fallbacks both runs: RAW ayoai patterns null_lift -0.012 (NO-GO, engine median 0.375 vs null 0.387 -- retrieval finds nothing better than random) vs GENERALIZED ayoai patterns (local qwen3.5-9b rewrite, domain nouns to generic roles) null_lift +0.178 (GO, engine 0.5375 vs null 0.36). The transform BOTH raises what retrieval finds (+0.16 engine) AND lowers the random baseline (-0.03 null): generalized text sharpens signal-to-noise. Sub-structure: the lift is a POOL-DIVERSITY effect -- within ARM3, framework-only patterns gave +0.018 and domain-only -0.013, but the full mixed pool gave +0.178 (per-query union retrieval beats any single shelf; null stays at mixture average). Product implication: the pearl engine thesis is REBORN as curate -> LLM-generalize (local model) -> privacy-gate -> share; commons value comes from breadth of the generalized pool, not domain shelving. Caveat for synthesis: judge = qwen3.5-9b scoring topical relevance; lift measures retrieval demand, not downstream task success.
original.when_to_use: When deciding what corpus the Lodestar commons shares, when polishing the pearl engine pipeline, when interpreting any Gate B arm result, or when designing future commons-value experiments

generalized.context: When evaluating a retrieval system where a local LLM rewrites domain-specific queries into generic role terms to query a shared knowledge pool.
approach: Run a controlled A/B test comparing raw domain-specific patterns against generalized patterns (local LLM rewrite of domain nouns to generic roles).
Ensure identical conditions: same seed, judge model, retrieval parameters, and query stratification.
Measure the lift in retrieval quality (engine score) and the shift in the random baseline (null lift).
Analyze sub-structure by testing framework-only, domain-only, and mixed pools to isolate the diversity effect.
generalized.outcome: The generalized approach yielded a +0.178 null lift (engine 0.5375 vs null 0.36), whereas the raw approach yielded a -0.012 null lift (engine 0.375 vs null 0.387). The transformation increased what the retrieval found (+0.16 engine) and lowered the random baseline (-0.03 null), proving that generalized text sharpens signal-to-noise.
generalized.lesson: When building a shared knowledge commons, transforming domain-specific queries into generic role terms via a local LLM significantly improves retrieval efficacy. This works because the generalization process both raises the quality of retrieved matches and lowers the random baseline, effectively sharpening the signal-to-noise ratio. The resulting lift is a pool-diversity effect: a mixed pool of generalized patterns outperforms single-domain or framework-only shelves, proving that the value of the commons comes from the breadth of the generalized pool rather than domain-specific shelving.

original.title: Inbound-reply OutreachTouch.contractId resolves via the matched OutreachSend, not the Prospect
original.content: To write a replied OutreachTouch for an inbound prospect reply, the required contractId FK is NOT on the Prospect row (lib/prospects.ts Prospect carries token/name/company/email/valueProp/variant/track -- no contractId). The chain is OutreachSend.contractId -> OutreachTouch.contractId (lib/outreach-dispatch.ts:167-176: 'if (send.contractId) persistOutreachTouch({contractId: send.contractId,...})'). So resolution order: matched prospectToken -> most-recent OutreachSend for that token -> send.contractId; fallback to a prior OutreachTouch's contractId; if still null, ROUTE TO REVIEW -- never forge a Contract just to satisfy the FK. Live caveat (2026-06-09): 10 of 12 OutreachSend rows have contractId=NONE, so most real replies currently route-to-review until opportunities are linked to Contracts at qualify time.
original.when_to_use: writing an OutreachTouch for an inbound reply; resolving a contractId for a zds-reachout pipeline row; building a reply/engagement consumer; go-to-market

generalized.context: When creating a reply record for an inbound prospect response, the required contract ID foreign key is not stored on the prospect entity itself.
approach: Identify that the prospect entity only contains contact details and value propositions, lacking a contract ID.
Resolve the contract ID by tracing the chain: matched prospect token -> most recent outbound send record for that token -> the send record's contract ID.
If the send record lacks a contract ID, fall back to a prior reply's contract ID if available.
If no contract ID is found after these steps, route the record to manual review rather than fabricating a contract.
generalized.outcome: Prevented data integrity violations by avoiding the creation of phantom contracts to satisfy foreign key constraints.
generalized.lesson: When resolving a contract ID for an inbound reply, do not assume it exists on the prospect entity. Instead, trace the lineage through the most recent outbound send record associated with the prospect. If the send record lacks a contract ID, check for a fallback from a previous reply. If no valid contract ID is found, route the record to manual review; never forge a contract record solely to satisfy a foreign key constraint.

original.content: When logging an inbound reply (or any OutreachTouch) for a prospect whose pursuit has no Contract row, the required contractId FK has nothing to point at. Do NOT leave the engagement unlogged and do NOT force the OutreachSend status flip. original.title: Gate B 2x2 complete: generalization is free within-domain and the generalized corpus is the only universally-GO artifact
original.content: Final 2x2 (null_lift, ALL-pattern stratum, 40q, seed 6976613, 0 fallbacks): raw-within +0.193 GO / gen-within +0.192 GO / raw-cross-domain -0.012 NO-GO / gen-cross-domain +0.178 GO / raw-cross-framework +0.301 GO / gen-cross-framework +0.230 GO. Four readings: (1) generalization costs NOTHING within-domain (0.193 vs 0.192 identical); (2) it is THE unlock for cross-domain (rb-249); (3) small toll on cross-framework (0.301 to 0.230, still GO) -- raw shares meta-vocabulary there; (4) raw-within GO anchors the metric itself (curated knowledge does retrieve over random at home, so cross-world NO-GO cells measure real transfer absence). The generalized corpus is the FIRST single artifact GO in every cell it appears in -- share one broad pool. Engine medians ceiling order: within-raw 0.825 > within-gen 0.795 > cross-fw 0.75-0.80 > cross-dom-gen 0.538 > cross-dom-raw 0.375. Total campaign tonight ~20,500 local model calls, $0.
original.when_to_use: When deciding the pearl Shared-tier pipeline shape, what artifact the commons ships, or defending the curate->LLM-generalize->privacy-gate->share architecture with data

generalized.context: When evaluating the architecture for a shared knowledge repository that must serve multiple distinct domains or frameworks, specifically comparing the performance of raw curated data versus generalized data across different strata.
approach: Measure retrieval scores for raw data and generalized data within the same domain (within-domain).
Measure retrieval scores for raw data and generalized data across different domains (cross-domain).
Measure retrieval scores for raw data and generalized data across different frameworks (cross-framework).
Analyze the delta between raw and generalized scores to determine the cost of generalization in each context.
generalized.outcome: Generalization incurs zero cost within the same domain (scores are identical), acts as a critical enabler for cross-domain transfer (turning NO-GO into GO), and incurs a small, acceptable penalty for cross-framework transfer while remaining viable.
generalized.lesson: When building a shared knowledge pipeline, generalization is free within the same domain (no performance loss) and is the necessary unlock for cross-domain applicability. While generalization incurs a small performance toll when moving across different frameworks, the generalized corpus remains a universally viable artifact that outperforms raw data in cross-domain scenarios and anchors the metric by ensuring curated knowledge retrieves better than random baselines.

original.content: When adding or upgrading @aws-sdk v3 packages: do NOT copy a client package version range (~3.10xx) onto a credential-provider package such as @aws-sdk/credential-provider-cognito-identity. AWS SDK v3 clients and credential-providers version on SEPARATE tracks (clients ~3.10xx, credential-providers ~3.972.x), so a copied range yields npm ETARGET. Query npm view <pkg> version per package. Also prefer fromCognitoIdentityPool({ identityPoolId, clientConfig: { region } }) over passing a standalone CognitoIdentityClient instance: the provider builds its own version-matched internal client, which avoids the cross-package client-type TS2322 mismatch and removes the @aws-sdk/client-cognito-identity dependency.

AWS SDK v3 clients and credential-providers version on SEPARATE tracks (clients ~3.10xx, credential-providers ~3.972.x), so a copied range yields npm ETARGET. Query npm view <pkg> version per package. Also prefer fromCognitoIdentityPool({ identityPoolId, clientConfig: { region } }) over passing a standalone CognitoIdentityClient instance: the provider builds its own version-matched internal client, which avoids the cross-package client-type TS2322 mismatch and removes the @aws-sdk/client-cognito-identity dependency.

generalized.context: When adding or upgrading AWS SDK v3 packages in a web application, specifically when mixing client libraries with credential providers.
approach: Do not copy the version range from a client package (e.g., ~3.10xx) onto a credential-provider package (e.g., @aws-sdk/credential-provider-...).
Query the specific latest version for each package individually using npm view, as clients and providers follow separate version tracks.
Prefer using the high-level provider function (e.g., fromCognitoIdentityPool) with a region config over passing a standalone client instance.
Allow the provider to build its own version-matched internal client to avoid cross-package type mismatches and unnecessary dependencies.
generalized.outcome: Avoids npm ETARGET errors caused by version track mismatches and eliminates TypeScript type errors (TS2322) between client types.
generalized.lesson: In AWS SDK v3, client packages and credential-provider packages follow separate version tracks; copying a client's version range onto a provider will cause dependency resolution failures. Always query the specific version for each package individually. Furthermore, prefer using high-level provider functions (like fromCognitoIdentityPool) with a region configuration over passing a standalone client instance. This approach allows the provider to construct its own version-matched internal client, preventing cross-package type mismatches and removing the need for the specific client dependency.
